System Credential

Organization Credential

User Credential

Tool Credential

Provider Credential

The AI model receives none of these directly.

The action/provider layer uses them after authorization.

# 13.31 Encryption

All network communication containing protected information must use secure transport.

At rest, sensitive data should be protected using the capabilities of the deployment environment/database/storage infrastructure.

Particular attention must be given to:

- authentication credentials;

- refresh tokens;

- API keys;

- sensitive documents;

- research datasets;

- private notes;

- organization data;

- audit records where appropriate.

Encryption architecture must not create unnecessary application complexity when secure managed infrastructure already provides appropriate protection.

# 13.32 File Upload Security

Uploaded files are untrusted.

The system must validate:

- file size;

- content type;

- extension;

- actual file signature where applicable;

- decompression behavior;

- filename;

- storage path;

- malware/security scanning where appropriate;

- parser safety.

Never trust:

filename extension

Content-Type header

user-provided MIME type

alone.

# 13.33 Malicious Documents

Documents may contain:

- malicious payloads;

- malformed structures;

- parser exploits;

- embedded scripts;

- prompt injection;

- excessive decompression;

- resource exhaustion;

- unexpected external references.

Document extraction must therefore occur in an appropriately isolated processing boundary where practical.

# 13.34 Path Traversal

Uploaded filenames must never determine arbitrary filesystem paths.

Reject or normalize dangerous path constructs including:

../

..\ 

absolute paths

device paths

unexpected control characters

Storage identifiers should be generated by the system.

# 13.35 SSRF Protection

Any feature that fetches a URL on behalf of a user or AI must defend against SSRF.

The network layer must control:

- allowed schemes;

- DNS resolution;

- private IP ranges;

- loopback;

- link-local addresses;

- internal service addresses;

- cloud metadata endpoints;

- redirects;

- ports;

- response size;

- timeout.

The model must not be allowed unrestricted network access.

# 13.36 Web Research Security

Web content is untrusted.

The web research layer must:

- fetch through a controlled boundary;

- validate destination;

- apply network restrictions;

- isolate credentials;

- limit response size;

- sanitize/normalize content;

- preserve source URL/provenance;

- identify external instructions as content;

- prevent content from directly invoking internal actions.

# 13.37 GitHub Security Boundary

GitHub repositories and code retrieved for research are untrusted content.

GitHub data may be used for:

- project research;

- dependency verification;

- scientific software discovery;

- implementation validation;

- source inspection.

Retrieved code must not automatically execute.

Any code execution requires the controlled computation boundary defined in Parts 10 and 11.

# 13.38 Code Execution Sandbox

If GSIR executes code for scientific computation, it must execute outside the privileged application process.

The sandbox must control:

- CPU;

- memory;

- execution time;

- filesystem;

- network;

- subprocesses;

- installed packages;

- environment variables;

- secrets;

- output size.

The sandbox must not inherit production credentials.

# 13.39 Database Security

Application database access must follow least privilege.

The application should not operate using a database administrator account.

Separate privileges should be considered for:

- application runtime;

- migration execution;

- development;

- testing;

- administration.

Queries must use parameterized mechanisms provided by the persistence framework.

Never construct SQL by concatenating untrusted user/model input.

# 13.40 AI-Generated Query Security

AI-generated SQL or database expressions must never be treated as trusted simply because they were generated by an AI model.

Preferred architecture:

Natural Language

      ↓

Structured Query Intent

      ↓

Authorization

      ↓

Validated Query Builder

      ↓

Database

rather than:

User

 ↓

AI

 ↓

arbitrary SQL

 ↓

production database

# 13.41 API Security

Every public API must have:

- authentication where required;

- authorization;

- schema validation;

- input size limits;

- rate limits where appropriate;

- consistent errors;

- safe logging;

- timeout behavior;

- abuse controls.

Never expose internal exceptions, stack traces, credentials, SQL, or provider secrets through production API responses.

# 13.42 Input Validation

Validation must occur at the API boundary.

Validate:

- identifiers;

- strings;

- lengths;

- enumerated values;

- numbers;

- dates;

- URLs;

- structured objects;

- uploaded file metadata;

- pagination;

- sorting;

- filters.

Validation must also occur at security-sensitive internal boundaries where necessary.

# 13.43 Output Encoding

Any data rendered into HTML or other executable contexts must be encoded appropriately.

Do not assume AI-generated content is safe HTML.

AI output should be treated as untrusted data unless explicitly sanitized and transformed into a safe representation.

# 13.44 CSRF

If browser authentication uses cookies, CSRF protections must be applied appropriately.

Possible controls include:

- SameSite cookie policy;

- CSRF tokens;

- origin validation;

- secure cookie flags.

If authentication uses a different architecture, apply the appropriate equivalent controls.

Do not add contradictory authentication mechanisms.

# 13.45 CORS

CORS must be explicitly configured.

Never use unrestricted:

Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *

with credentialed requests.

Allowed origins should come from controlled configuration.

# 13.46 Security Headers

The deployed web application/API should use appropriate security headers, including protections against:

- clickjacking;

- MIME sniffing;

- unsafe framing;

- insecure transport;

- inappropriate browser capabilities.

The exact headers must be tested against the actual frontend architecture.

# 13.47 Rate Limiting

Rate limits should exist at appropriate boundaries:

- authentication;

- password recovery;

- public APIs;

- AI inference;

- expensive research;

- external tool calls;

- file upload;

- code execution;

- administrative APIs.

Limits should protect both security and cost.

# 13.48 Abuse Prevention

GSIR must protect against:

- credential stuffing;

- brute-force authentication;

- request flooding;

- AI-cost abuse;

- tool abuse;

- excessive research requests;

- file-based resource exhaustion;

- computation abuse;

- API-key abuse.

Rate limits should be resource-aware rather than blindly uniform.

# 13.49 Background Job Security

Background workers must preserve:

- tenant context;

- authorization context where appropriate;

- resource ownership;

- job identity;

- provenance;

- retry boundaries.

A queued job must not become an authorization bypass.

Workers must validate that the requested operation remains authorized when the job executes.

# 13.50 Job Retry Security

Retries must not duplicate dangerous operations.

For write operations, use:

- idempotency keys;

- operation identifiers;

- transactional state;

- postcondition checks.

Do not blindly retry destructive operations.

# 13.51 Webhook Security

Incoming webhooks must validate:

- source authenticity;

- signatures;

- timestamp/replay protection;

- payload schema;

- event type;

- target tenant/resource.

Webhook data remains untrusted until verified.

# 13.52 Audit Architecture

Security-relevant operations must generate audit events.

Examples:

- authentication;

- failed authentication;

- session creation/revocation;

- permission changes;

- organization membership changes;

- API key changes;

- tool authorization;

- high-risk action approval;

- sensitive data export;

- model/provider changes;

- security configuration changes;

- destructive operations.

The existing audit_events data model should remain the authoritative application audit boundary unless repository evidence requires a controlled change.

# 13.53 Audit Event Minimum Contract

An audit event should capture sufficient information to answer:

WHO

WHAT

WHEN

WHERE/CONTEXT

TARGET

RESULT

RISK

CORRELATION

Conceptually:

eventId

timestamp

actor

organization

workspace/project if applicable

action

resource

result

risk

request/correlation identifier

source

metadata

Do not store unnecessary sensitive payloads.

# 13.54 Audit Integrity

Audit records should be difficult to alter without detection.

Depending on deployment requirements, integrity mechanisms may include:

- append-oriented storage;

- restricted write permissions;

- database constraints;

- immutable storage;

- hash chaining;

- external archival.

Do not implement cryptographic audit chaining merely for appearance.

The chosen mechanism must provide measurable security value.

# 13.55 Logging vs Audit

Operational logs and audit events are different.

### Operational logs

Used for:

- debugging;

- performance;

- failures;

- service operation.

### Audit events

Used for:

- accountability;

- security;

- governance;

- compliance-readiness;

- investigation.

Do not use arbitrary application logs as the authoritative audit trail.

# 13.56 PII and Sensitive Data in Logs

Never log:

- passwords;

- authentication tokens;

- API keys;

- refresh tokens;

- raw authorization headers;

- unnecessary private document contents;

- unnecessary personal information.

AI prompts/responses must not automatically be copied into unrestricted logs.

Where logging AI interactions is required, apply data minimization and classification.

# 13.57 Correlation and Traceability

Security and research operations should be traceable through correlation identifiers.

A request may produce:

HTTP request

   ↓

research task

   ↓

AI run

   ↓

tool invocation

   ↓

job

   ↓

external result

   ↓

audit event

These records should be linkable without duplicating sensitive data.

# 13.58 Privacy by Design

GSIR must collect and retain only information necessary for:

- product functionality;

- security;

- research provenance;

- user-requested persistence;

- legally/operationally required purposes.

Do not collect data simply because future functionality might need it.

# 13.59 Data Minimization

Before processing data:

What is required?

What is optional?

What can be removed?

What can be redacted?

What must remain?

This applies particularly to AI context assembly.

More context is not automatically better.

# 13.60 Data Retention

Each major data class should have a defined lifecycle.

Examples:

Session → short-lived

Temporary tool result → limited retention

Raw uploaded file → user/project lifecycle

Research evidence → research lifecycle

Audit event → security/governance lifecycle

Derived knowledge → controlled lifecycle

Retention periods should be configurable where necessary.

Do not create arbitrary permanent retention.

# 13.61 Deletion

Deletion must respect dependencies and provenance.

The system must distinguish:

- user-visible deletion;

- soft deletion;

- permanent deletion;

- legal/administrative retention;

- derived data;

- cached copies;

- external-provider copies.

Deletion behavior must be documented rather than implied.

# 13.62 Data Export

Users/organizations may require export of their data.

Export must:

- enforce authorization;

- preserve tenant boundaries;

- avoid exposing secrets;

- record appropriate audit events;

- avoid uncontrolled server resource usage;

- use asynchronous processing for large exports.

# 13.63 AI Memory Privacy

Memory must obey scope.

Examples:

User memory

Organization knowledge

Workspace knowledge

Project research memory

Conversation context

These are not interchangeable.

A project-specific fact must not silently become global organizational knowledge.

# 13.64 Cross-Project Isolation

Research retrieval must not accidentally expose information from another project.

Retrieval filters must enforce:

tenant

+

scope

+

authorization

+

classification

+

resource status

Vector similarity must never override authorization.

# 13.65 Retrieval Security Rule

The following is mandatory:

Retrieval can discover information; retrieval cannot grant permission.

A highly similar document belonging to another tenant remains inaccessible.

# 13.66 Knowledge Promotion Security

Knowledge promotion must not bypass access control.

When information moves from:

document

→ evidence

→ claim

→ knowledge

its authorization and classification metadata must remain explicit.

Promotion does not automatically make information public.

# 13.67 Scientific Integrity and Security

Security must protect scientific integrity.

The system must preserve:

- source identity;

- evidence provenance;

- calculation provenance;

- experiment provenance;

- model/version identity;

- tool/version identity;

- timestamps;

- research-state history.

Security controls must not make scientific results impossible to reproduce.

# 13.68 Provenance Trust

A source being authenticated does not automatically make its scientific claims true.

GSIR must maintain the distinction:

Authenticity

≠

Scientific Validity

Security verifies system trust.

Scientific evaluation determines evidence quality.

# 13.69 Model Output Trust

AI output is untrusted until evaluated.

A model can be:

- wrong;

- manipulated;

- outdated;

- hallucinating;

- prompt-injected;

- inconsistent.

Therefore:

Model Output

     ↓

Validation

     ↓

Evidence / Policy / Schema Checks

     ↓

Allowed Use

# 13.70 Model Routing Security

Model routing must consider security.

Routing may depend on:

- data classification;

- provider trust;

- contractual policy;

- geographic/data residency requirements where applicable;

- model capabilities;

- provider configuration;

- task sensitivity.

A cheaper model is not automatically acceptable for sensitive information.

# 13.71 Provider Failure and Security

If an AI provider fails:

- do not automatically fall back to an unauthorized provider;

- preserve data-classification restrictions;

- preserve tenant context;

- preserve auditability;

- preserve user/provider policy;

- fail closed when no compliant provider exists.

# 13.72 External API Credential Security

Scientific APIs may require credentials.

The credential boundary must be:

GSIR

  ↓

Credential Store

  ↓

Authorized Connector

  ↓

External API

not:

GSIR

  ↓

AI prompt

  ↓

API key

The model should receive only the result required for reasoning.

# 13.73 Tool Data Egress

Before sending data externally, the action layer should determine:

- destination;

- data classification;

- user authorization;

- organization policy;

- tool permission;

- provider policy;

- amount of data;

- purpose.

Potentially sensitive external transmission should be blocked or require approval according to policy.

# 13.74 High-Impact Scientific Operations

Medicine, biological experimentation, hazardous chemistry, engineering systems, physical equipment, and other high-impact areas require stronger governance.

GSIR may assist with:

- analysis;

- literature review;

- calculations;

- experimental planning;

- SOP drafting;

- comparison;

- simulation;

- data interpretation.

Actual high-impact execution must remain subject to:

- authorization;

- domain-specific safety constraints;

- human oversight;

- validated equipment/tool interfaces;

- appropriate approval;

- emergency controls where applicable.

The AI must not become an unrestricted autonomous operator.

# 13.75 Physical System Boundary

Future physical systems must have a hard boundary:

AI Proposal

 ↓

Safety Validation

 ↓

Authorization

 ↓

Human Approval where required

 ↓

Physical Controller

 ↓

Action

 ↓

Sensor Observation

 ↓

Validation

Emergency stop mechanisms must remain independent of the AI system.

# 13.76 Governance Architecture

Governance defines what GSIR is permitted to do.

Governance policies should cover:

- model usage;

- tool usage;

- data handling;

- retention;

- external data transmission;

- research integrity;

- high-risk operations;

- human approval;

- security;

- account administration;

- deployment;

- model/provider changes.

Policies must be versioned.

# 13.77 Policy Versioning

Security-sensitive policies must have:

policyId

version

status

effectiveAt

createdBy

approvedBy where required

scope

rules

A change must be attributable.

Do not silently change security behavior through undocumented configuration.

# 13.78 Configuration Security

Configuration must be separated into:

### Safe operational configuration

Examples:

- timeouts;

- limits;

- UI preferences.

### Security-sensitive configuration

Examples:

- authentication;

- authorization;

- allowed providers;

- allowed tools;

- network egress;

- retention;

- secret locations.

Security-sensitive configuration requires stronger change controls.

# 13.79 Administrative Actions

Administrative actions must be:

- authenticated;

- authorized;

- auditable;

- appropriately rate limited;

- protected against accidental execution.

High-impact administrative operations should support confirmation/step-up authentication where appropriate.

# 13.80 Emergency Controls

GSIR should provide controlled emergency mechanisms for:

- disabling a tool;

- disabling a provider;

- revoking credentials;

- stopping jobs;

- disabling external writes;

- disabling physical interfaces;

- restricting affected tenants.

Emergency controls must not depend on the AI model cooperating.

# 13.81 Incident Detection

Security monitoring should detect patterns such as:

- repeated failed authentication;

- unusual token use;

- privilege changes;

- unexpected tool usage;

- excessive external requests;

- abnormal data exports;

- repeated sandbox failures;

- SSRF attempts;

- suspicious file uploads;

- anomalous AI/tool behavior.

Detection should produce actionable signals rather than excessive noise.

# 13.82 Incident Response

A basic incident lifecycle:

Detect

 ↓

Contain

 ↓

Investigate

 ↓

Eradicate

 ↓

Recover

 ↓

Validate

 ↓

Document

 ↓

Improve

The system must preserve relevant audit and operational evidence during incidents.

# 13.83 Security Failure Modes

Security failures should be classified.

### Authentication failure

Reject request.

### Authorization failure

Reject request.

### Invalid tool permission

Do not invoke tool.

### Invalid provider policy

Do not send data.

### Unsafe file

Quarantine/reject.

### SSRF attempt

Block.

### Sandbox violation

Terminate execution.

### Suspicious external content

Treat as untrusted and continue only within safe boundaries.

### High-risk action without approval

Block.

### Security service unavailable

Fail closed for security-critical operations.

# 13.84 Fail-Closed Principle

For security-critical decisions:

unknown permission

→ deny

unknown identity

→ deny

unknown policy

→ deny

invalid approval

→ deny

invalid tool state

→ deny

Do not interpret missing information as permission.

# 13.85 Availability vs Security

Fail-closed behavior must not unnecessarily destroy availability.

For example:

- informational research may continue if a noncritical auxiliary service fails;

- a destructive external action should not continue if authorization cannot be verified.

The system must distinguish:

critical security dependency

from:

optional enhancement

# 13.86 Supply-Chain Security

Dependencies are part of the attack surface.

The project must use:

- pinned/controlled versions where appropriate;

- dependency vulnerability scanning;

- lockfiles;

- controlled upgrades;

- removal of unused dependencies;

- provenance-aware dependency review;

- software bill of materials where appropriate.

Do not add libraries simply because they provide convenience.

# 13.87 SBOM

The build/release process should be capable of producing an SBOM for production artifacts when practical.

The SBOM should support:

- dependency identification;

- vulnerability investigation;

- incident response;

- upgrade planning.

# 13.88 Secrets Scanning

Repository CI should detect accidentally committed:

- API keys;

- tokens;

- private keys;

- passwords;

- cloud credentials;

- database credentials.

A detected secret must trigger appropriate remediation, including rotation when exposure is real.

# 13.89 Secure Development Lifecycle

Every implementation change should follow:

Requirement

 ↓

Threat Consideration

 ↓

Design

 ↓

Implementation

 ↓

Unit Tests

 ↓

Security Tests

 ↓

Integration Tests

 ↓

Regression Tests

 ↓

Review

 ↓

Deployment

 ↓

Monitoring

Security review must happen before exposing new external capabilities.

# 13.90 Dependency and Code Review

Before adding a dependency, the coding agent must answer:

- Why is it required?

- Can existing functionality provide the capability?

- Is it maintained?

- What permissions does it require?

- Does it expand the attack surface?

- Does it introduce transitive vulnerabilities?

- Can the same result be implemented more simply?

Prefer existing trusted dependencies already present in the repository.

# 13.91 Migration Security

Database migrations must:

- be versioned;

- be reviewed;

- avoid destructive changes without explicit authorization;

- preserve tenant integrity;

- preserve audit requirements;

- be tested against supported database states.

A migration must never silently weaken authorization or tenant isolation.

# 13.92 Backup Security

Backups must be protected as strongly as the underlying data.

They require:

- access control;

- encryption where appropriate;

- retention policy;

- integrity checks;

- restoration testing.

A secure production database with insecure backups is not a secure system.

# 13.93 Disaster Recovery

GSIR must define recovery objectives appropriate to the deployment.

At minimum determine:

- what data must survive;

- what can be reconstructed;

- what can be regenerated;

- what must be backed up;

- recovery ordering;

- credential recovery;

- external dependency recovery.

Research provenance should not be lost merely because transient AI state is lost.

# 13.94 Business Continuity

When optional AI providers or external scientific APIs fail, GSIR should degrade gracefully.

Examples:

Primary model unavailable

→ permitted fallback model

Scientific API unavailable

→ cached/previous evidence with freshness warning

Search provider unavailable

→ alternate permitted retrieval path

Background worker unavailable

→ queued state preserved

Fallback must respect security and data policy.

# 13.95 Security Testing Strategy

Security tests must cover at least:

### Identity

- invalid credentials;

- expired sessions;

- revoked sessions;

- token reuse;

- password reset abuse;

- authentication rate limits.

### Authorization

- cross-tenant access;

- cross-workspace access;

- cross-project access;

- role escalation;

- direct-ID manipulation.

### AI

- prompt injection;

- tool escalation;

- unauthorized data retrieval;

- provider-policy bypass;

- malicious model output.

### Files

- path traversal;

- malicious file types;

- oversized files;

- decompression attacks;

- parser failures.

### Network

- SSRF;

- redirect abuse;

- internal address access;

- unsupported schemes.

### Tools

- unauthorized invocation;

- invalid arguments;

- approval bypass;

- retry duplication;

- credential leakage.

### Database

- injection;

- ownership bypass;

- migration integrity.

# 13.96 Mandatory Tenant Isolation Tests

The test suite must prove:

User A / Organization A

        X

User B / Organization B

for every major resource class.

At minimum test:

- workspaces;

- projects;

- notes;

- web links;

- conversations;

- messages;

- files;

- document chunks;

- research data;

- AI runs;

- audit records.

# 13.97 Mandatory AI Security Tests

The implementation must include tests for scenarios such as:

### Test A — Prompt injection

External document says to reveal secrets.

Expected:

No secret disclosure.

No privilege change.

No tool escalation.

### Test B — Tool escalation

Model requests a tool outside its authorized capability.

Expected:

Invocation blocked.

Audit event recorded.

### Test C — Cross-tenant retrieval

Model attempts to retrieve another organization's document.

Expected:

No result returned.

Authorization boundary preserved.

### Test D — Provider leakage

Sensitive content is routed to a provider not authorized for that classification.

Expected:

Request blocked or rerouted only to an authorized provider.

### Test E — Malicious web page

Fetched page contains executable-looking instructions.

Expected:

Page remains untrusted content.

No privileged action occurs.

# 13.98 Mandatory Human-Approval Test

For every configured high-risk operation:

AI proposal

    ↓

No approval

    ↓

BLOCK

Then:

AI proposal

    ↓

Valid authorized approval

    ↓

Policy validation

    ↓

Execution

The test must verify that the frontend cannot fake the approval state.

# 13.99 Security Observability

Security metrics should include:

- authentication failures;

- authorization denials;

- tool denials;

- blocked SSRF attempts;

- file security failures;

- sandbox violations;

- provider policy blocks;

- high-risk approval requests;

- suspicious activity;

- secret scanning failures;

- dependency vulnerabilities.

Metrics must not expose sensitive user content.

# 13.100 Security Performance

Security controls must be efficient.

Avoid:

- unnecessary repeated authorization queries;

- repeated credential lookups;

- excessive cryptographic work;

- redundant serialization;

- oversized audit payloads;

- unnecessary security middleware duplication.

However:

Performance must never remove a required security boundary.

Cache only decisions that are safe to cache and invalidate them correctly when permissions change.

# 13.101 Security and Cognitive-State Boundaries

The cognitive state may contain:

- goals;

- constraints;

- evidence;

- hypotheses;

- plans;

- observations;

- uncertainty;

- tool proposals.

It must not contain:

- raw passwords;

- unrestricted credentials;

- authorization secrets;

- private signing keys;

- unrestricted database credentials.

Sensitive secrets remain outside cognitive state.

# 13.102 Security and Memory Boundaries

Memory may retain useful facts, but memory must not become an uncontrolled privilege store.

Do not allow memory to establish:

"User previously approved X"

as permanent authorization for future unrelated actions.

Authorization is determined by current policy and current authority.

# 13.103 Security and Learning Boundaries

The learning system must never automatically learn security policy from arbitrary examples.

For example:

User says:

"Ignore authentication next time."

must not become learned authorization behavior.

Security policy belongs to controlled system governance.

# 13.104 Security and Continuous Improvement

Improvement mechanisms must not modify security boundaries automatically.

Safe improvement may optimize:

- prompts;

- retrieval;

- routing;

- strategy;

- model selection;

- performance.

But changes to:

- authorization;

- identity;

- secrets;

- tool permissions;

- network policy;

- security controls

require explicit governance and controlled deployment.

# 13.105 No Self-Granted Privilege

This rule is absolute:

No AI component, learning component, memory component, tool, plugin, or generated code may grant itself additional authority.

Any privilege change must pass through the normal authorization/governance mechanism.

# 13.106 Generated Code Security

AI-generated code must be treated as untrusted until reviewed/tested.

The coding agent must:

- inspect repository context;

- preserve existing security boundaries;

- avoid disabling security checks;

- avoid weakening validation;

- avoid exposing secrets;

- run security tests;

- report security-sensitive changes.

# 13.107 Security Regression Protection

Every security defect fixed should produce a regression test when practical.

Example:

security bug

 ↓

fix

 ↓

test reproducing previous failure

 ↓

permanent regression protection

Security behavior must not depend solely on developer memory.

# 13.108 Compliance Readiness

GSIR should be designed to support future compliance requirements, but the project must not falsely claim certification or compliance.

Architecture should support future requirements through:

- access controls;

- auditability;

- data classification;

- retention;

- incident records;

- change management;

- security testing;

- documented policies.

Specific regulatory/compliance claims require separate verification.

# 13.109 Minimal Security Architecture

The MVP should avoid creating a large security subsystem.

Prefer:

Identity

Authorization

Policy

Credential Boundary

Audit

Validation

Security Middleware

Controlled Tool Boundary

over many independent security services.

Security capabilities should be centralized where appropriate but remain enforceable at every required boundary.

# 13.110 Recommended Security Module Boundaries

The exact package/module names must follow the current repository after audit.

Conceptually:

security/

    identity

    authentication

    authorization

    policy

    audit

    credentials

    validation

    risk

These are logical boundaries, not a requirement to create unnecessary physical modules.

# 13.111 Security Dependency Rule

No business component should directly implement its own independent authentication or authorization mechanism.

Instead:

Business Operation

       ↓

Security Context

       ↓

Authorization Policy

       ↓

Operation

This prevents inconsistent security behavior.

# 13.112 Security Context

Each protected operation should have access to a normalized security context containing only necessary information, such as:

principalId

organizationId

roles

resourceScope

authenticationState

authorizationContext

correlationId

Do not place secrets in this context.

# 13.113 Authorization Decision

Authorization should produce a structured decision:

ALLOW

DENY

REQUIRE_APPROVAL

rather than relying on arbitrary model text.

Additional internal reasons may support observability.

# 13.114 Risk Decision

Action risk should similarly be structured:

riskLevel

requiredScopes

approvalRequired

allowed

reason

The model cannot override the result.

# 13.115 Security State Machine for Actions

A high-risk action should follow:

PROPOSED

   ↓

VALIDATING

   ↓

AUTHORIZED

   ↓

APPROVAL_REQUIRED ──→ APPROVED

   ↓                      ↓

REJECTED ←──────────── EXECUTING

                          ↓

                       COMPLETED

                          ↓

                       AUDITED

Invalid transitions must be rejected.

# 13.116 Security Acceptance Criteria

Part 13 is accepted only when the implementation can demonstrate:

### Identity

- secure authentication;

- secure session lifecycle;

- credential recovery;

- session revocation.

### Authorization

- organization isolation;

- workspace isolation;

- project isolation;

- resource authorization;

- least privilege.

### AI security

- model has no implicit authority;

- prompt injection does not grant privilege;

- tool authorization is enforced outside the model;

- sensitive provider routing is policy-controlled.

### Data

- secrets are isolated;

- sensitive information is minimized;

- files are treated as untrusted;

- memory respects scope;

- retrieval cannot bypass authorization.

### External systems

- SSRF protection exists;

- tool permissions are enforced;

- external credentials are isolated;

- code execution is sandboxed where supported.

### Audit

- security-sensitive operations are attributable;

- audit records contain sufficient context;

- sensitive data is not unnecessarily logged.

### Operations

- rate limits exist where required;

- security failures fail safely;

- dependencies are monitored;

- backup/recovery strategy exists.

# 13.117 Coding-Agent Audit Prompt

The coding agent must execute the following before implementing Part 13:

GSIR SECURITY ARCHITECTURE AUDIT

Inspect the current repository before changing code.

Determine:

- Current authentication implementation.

- Current session/token implementation.

- Current user/organization/workspace/project authorization.

- Existing security middleware/configuration.

- Existing CORS/CSRF/security-header configuration.

- Existing rate limiting.

- Existing file-upload handling.

- Existing external API/tool boundary.

- Existing AI provider boundary.

- Existing secret/configuration handling.

- Existing audit implementation.

- Existing logging and sensitive-data exposure.

- Existing database ownership/tenant constraints.

- Existing background jobs and authorization context.

- Existing web/network fetching.

- Existing code execution or sandboxing.

- Existing tests covering security.

- Existing dependencies with security relevance.

Do not assume historical GSIR architecture is current.

Produce:

- CURRENT architecture;

- security gaps;

- verified controls;

- missing controls;

- duplicate security mechanisms;

- vulnerabilities;

- required changes;

- files affected;

- dependency changes;

- migration requirements;

- tests required.

Do not implement anything during the audit.

If a security or architecture decision cannot be determined from repository evidence, mark it BLOCKED / NEEDS DECISION rather than guessing.

# 13.118 Coding-Agent Implementation Prompt

GSIR PART 13 — SECURE IMPLEMENTATION

Implement only the security changes justified by the completed repository audit.

Requirements:

- preserve the existing architecture where correct;

- do not create unnecessary services/modules;

- do not duplicate authentication/authorization logic;

- enforce authorization server-side;

- preserve tenant isolation;

- keep secrets outside model context;

- treat external content as untrusted;

- enforce AI tool permissions outside the model;

- protect file uploads;

- enforce network/SSRF boundaries where applicable;

- preserve auditability;

- avoid sensitive information in logs;

- preserve existing API contracts unless a required security correction is documented;

- add migrations only when necessary;

- add dependencies only when necessary;

- add security regression tests for every material security change.

Do not weaken an existing security control to make a test pass.

Do not mark a control complete without executable evidence.

# 13.119 Final Verification Prompt

GSIR PART 13 — SECURITY FINAL VERIFICATION

Verify the completed implementation from the repository itself.

Check:

- Authentication.

- Session security.

- Authorization.

- Tenant isolation.

- Resource ownership.

- Input validation.

- CORS/CSRF/security headers where applicable.

- Rate limiting.

- Secret handling.

- File security.

- SSRF/network controls.

- AI/tool authorization.

- Provider data boundaries.

- Background-job security.

- Audit events.

- Sensitive logging.

- Database security.

- Dependency security.

- Security regression tests.

- Build/test status.

Run the complete applicable test suite.

Report:

- PASS;

- FAIL;

- BLOCKED;

- NOT APPLICABLE;

with evidence for every category.

Do not claim security completion based solely on code inspection.

# 13.120 Required Security Test Matrix

The implementation report must include a matrix:

| **Security Area** | **Control** | **Test** | **Expected Result** | **Actual Result** | **Status** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Authentication | invalid credential rejection | auth test | rejected | — | — |
| Session | revoked session | session test | rejected | — | — |
| Authorization | cross-tenant access | isolation test | denied | — | — |
| RBAC | unauthorized role | role test | denied | — | — |
| File | malicious path | upload test | rejected | — | — |
| SSRF | private target | network test | blocked | — | — |
| AI | prompt injection | adversarial test | contained | — | — |
| Tool | unauthorized action | tool test | blocked | — | — |
| Provider | restricted data | routing test | blocked/rerouted | — | — |
| Audit | privileged action | audit test | recorded | — | — |
| Secrets | log inspection | secret test | absent | — | — |
| Database | injection | API test | prevented | — | — |

# 13.121 MVP Security Implementation Order

Implementation should proceed in this order:

### Security Phase 1 — Repository security audit

No code changes.

### Security Phase 2 — Identity/authentication

Implement/fix:

- authentication;

- session lifecycle;

- credential security;

- recovery;

- revocation.

### Security Phase 3 — Authorization

Implement/fix:

- organization;

- workspace;

- project;

- resource-level authorization;

- tenant isolation.

### Security Phase 4 — API hardening

Implement:

- validation;

- safe errors;

- CORS;

- CSRF where applicable;

- security headers;

- rate limits.

### Security Phase 5 — Secrets/data

Implement:

- secret isolation;

- sensitive-data handling;

- logging redaction;

- provider credential boundaries.

### Security Phase 6 — AI/tool security

Implement:

- model authority boundary;

- tool authorization;

- risk checks;

- approval mechanism;

- provider data policies.

### Security Phase 7 — Files/network

Implement:

- upload validation;

- path protection;

- SSRF controls;

- external-content isolation.

### Security Phase 8 — Audit/observability

Implement:

- security audit events;

- correlation;

- security metrics;

- monitoring.

### Security Phase 9 — Testing

Run:

- unit;

- integration;

- API;

- tenant isolation;

- security regression;

- AI adversarial;

- tool authorization;

- dependency/security checks.

### Security Phase 10 — Final verification

No completion claim until evidence is recorded.

# 13.122 Security Architecture Completion Rule

Part 13 is not complete merely because authentication works.

Completion requires demonstrated protection of the complete path:

Identity

 ↓

Authorization

 ↓

Data

 ↓

AI

 ↓

Memory

 ↓

Research

 ↓

Tool

 ↓

External System

 ↓

Audit

Every transition that can cross a security boundary must have an explicit control.

# 13.123 Master Security Principle

The final governing rule for Part 13 is:

GSIR must remain secure even when its AI is wrong, manipulated, prompt-injected, compromised, or overconfident. Security authority therefore belongs to deterministic system controls, authorization policy, controlled action boundaries, and human governance—not to the model itself.

# 13.124 Transition to Part 14

With the security/trust architecture defined, the next part will address the enterprise application/API architecture and production runtime, including:

- backend application boundaries;

- REST/API contracts;

- WebSocket/realtime behavior where required;

- request lifecycle;

- service boundaries;

- transaction boundaries;

- background processing;

- event/outbox behavior;

- frontend/backend contract;

- error architecture;

- configuration;

- deployment;

- observability;

- health/readiness;

- production runtime;

- scalability without premature microservices;

- exact implementation structure based on the audited repository.

Part 14 must continue from the actual repository state and must not blindly preserve historical stack assumptions.

# GSIR MASTER DEVELOPMENT PLAN

## PART 14 — ENTERPRISE APPLICATION, API, RUNTIME, DEPLOYMENT AND PRODUCTION OPERATIONS ARCHITECTURE

## 14.1 Purpose

Part 14 defines how GSIR operates as a reliable production application.

The preceding parts established:

- the product and engineering principles;

- the coding-agent operating model;

- the data architecture;

- the AI architecture;

- the unified cognitive architecture;

- the scientific research engine;

- the controlled action/tool boundary;

- learning and continuous improvement;

- security, privacy, identity, authorization, governance, audit, and trust.

Part 14 converts those architectural principles into a practical application/runtime architecture.

The objective is:

One coherent production system with clear internal boundaries, reliable APIs, predictable state transitions, efficient background processing, strong observability, and a deployment model that can scale without premature architectural complexity.

# 14.2 Primary Runtime Principle

GSIR should initially operate as:

One Application

+

One Primary Database

+

One Controlled Background Processing Mechanism

+

External AI/Scientific Services

rather than prematurely becoming:

10–50 Microservices

+

Service Mesh

+

Multiple Databases

+

Multiple Message Brokers

+

Multiple Deployment Systems

The architecture must remain modular internally so that future extraction is possible if real scaling evidence requires it.

# 14.3 Application Architecture

The preferred logical architecture is:

Client

  ↓

API / Web Boundary

  ↓

Application Layer

  ↓

Domain / Core Logic

  ↓

Persistence

  ↓

PostgreSQL

with controlled side paths:

Application

 ├── AI Gateway

 ├── Tool/Action Boundary

 ├── File/Storage Boundary

 ├── Background Jobs

 └── Event/Outbox Boundary

These are logical boundaries.

They do not automatically require separate deployable services.

# 14.4 Repository-First Rule

Before implementing Part 14, the coding agent must inspect the actual repository.

The historical architecture documents may contain:

- previous technologies;

- superseded modules;

- old API assumptions;

- obsolete database structures;

- previous deployment approaches.

The repository is the implementation source of truth unless a higher-authority approved specification explicitly changes it.

The coding agent must not replace an existing working architecture simply because a newer theoretical architecture appears cleaner.

# 14.5 Runtime Architecture Decision Hierarchy

When selecting implementation details:

Current verified repository

        ↓

Approved GSIR architecture

        ↓

Current phase requirements

        ↓

Security constraints

        ↓

Production evidence

        ↓

Engineering judgment

If a decision cannot be determined safely, mark it:

BLOCKED / NEEDS DECISION

Do not guess.

# 14.6 Application Boundary

The application boundary owns:

- authentication;

- authorization;

- API handling;

- domain operations;

- research state;

- AI orchestration;

- tool authorization;

- persistence;

- job submission;

- audit;

- observability.

External systems remain outside the application boundary.

# 14.7 Layering

The application should use a small number of meaningful layers:

API

 ↓

Application

 ↓

Domain

 ↓

Infrastructure

### API

Responsible for:

- HTTP;

- authentication context;

- request validation;

- DTO mapping;

- response formatting;

- API errors.

### Application

Responsible for:

- use cases;

- transactions;

- orchestration;

- authorization invocation;

- state transitions.

### Domain

Responsible for:

- business rules;

- invariants;

- research logic;

- state transitions.

### Infrastructure

Responsible for:

- database;

- external APIs;

- AI providers;

- storage;

- queues;

- network clients.

Do not create unnecessary abstraction layers between these.

# 14.8 Controller/API Rule

Controllers must remain thin.

A controller should:

receive request

→ validate/map

→ invoke application operation

→ return result

A controller must not contain:

- complex scientific reasoning;

- database business logic;

- provider-specific AI logic;

- authorization rules duplicated from the security layer;

- long-running computation.

# 14.9 Application-Service Rule

Application services coordinate use cases.

Example:

CreateResearchTask

RunResearchStep

CreateConversation

SendMessage

UploadFile

RunAIRequest

InvokeTool

PromoteKnowledge

CreateExperiment

They should coordinate rather than become enormous “god services”.

# 14.10 Domain Logic

Domain logic should contain rules that remain true regardless of transport.

Examples:

- research-state transitions;

- evidence status;

- hypothesis lifecycle;

- experiment state;

- tool-risk rules;

- knowledge promotion conditions.

Domain logic must not depend unnecessarily on HTTP.

# 14.11 Repository Interfaces

Persistence access should be isolated behind the application's persistence mechanism.

The application should not scatter database queries throughout controllers and unrelated services.

Repositories should expose operations meaningful to the domain/use case.

Avoid creating generic abstractions such as:

GenericRepository<T>

unless the actual codebase demonstrates a real benefit.

# 14.12 Transaction Boundaries

Transactions should correspond to meaningful state changes.

Example:

Create research task

+

Initial state

+

Audit event

may form one transaction where appropriate.

Do not hold a database transaction open while waiting for:

- an AI provider;

- a web request;

- a scientific API;

- a long computation;

- user approval.

Long-running external work must occur outside database transactions.

# 14.13 External Call Boundary

External calls should follow:

Validate

 ↓

Authorize

 ↓

Prepare

 ↓

Invoke

 ↓

Validate result

 ↓

Persist relevant state

 ↓

Audit

The application should not assume external success.

# 14.14 Request Lifecycle

A normal protected request should follow:

HTTP Request

 ↓

Request ID / Correlation

 ↓

Authentication

 ↓

Authorization

 ↓

Input Validation

 ↓

Application Use Case

 ↓

Domain Rules

 ↓

Persistence / External Boundary

 ↓

Audit where required

 ↓

Response

Security checks must occur before sensitive operations.

# 14.15 Request Context

A request context should provide only the necessary metadata, such as:

requestId

principalId

organizationId

workspaceId

projectId

locale if required

timestamp

Do not store arbitrary user/model content in request context.

Do not store secrets.

# 14.16 API Contract Architecture

APIs must have explicit contracts.

Every endpoint should define:

- method;

- path;

- authentication;

- authorization;

- request schema;

- response schema;

- errors;

- pagination where applicable;

- idempotency where applicable;

- side effects;

- audit behavior.

OpenAPI or the repository's equivalent contract mechanism should remain synchronized with implementation.

# 14.17 API Naming

API naming should remain consistent.

Prefer predictable resource-oriented naming.

Examples:

/users

/organizations

/workspaces

/projects

/notes

/web-links

/conversations

/messages

/files

/research

/tasks

Do not create multiple naming styles for equivalent operations.

# 14.18 API Versioning

Do not introduce API versions simply because versioning is theoretically useful.

Version when there is a genuine compatibility requirement.

If versioning is necessary, it must be explicit and documented.

Existing clients must not be silently broken.

# 14.19 DTO Boundary

API DTOs must remain separate from persistence entities.

Reasons:

- prevent accidental data exposure;

- preserve API stability;

- avoid coupling database structure to public contracts;

- support validation;

- allow internal schema evolution.

Never return database entities directly from public APIs when doing so exposes internal fields or persistence assumptions.

# 14.20 Pagination

Collection endpoints must use bounded pagination.

Never allow an endpoint to return an unbounded collection.

Pagination should support a predictable contract such as:

items

page/offset/cursor

limit

hasNext

The exact mechanism should follow repository conventions.

# 14.21 Filtering and Sorting

Filtering/sorting must use explicit allowlists.

Never pass arbitrary client-provided database expressions directly to persistence.

Example:

sort=createdAt

must map to an approved field.

Not:

sort=<arbitrary SQL>

# 14.22 Idempotency

Idempotency should be used for operations where duplicate execution would be harmful.

Examples:

- payment-like future integrations;

- external writes;

- high-cost jobs;

- irreversible requests;

- retryable tool operations.

The implementation must not add idempotency complexity to operations where duplicates are harmless.

# 14.23 API Error Architecture

All API errors must follow a consistent structure.

Conceptually:

code

message

requestId

details where safe

Internal stack traces must never be exposed.

Errors should distinguish:

validation

authentication

authorization

not found

conflict

rate limited

dependency failure

internal failure

# 14.24 Error Ownership

Errors should be handled at the correct layer.

Domain error

→ application mapping

Infrastructure error

→ infrastructure/application mapping

HTTP formatting

→ API layer

Do not expose low-level database/provider exceptions directly.

# 14.25 Exception Handling

Do not use broad exception handling to hide failures.

Bad:

catch everything

→ return success

Good:

known failure

→ structured failure

unexpected failure

→ safe internal error

+

diagnostic logging

+

correlation ID

# 14.26 AI Request Lifecycle

AI requests must follow the established architecture:

User Goal

 ↓

Application Request

 ↓

Authorization

 ↓

Research/Cognitive State

 ↓

Context Assembly

 ↓

Model Routing

 ↓

Provider Adapter

 ↓

AI Provider

 ↓

Output Validation

 ↓

Research/Cognitive Update

 ↓

Persistence

 ↓

Response

The API layer must not contain provider-specific logic.

# 14.27 Long-Running AI Requests

Long-running AI/research operations should not unnecessarily occupy HTTP connections.

Where appropriate:

POST request

 ↓

create task/job

 ↓

return task identifier

 ↓

background processing

 ↓

status/result

The exact mechanism must follow the actual product UX and repository architecture.

# 14.28 Synchronous vs Asynchronous Work

### Synchronous

Suitable for:

- authentication;

- small CRUD operations;

- lightweight validation;

- short AI operations where latency is bounded.

### Asynchronous

Suitable for:

- large document processing;

- deep research;

- large computations;

- batch analysis;

- long external API workflows;

- report generation;

- large exports.

Do not make every operation asynchronous.

# 14.29 Background Job Architecture

Background jobs must have:

jobId

type

tenant scope

resource reference

status

attempt count

createdAt

startedAt

completedAt

failure information

The existing job/job-attempt architecture should be reused where applicable.

# 14.30 Job State Machine

A job should use explicit states:

QUEUED

 ↓

RUNNING

 ↓

SUCCEEDED

with controlled alternatives:

QUEUED → CANCELLED

RUNNING → CANCELLED

RUNNING → FAILED

FAILED → RETRYING

RETRYING → RUNNING

Invalid state transitions must be rejected.

# 14.31 Job Ownership

Every job must have an explicit scope.

A worker must verify that:

- the referenced resource exists;

- the tenant remains valid;

- required authorization conditions remain valid;

- the job has not already completed;

- the job has not been cancelled.

# 14.32 Job Retry

Retries must be bounded.

Each retry should have:

- attempt number;

- reason;

- delay;

- error category;

- timestamp.

Do not retry:

- invalid authorization;

- malformed input;

- permanent external errors;

- destructive operations without idempotency.

# 14.33 Backoff

Transient failures may use exponential backoff with jitter.

Example conceptual sequence:

1s

2s

4s

8s

...

bounded maximum

Actual values must be selected from workload measurements.

# 14.34 Dead-Letter Handling

Jobs that repeatedly fail should become inspectable rather than retry forever.

The system should preserve:

- job identity;

- attempts;

- failure reason;

- last state;

- tenant/resource context.

Automatic retry loops must have a hard limit.

# 14.35 Cancellation

Cancellation must be cooperative where possible.

For example:

RUNNING

 ↓

CANCEL_REQUESTED

 ↓

worker checks cancellation

 ↓

CANCELLED

External operations that cannot be cancelled must be handled safely and marked appropriately.

# 14.36 Outbox Architecture

When database state and external event publication must remain consistent, use the existing outbox pattern.

Conceptually:

Database Transaction

 ├── Domain State

 └── Outbox Event

Then:

Outbox

 ↓

Publisher

 ↓

External Consumer

Do not publish an external event before the corresponding transaction is safely committed.

# 14.37 Outbox Reliability

Outbox processing must support:

- retry;

- idempotent publication;

- failure tracking;

- bounded retries;

- observability.

The system must tolerate publisher restarts without silently losing events.

# 14.38 Event Semantics

Events should represent meaningful facts.

Examples:

ResearchTaskCreated

ResearchTaskCompleted

FileUploaded

DocumentProcessed

AIRunCompleted

ToolInvocationCompleted

KnowledgePromoted

Do not create events for every internal method call.

# 14.39 Event Payload Security

Events must contain the minimum necessary information.

Do not publish:

- passwords;

- credentials;

- unnecessary document contents;

- secrets;

- full AI prompts/responses unless explicitly required and protected.

# 14.40 WebSocket / Realtime Architecture

Realtime communication should be used only where it materially improves UX.

Appropriate uses include:

- job progress;

- AI generation state;

- notifications;

- collaboration updates;

- task completion.

Do not use WebSockets for everything.

# 14.41 Realtime Authorization

Every realtime connection must be authenticated and scoped.

Subscriptions must be authorized.

A user subscribed to:

Project A

must not receive:

Project B

events.

# 14.42 Realtime Reliability

The frontend must not assume realtime delivery is perfect.

The architecture should support:

Realtime update

+

authoritative REST/state refresh

where appropriate.

If a connection drops, the client must be able to recover state.

# 14.43 Frontend/Backend Contract

The frontend must consume stable API contracts.

The frontend must not:

- directly access the database;

- contain authorization logic as the authority;

- duplicate business rules unnecessarily;

- depend on internal entity structure.

Frontend behavior should reflect server state.

# 14.44 Frontend State

The frontend should distinguish:

server state

UI state

session state

temporary interaction state

Do not duplicate entire backend state unnecessarily in the browser.

# 14.45 API Client

The React frontend should use a centralized API client or equivalent existing repository mechanism.

It should handle:

- base URL;

- authentication;

- common errors;

- request IDs where appropriate;

- serialization;

- retries only when safe.

Do not scatter raw HTTP implementation throughout UI components.

# 14.46 Authentication State in Frontend

The frontend should maintain a controlled authentication state.

It must handle:

- login;

- logout;

- expired session;

- unauthorized response;

- session restoration;

- protected routes.

Never store secrets in insecure persistent browser storage merely for convenience.

# 14.47 Configuration Architecture

Configuration should be externalized.

Separate:

source code

configuration

secrets

runtime environment

Never commit environment-specific secrets.

# 14.48 Configuration Validation

Application startup should validate required configuration.

If a required production secret/configuration is missing:

startup

→ clear configuration error

→ no unsafe partial operation

Do not silently substitute insecure defaults in production.

# 14.49 Environment Separation

At minimum distinguish:

development

test

staging

production

Environment-specific configuration must not accidentally cross boundaries.

Production credentials must never be used by tests.

# 14.50 Database Runtime

The production database should be treated as authoritative persistent state.

The application must use:

- connection pooling;

- transaction management;

- migration control;

- appropriate indexes;

- timeouts;

- safe connection limits.

Do not open one new database connection per request manually.

# 14.51 Database Connection Pooling

Pool configuration must be based on:

- application concurrency;

- database capacity;

- query duration;

- number of application instances.

More connections do not automatically improve performance.

# 14.52 Database Migrations

Schema changes must use the repository's approved migration mechanism.

Migrations must be:

- versioned;

- repeatable only where explicitly designed;

- tested;

- ordered;

- compatible with deployment strategy.

Do not modify production schema manually as the normal workflow.

# 14.53 Zero-Downtime Migration Principle

When production availability matters, schema changes should prefer:

expand

→ deploy compatible code

→ migrate/backfill

→ switch behavior

→ contract/remove obsolete structure

rather than an immediate destructive change.

# 14.54 Database Indexing

Indexes must be created from actual access patterns.

Important candidates include:

- tenant scope;

- ownership;

- foreign keys;

- frequently queried status;

- timestamps used for ordering;

- unique business identifiers.

Do not index every column.

# 14.55 Query Performance

Production queries must be evaluated for:

- full-table scans;

- N+1 behavior;

- unnecessary joins;

- excessive result size;

- missing indexes;

- repeated identical queries.

Performance optimization must use measurements.

# 14.56 Caching

Caching should be introduced selectively.

Good candidates:

- stable external metadata;

- model metadata;

- tool manifests;

- expensive immutable research retrieval;

- short-lived derived state.

Do not cache authorization decisions indefinitely.

# 14.57 Cache Correctness

Every cache requires:

owner

key

scope

TTL

invalidation rule

staleness behavior

A cache without a correctness model is a hidden data-consistency bug.

# 14.58 AI Response Caching

AI caching must consider:

- model/version;

- prompt/context;

- tools used;

- research state;

- temperature/randomness;

- provider;

- user/project scope.

Never reuse an AI response across incompatible security scopes.

# 14.59 Scientific Data Caching

Scientific data must include freshness metadata.

A cached result should identify:

source

retrievedAt

sourceVersion if available

expiration/freshness

A cached old result must not silently appear current.

# 14.60 Storage Architecture

Files should follow the established separation:

Database

→ metadata/version/provenance

Object Storage

→ actual file bytes

The database should not unnecessarily contain large binary objects.

# 14.61 File Processing

Large files should be processed asynchronously.

The lifecycle may be:

Upload

 ↓

Validate

 ↓

Store

 ↓

Create version

 ↓

Queue extraction

 ↓

Extract

 ↓

Chunk

 ↓

Index

 ↓

Research-ready

Each step must be observable.

# 14.62 File Processing Failure

If extraction fails:

file remains preserved

+

processing state = FAILED

+

failure reason recorded

Do not delete the user's source file merely because processing failed.

# 14.63 External Dependency Architecture

External dependencies should be accessed through adapters.

Examples:

AI Provider Adapter

Scientific API Adapter

Storage Adapter

Search Adapter

GitHub Adapter

The core application must not depend on provider-specific implementation details.

# 14.64 Provider Timeout

Every external request requires a bounded timeout.

Never allow an external provider to hold application resources indefinitely.

# 14.65 Circuit Breaking

Circuit breakers should be introduced for genuinely unstable/high-volume dependencies.

They should prevent repeated failures from consuming application resources.

Do not add circuit breakers to every function.

# 14.66 External Fallback

Fallback should be policy-aware.

For example:

AI provider unavailable

→ permitted alternative provider

but:

restricted data provider unavailable

→ arbitrary provider

is prohibited.

# 14.67 Deployment Architecture

The initial deployment should remain simple.

Conceptually:

Internet

  ↓

TLS / Reverse Proxy

  ↓

GSIR Application

  ├── API

  ├── Realtime

  └── Background Processing

  ↓

PostgreSQL

  ↓

Object Storage

External AI/scientific services remain controlled dependencies.

# 14.68 Containerization

If the repository already uses containers, preserve that architecture where appropriate.

Containers should provide:

- reproducible environments;

- dependency isolation;

- deployment consistency.

Do not create a separate container for every internal module.

# 14.69 Production Process Separation

Even in one deployable application, processes may be separated logically or operationally:

Web/API process

Worker process

Migration process

Only separate them if the runtime architecture benefits.

# 14.70 Horizontal Scaling

The application should be designed so that stateless API instances can scale horizontally where practical.

Persistent state belongs in:

- PostgreSQL;

- object storage;

- controlled queues;

- other explicit shared infrastructure.

Do not rely on local application memory for authoritative persistent state.

# 14.71 Stateless Application Principle

Application instances should not require local state to survive between requests.

Local memory may be used for:

- temporary computation;

- safe caches;

- short-lived processing.

It must not be the only location of:

- authentication state;

- research state;

- user data;

- task state;

- audit records.

# 14.72 Health Endpoints

Production deployment should expose appropriate health information.

Separate:

liveness

readiness

where the deployment environment benefits from this distinction.

Liveness answers:

Is the process alive?

Readiness answers:

Can this instance safely serve traffic?

# 14.73 Dependency Health

Readiness must not blindly fail because every optional external service is unavailable.

Distinguish:

critical dependency

from:

optional dependency

For example, a temporary scientific API outage should not necessarily make authentication unavailable.

# 14.74 Startup Behavior

Startup should:

- load configuration;

- validate configuration;

- initialize required infrastructure;

- verify required dependencies;

- initialize application components;

- expose readiness only when safe.

Do not perform long research operations during startup.

# 14.75 Graceful Shutdown

The application must support graceful shutdown.

On shutdown:

stop accepting new work

 ↓

finish safe in-flight work

 ↓

persist necessary state

 ↓

stop workers

 ↓

close connections

Long-running jobs should remain resumable or safely recoverable.

# 14.76 Deployment Safety

Deployments must avoid:

- mixed incompatible schema/code states;

- secret replacement without validation;

- uncontrolled migration execution;

- accidental deletion;

- untested configuration changes.

Production deployment should have a rollback/recovery strategy.

# 14.77 Release Artifacts

A production release should identify:

application version

commit/build identifier

database migration version

configuration version where applicable

AI/provider compatibility

This enables reproducibility.

# 14.78 Observability Architecture

GSIR requires three primary observability layers:

Logs

Metrics

Traces

plus:

Audit events

for security/governance.

These are complementary, not interchangeable.

# 14.79 Structured Logging

Production logs should be structured.

Include fields such as:

timestamp

level

service/process

requestId

operation

resource

duration

result

errorCode

Avoid arbitrary unstructured diagnostic output for critical workflows.

# 14.80 Metrics

Important metrics include:

### API

- request rate;

- latency;

- error rate;

- status-code distribution.

### Database

- query latency;

- connection pool utilization;

- transaction failures.

### AI

- inference latency;

- token usage where available;

- cost where available;

- provider failure rate;

- routing distribution.

### Research

- research task duration;

- retrieval success;

- evidence processing;

- computation duration.

### Tools

- invocation count;

- latency;

- failure rate;

- authorization denials.

### Jobs

- queue depth;

- processing time;

- retry count;

- failure rate.

# 14.81 Distributed Tracing

Tracing should be added where it materially helps understand multi-step operations.

Example:

API request

 ↓

Research task

 ↓

AI run

 ↓

Tool invocation

 ↓

External API

 ↓

Persistence

Tracing must not capture secrets or unnecessary sensitive content.

# 14.82 AI Observability

AI operations should record safe metadata such as:

aiRunId

model

provider

modelVersion

latency

token usage if available

cost if available

status

tool count

research task

Do not automatically log hidden reasoning or sensitive prompt content.

# 14.83 Research Observability

Scientific operations should preserve:

- source;

- retrieval time;

- tool version;

- model version;

- calculation identifier;

- dataset version;

- result status.

This supports reproducibility and scientific auditability.

# 14.84 Performance Budgets

Every major workflow should eventually have measurable targets.

Examples:

authentication latency

CRUD latency

AI first-token latency

research task latency

file processing throughput

database query latency

Targets must be based on actual workload rather than arbitrary numbers.

# 14.85 Resource Budgets

AI/research operations should be bounded by:

- time;

- tokens;

- tool calls;

- network requests;

- computation;

- memory;

- cost.

The cognitive loop must respect these budgets.

# 14.86 Backpressure

When system capacity is reached:

incoming work

 ↓

queue/backpressure

 ↓

controlled admission

rather than allowing unlimited resource consumption.

Examples:

- maximum concurrent research tasks;

- maximum file processing;

- maximum AI calls;

- maximum sandbox jobs.

# 14.87 Concurrency Control

Concurrent operations modifying the same resource must have explicit behavior.

Possible mechanisms:

- optimistic locking;

- version checks;

- database constraints;

- idempotency;

- serialized processing.

Do not silently overwrite newer state.

# 14.88 Research-State Concurrency

If two AI/research operations update the same research state:

State V10

 ├── Operation A → V11

 └── Operation B → V11

the system must detect the conflict.

Possible result:

A succeeds

B detects stale state

B retries/rebases/requires resolution

Never silently lose one update.

# 14.89 User Collaboration

Future collaboration features should use explicit resource versions/events.

Do not rely only on realtime messages.

The database remains authoritative.

# 14.90 Reliability Principle

Every important operation should have:

known state

+

failure state

+

recovery path

There must not be a large category of:

something failed

→ unknown what happened

# 14.91 Recovery Architecture

For a failed operation:

Detect

 ↓

Classify

 ↓

Persist failure

 ↓

Retry if safe

 ↓

Fallback if permitted

 ↓

Require user intervention if necessary

# 14.92 Data Consistency

GSIR must distinguish:

strongly consistent state

from:

eventually consistent derived state

Examples:

### Strong/authoritative

- permissions;

- organization membership;

- project ownership;

- core research-state transitions.

### Potentially eventually consistent

- search index;

- analytics;

- cached metadata;

- notifications.

The user must not see stale authorization as valid.

# 14.93 Search Index Consistency

If search/indexing is asynchronous:

database

 ↓

outbox/event

 ↓

indexing

The database remains authoritative.

Search results must never be used as an authorization source.

# 14.94 Deployment Environment

The exact deployment platform must be selected after repository and infrastructure inspection.

The coding agent must not introduce:

- Kubernetes;

- service mesh;

- serverless decomposition;

- multiple databases;

- complex cloud orchestration

unless justified by actual requirements.

# 14.95 Scaling Trigger

A component may be extracted from the main application when evidence demonstrates:

- independent scaling requirement;

- independent deployment requirement;

- fault isolation requirement;

- security isolation requirement;

- resource isolation requirement;

- organizational ownership requirement.

Architecture should not be fragmented merely because it can be.

# 14.96 Microservice Extraction Rule

If extraction becomes necessary:

existing module

 ↓

stable interface

 ↓

measured bottleneck

 ↓

independent deployment need

 ↓

extract

not:

design first

→ create 20 services

→ discover actual requirements later

# 14.97 Production Security Integration

Part 14 must preserve all Part 13 controls.

Every runtime path must retain:

- identity;

- authorization;

- tenant scope;

- secret isolation;

- auditability;

- input validation;

- safe failure.

Performance optimizations must never bypass these.

# 14.98 Production Data Protection

Production environments must never use real sensitive production data for development/testing unless explicitly authorized and appropriately protected.

Test data should be synthetic or appropriately sanitized.

# 14.99 Environment Access

Production access should follow least privilege.

Developers and automated systems should receive only the access required for their role.

Administrative access should be auditable.

# 14.100 Operational Runbooks

Important operational failures require documented recovery procedures.

At minimum:

- database unavailable;

- database migration failure;

- storage unavailable;

- AI provider outage;

- external API outage;

- queue failure;

- worker failure;

- authentication failure;

### Code

package com.gsir.common.error;

import org.springframework.http.HttpStatus;

public class GsirException extends RuntimeException {

    private final String code;

    private final HttpStatus status;

    public GsirException(

            String code,

            String message,

            HttpStatus status

    ) {

        super(message);

        this.code = code;

        this.status = status;

    }

    public String getCode() {

        return code;

    }

    public HttpStatus getStatus() {

        return status;

    }

}

## 2.3 Common errors

### File

src/main/java/com/gsir/common/error/CommonErrors.java

### Code

package com.gsir.common.error;

import org.springframework.http.HttpStatus;

public final class CommonErrors {

    private CommonErrors() {}

    public static GsirException notFound(String resource) {

        return new GsirException(

                "RESOURCE_NOT_FOUND",

                resource + " was not found",

                HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND

        );

    }

    public static GsirException forbidden() {

        return new GsirException(

                "FORBIDDEN",

                "You do not have permission to perform this operation",

                HttpStatus.FORBIDDEN

        );

    }

    public static GsirException unauthorized() {

        return new GsirException(

                "UNAUTHORIZED",

                "Authentication is required",

                HttpStatus.UNAUTHORIZED

        );

    }

    public static GsirException conflict(String message) {

        return new GsirException(

                "CONFLICT",

                message,

                HttpStatus.CONFLICT

        );

    }

    public static GsirException invalid(String message) {

        return new GsirException(

                "INVALID_REQUEST",

                message,

                HttpStatus.BAD_REQUEST

        );

    }

}

## 3.1 Request ID filter

### File

src/main/java/com/gsir/common/web/RequestIdFilter.java

### Code

package com.gsir.common.web;

import jakarta.servlet.FilterChain;

import jakarta.servlet.ServletException;

import jakarta.servlet.http.HttpServletRequest;

import jakarta.servlet.http.HttpServletResponse;

import org.slf4j.MDC;

import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;

import org.springframework.web.filter.OncePerRequestFilter;

import java.io.IOException;

import java.util.UUID;

@Component

public class RequestIdFilter extends OncePerRequestFilter {

    public static final String REQUEST_ID = "requestId";

    @Override

    protected void doFilterInternal(

            HttpServletRequest request,

            HttpServletResponse response,

            FilterChain filterChain

    ) throws ServletException, IOException {

        String requestId = request.getHeader("X-Request-ID");

        if (requestId == null || requestId.isBlank()) {

            requestId = UUID.randomUUID().toString();

        }

        MDC.put(REQUEST_ID, requestId);

        response.setHeader("X-Request-ID", requestId);

        try {

            filterChain.doFilter(request, response);

        } finally {

            MDC.remove(REQUEST_ID);

        }

    }

}

package com.gsir.common.error;

import jakarta.servlet.http.HttpServletRequest;

import org.slf4j.MDC;

import org.springframework.http.HttpStatus;

import org.springframework.http.ResponseEntity;

import org.springframework.web.bind.MethodArgumentNotValidException;

import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.ExceptionHandler;

import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RestControllerAdvice;

import java.time.Instant;

import java.util.List;

@RestControllerAdvice

public class GlobalExceptionHandler {

    @ExceptionHandler(GsirException.class)

    public ResponseEntity<ApiError> handleGsirException(

            GsirException exception

    ) {

        return ResponseEntity

                .status(exception.getStatus())

                .body(error(

                        exception.getCode(),

                        exception.getMessage(),

                        List.of()

                ));

    }

    @ExceptionHandler(MethodArgumentNotValidException.class)

    public ResponseEntity<ApiError> handleValidation(

            MethodArgumentNotValidException exception

    ) {

        List<ApiError.FieldError> fields =

                exception.getBindingResult()

                        .getFieldErrors()

                        .stream()

                        .map(error ->

                                new ApiError.FieldError(

                                        error.getField(),

                                        error.getDefaultMessage()

                                )

                        )

                        .toList();

        return ResponseEntity

                .status(HttpStatus.BAD_REQUEST)

                .body(error(

                        "VALIDATION_ERROR",

                        "Request validation failed",

                        fields

                ));

    }

    @ExceptionHandler(Exception.class)

    public ResponseEntity<ApiError> handleUnexpected(

            Exception exception,

            HttpServletRequest request

    ) {

        return ResponseEntity

                .status(HttpStatus.INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR)

                .body(error(

                        "INTERNAL_ERROR",

                        "An unexpected server error occurred",

                        List.of()

                ));

    }

    private ApiError error(

            String code,

            String message,

            List<ApiError.FieldError> fields

    ) {

        return new ApiError(

                code,

                message,

                MDC.get("requestId"),

                Instant.now(),

                fields

        );

    }

}

# PART 5 — DATABASE FOUNDATION

### Aim of the code

Make PostgreSQL the authoritative transactional database while keeping migrations controlled.

The current GSIR decision is:

PostgreSQL

    ↓

Transactional source of truth

while:

Redis

Object Storage

Search

Vector

Analytics

Queues

serve specialized workloads rather than silently becoming the relational system of record.

The current final MVP design contains the following groups: identity, tenancy, projects, notes/links, conversations, files/documents, AI execution, jobs/outbox, and audit.

JOBS

AUDIT

The current design specifically defers premature research-specific tables such as:

experiments

sources

citations

evidence

knowledge_objects

embeddings

workflow_definitions

memory_items

...

until concrete workflows require them. 

This is important because adding every future table now would make the MVP unnecessarily complex.

### Important note

This is the implementation baseline, not permission to immediately replace the current repository schema blindly.

existing schema
