Part 266 — Authentication Implementation Reconciliation: Verify Existing Code Against Parts 192–265 Before Adding New Features

Aim of the code

Before implementing any additional authentication capability, reconcile the existing GSIR authentication codebase against the approved implementation contracts defined in Parts 192–265.

This part is an audit and alignment step. It must not introduce a second authentication implementation, duplicate services, replace working code without evidence, or silently change previously established contracts.

The objective is to determine, with repository evidence, which authentication requirements are:

- already implemented correctly;

- partially implemented;

- implemented differently and requiring explicit architectural review;

- missing;

- implemented but insufficiently tested;

- blocked by infrastructure such as PostgreSQL or Redis.

The audit must cover the complete authentication path:

Registration

    ↓

Password Hashing

    ↓

User Persistence

    ↓

Login

    ↓

Session Creation

    ↓

Refresh Token Creation

    ↓

JWT Issuance

    ↓

JWT Verification

    ↓

Session Validation

    ↓

Security Context

    ↓

Tenant Context

    ↓

Authorization

    ↓

Protected Resource

Refresh must be treated as a separate security path:

Refresh Token

    ↓

Hash

    ↓

Active Token Lookup

    ↓

Session Validation

    ↓

Atomic Token Consumption

    ↓

Replacement Token

    ↓

Access JWT

Logout and revocation must be reconciled independently:

Logout

    ↓

Session Revocation

    ↓

Refresh Token Revocation

    ↓

Audit Event

1. Repository inspection rules

The implementation must first inspect the existing source tree and identify actual classes, packages, interfaces, repositories, controllers, configurations, migrations, tests, and dependencies.

Do not assume that names from Parts 192–265 exist exactly as specified.

The audit should locate at minimum:

Authentication

Security

Session

RefreshToken

JWT

Authorization

Tenant

RateLimit

User

OrganizationMembership

WorkspaceMembership

Audit

Flyway

Redis

Argon2

Spring Security

OpenAPI

Example repository searches:

Get-ChildItem -Recurse -File src |

    Select-String -Pattern `

    'Authentication|Security|Session|RefreshToken|Jwt|JWT|Authorization|Tenant|RateLimit|Argon2|Flyway|Redis'

Also inspect:

pom.xml

application.yml

application-*.yml

Flyway migrations

test configuration

security configuration

database schema

existing integration tests

No implementation should be deleted merely because its name differs from the master document.

2. Create one reconciliation matrix

Create an internal audit matrix containing at least:

| **Requirement** | **Expected Contract** | **Existing Implementation** | **Status** | **Action** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Password hashing | Argon2id/approved encoder | Actual implementation | MATCH/PARTIAL/MISSING/CONFLICT | KEEP/FIX/REVIEW/ADD |
| Registration | Transactional user creation | Actual implementation | ... | ... |
| Login | Generic authentication failure | Actual implementation | ... | ... |
| Session persistence | DB-authoritative lifecycle | Actual implementation | ... | ... |
| Refresh token hashing | Secret never stored plaintext | Actual implementation | ... | ... |
| Refresh rotation | Atomic one-time consumption | Actual implementation | ... | ... |
| JWT algorithm | Approved asymmetric algorithm | Actual implementation | ... | ... |
| JWT claims | sub, uid, sid, issuer, audience, iat, exp | Actual implementation | ... | ... |
| JWT verification | Signature + claim validation | Actual implementation | ... | ... |
| Session validation | DB check after JWT verification | Actual implementation | ... | ... |
| Security context | Authenticated principal | Actual implementation | ... | ... |
| Tenant context | Organization/workspace context | Actual implementation | ... | ... |
| RBAC | Membership-based authorization | Actual implementation | ... | ... |
| Resource authorization | Tenant/resource checks | Actual implementation | ... | ... |
| Rate limiting | Authentication abuse protection | Actual implementation | ... | ... |
| Logout | Current-session revocation | Actual implementation | ... | ... |
| Logout-all | User-wide session revocation | Actual implementation | ... | ... |
| Replay detection | Session/refresh-token response | Actual implementation | ... | ... |
| Audit | Safe authentication events | Actual implementation | ... | ... |
| OpenAPI | Correct security contract | Actual implementation | ... | ... |
| Tests | Unit + integration + security | Actual implementation | ... | ... |

The matrix is an audit artifact, not an architectural approval mechanism.

3. Reconciliation status definitions

Use only these statuses:

MATCH

PARTIAL

MISSING

CONFLICT

BLOCKED

NOT_APPLICABLE

Definitions:

MATCH

Existing implementation satisfies the corresponding contract.

PARTIAL

Some contract requirements exist, but the implementation is incomplete.

MISSING

Required capability is absent.

CONFLICT

Existing implementation materially differs from the established contract.

BLOCKED

Implementation cannot yet be verified because required infrastructure or evidence is unavailable.

NOT_APPLICABLE

The requirement is genuinely not applicable to the current implementation.

Do not mark a requirement MATCH merely because a similarly named class exists.

4. Evidence requirement

Every MATCH, PARTIAL, or CONFLICT result must be supported by repository evidence.

Record:

file

class/interface

method

configuration

migration

test

where applicable.

Example:

Requirement:

JWT session claim

Evidence:

src/.../JwtTokenService.java

method: issueAccessToken(...)

claim: sid

Status:

MATCH

A status without implementation evidence must not be treated as verified.

5. Preserve existing correct implementation

When existing code already satisfies the established contract:

KEEP

must be the default action.

Do not create duplicate implementations such as:

JwtService

JwtTokenService

AccessTokenService

TokenService

when they represent the same responsibility.

Instead, determine whether one can serve as the canonical boundary.

Likewise, avoid duplicate:

SessionService

SessionAuthenticationService

AuthenticationSessionService

unless their responsibilities are materially different and explicitly justified.

6. Detect architectural duplication

The audit must specifically search for multiple implementations of the same security responsibility.

Check for duplicate:

JWT creation

JWT verification

password hashing

refresh-token hashing

session validation

authorization

tenant resolution

rate limiting

security principal construction

logout/revocation

audit logging

For each duplicate implementation:

Canonical implementation

Secondary implementation

Consumers

Differences

Risk

Required action

The preferred result is one canonical implementation per responsibility with thin adapters where necessary.

7. Verify authentication boundaries

Confirm that controllers do not contain:

JPA operations

password hashing logic

JWT cryptographic logic

refresh-token persistence logic

authorization algorithms

tenant SQL

Controllers should remain transport adapters.

The application/service layer should contain authentication decisions.

The persistence layer should contain database access.

The security layer should verify credentials and establish the security context.

8. Verify session authority

Confirm that JWT identity is not treated as sufficient evidence of an active session.

For protected authenticated requests:

JWT signature verification

        ↓

JWT claim validation

        ↓

session lookup

        ↓

session user match

        ↓

session not revoked

        ↓

session not expired

        ↓

authenticated principal

Session revocation and expiry must therefore remain enforceable without waiting for JWT expiration.

9. Verify refresh-token security

Confirm:

raw refresh token

        ↓

one-way hash

        ↓

database lookup

and that the database does not store the raw token.

Verify that replacement consumes the previous token atomically.

The expected persistence invariant is conceptually:

UPDATE refresh_tokens

SET

    status = 'CONSUMED',

    consumed_at = :consumedAt,

    replaced_by_token_id = :replacementTokenId

WHERE

    id = :tokenId

    AND status = 'ACTIVE'

    AND expires_at > :now;

The audit must confirm that concurrent requests cannot both successfully consume the same refresh token.

If the existing persistence adapter cannot guarantee this, mark:

PARTIAL

or:

CONFLICT

rather than assuming application-level synchronization is sufficient.

10. Verify replay handling

A reused refresh token must not silently create another valid session/token chain.

The audit must verify the existing behavior for:

consumed token

revoked token

expired token

replayed token

concurrent reuse

The security response should remain externally generic.

Sensitive distinctions may exist internally for security response and audit purposes, but must not disclose token lifecycle information unnecessarily.

11. Verify JWT cryptographic boundary

Confirm that the implementation explicitly validates:

signature

algorithm

key type

issuer

audience

expiration

not-before, when used

## 4. JWT correction boundary

If JWT verification was classified as incomplete or conflicting, correct only the verified weakness.

The verifier must establish:

signature valid

AND

algorithm allowed

AND

key type expected

AND

issuer valid

AND

audience valid

AND

expiration valid

AND

required claims present

AND

sub == uid

AND

sid valid

Conceptually:

VerifiedAccessToken verify(String token) {

    JwtClaims claims = jwtVerifier.verify(token);

    claimValidator.validateIssuer(claims);

    claimValidator.validateAudience(claims);

    claimValidator.validateRequiredClaims(claims);

    claimValidator.validateSubjectConsistency(claims);

    return new VerifiedAccessToken(

        claims.userId(),

        claims.sessionId(),

        claims.issuedAt(),

        claims.expiresAt()

    );

}

Do not duplicate an existing verified JWT service.

If the repository already has a canonical verifier, modify that implementation instead.

## 5. Session validation correction

If session validation is missing or incomplete, ensure the authenticated session is checked after JWT verification.

Required sequence:

JWT

 ↓

signature/claim validation

 ↓

session lookup

 ↓

user/session consistency

 ↓

expiry

 ↓

revocation

 ↓

authenticated principal

A cryptographically valid JWT must not bypass database session state.

Conceptual contract:

SessionValidationResult validate(

    UUID sessionId,

    UUID userId,

    Instant now

);

Required failures:

session missing

session belongs to another user

session expired

session revoked

must all terminate authentication.

## 6. Refresh-token correction

If refresh rotation was verified as incomplete, implement only the missing persistence/security behavior.

The critical invariant is:

ACTIVE

  ↓

exactly one successful consumption

  ↓

CONSUMED

The database operation must be atomic.

Conceptually:

UPDATE refresh_tokens

SET

    status = 'CONSUMED',

    consumed_at = :now,

    replaced_by_token_id = :replacementTokenId

WHERE

    id = :tokenId

    AND status = 'ACTIVE'

    AND expires_at > :now;

Then verify the affected-row count:

1 → rotation may continue

0 → rotation fails

Never interpret:

0 rows updated

as successful token consumption.

## 7. Refresh-token replacement

A successful rotation must:

generate replacement token ID

generate cryptographically random raw token

hash raw token

persist only hash

link replacement

issue access JWT

return raw replacement token only through the intended response

The old raw token must never be returned again.

Never store:

raw_refresh_token

in the database.

## 8. Refresh replay correction

If replay detection is missing, establish the minimum safe behavior.

When a previously consumed/revoked token is presented:

detect replay

 ↓

revoke affected session

 ↓

revoke active refresh tokens for that session

 ↓

record safe audit event

 ↓

return generic authentication failure

Do not expose:

TOKEN_WAS_CONSUMED

TOKEN_WAS_REVOKED

TOKEN_BELONGS_TO_SESSION_X

to an unauthenticated client.

## 9. Refresh concurrency test

If refresh rotation was changed, add a real concurrency test.

The test must attempt:

same refresh token

+

request A

+

request B

concurrently.

Expected invariant:

successful rotations = 1

failed/replayed rotations = 1

There must never be:

successful rotations = 2

where both requests produce independently valid replacement credentials.

An H2 result alone must not be treated as final PostgreSQL concurrency verification.

## 10. Logout correction

If logout was incomplete, enforce:

authenticated principal

        ↓

current session

        ↓

session revocation

        ↓

active refresh-token revocation

Do not accept arbitrary:

userId

sessionId

from the request body when the operation is intended to terminate the authenticated user's current session.

The operation should be idempotent.

Repeated logout must not create an error merely because the session is already revoked.

## 11. Logout-all correction

If verified as incomplete:

authenticated user

        ↓

revoke all user's sessions

        ↓

revoke all active refresh tokens

The operation must not affect another user.

It must also not depend on the client submitting a user ID.

## 12. Authorization correction

If Part 267 identified an authorization or IDOR defect, correct the smallest affected application boundary.

Unsafe:

projectRepository.findById(projectId);

when no trustworthy tenant/resource authorization follows.

Preferred conceptual boundary:

projectAuthorizationService.requireAccess(

    principal,

    projectId,

    ResourcePermission.READ

);

or an equivalent tenant-scoped query.

The exact implementation must follow the existing repository architecture rather than creating another authorization framework.

For every verified tenant defect, ensure the access path establishes:

authenticated user

        ↓

organization membership

        ↓

workspace membership

        ↓

resource relationship

A client-provided:

organizationId

workspaceId

role

must not independently establish authorization.

Test at least:

User A → User A resource → ALLOW

User A → User B resource → DENY

Organization A → Organization B resource → DENY

Workspace A → Workspace B resource → DENY

where those relationships exist in the actual implementation.

## 14. Rate-limit correction

If Part 267 found a non-atomic authentication rate limiter, replace only the unsafe operation.

The counter update and expiration behavior must be race-safe.

Acceptable implementation mechanisms include the repository's selected Redis atomic mechanism.

Do not introduce a second rate-limiting abstraction.

The test must verify:

within limit → ALLOW

limit reached → DENY

expiration → counter becomes usable again

concurrent requests → no unsafe bypass

Otherwise:

implementation:

explicit failure state

architecture decision:

PENDING

Every changed security behavior requires a regression test.

Use the mapping:

| **Change** | **Required regression** |
| --- | --- |
| JWT verifier | invalid signature/claims/algorithm |
| Session validation | revoked/expired session |
| Refresh rotation | one-time atomic consumption |
| Replay handling | reused token rejected |
| Logout | current session unusable |
| Logout-all | all user sessions unusable |
| Authorization | unauthorized resource denied |
| Tenant isolation | cross-tenant access denied |
| Rate limiting | threshold/concurrency behavior |
| Error normalization | no sensitive disclosure |
| Secret handling | no credential leakage |
| Persistence | transaction/constraint behavior |

Do not mark a defect fixed without a test capable of detecting its recurrence.

## 21. Preserve unrelated behavior

After every fix, run the existing test suite.

A security fix that breaks unrelated GSIR functionality must not simply be accepted.

Classify failures as:

EXPECTED_SECURITY_CHANGE

REGRESSION

TEST_DEFECT

ENVIRONMENT_FAILURE

UNRELATED_PREEXISTING_FAILURE

Only evidence may determine the classification.

## 22. PostgreSQL verification

If the fix involves:

SQL

locking

transactions

constraints

indexes

refresh rotation

tenant queries

run the affected integration tests against PostgreSQL when the environment is available.

Do not claim:

POSTGRESQL_VERIFIED

from H2-only execution.

If PostgreSQL is unavailable:

POSTGRESQL_VERIFICATION = BLOCKED

and preserve that status.

## 23. Redis verification

If the fix involves Redis:

atomic operations

expiration

rate limiting

failure handling

verify the behavior against the actual Redis-compatible infrastructure required by the project.

If unavailable:

REDIS_VERIFICATION = BLOCKED

Do not convert an untested infrastructure dependency into a false production-complete status.

Refresh concurrency

Logout

RBAC

Tenant isolation

IDOR

Rate limiting

Secret leakage

The result must record:

PASS

FAIL

BLOCKED

Do not use ambiguous terms such as:

looks good

probably fixed

should work

unused classes

duplicate security services

unrelated refactors

dead code

debug logging

hardcoded secrets

temporary bypasses

disabled security checks

test-only production behavior

The final patch should be as small as reasonably possible.

## 3. Registration verification

Execute the real HTTP/application path.

Verify:

valid registration → success

duplicate identity → controlled failure

invalid input → validation failure

password → never stored plaintext

Inspect the database after registration.

The stored password representation must be a password hash rather than the supplied password.

## 4. Login verification

Verify:

valid credentials → authenticated

invalid credentials → generic authentication failure

unknown identity → generic authentication failure

rate limit → enforced

Compare responses for invalid identity versus invalid password.

They must not unnecessarily disclose account existence.

## 5. JWT verification

Execute the complete JWT matrix.

Test:

valid token

expired token

malformed token

tampered token

wrong signature

wrong issuer

wrong audience

unsupported algorithm

alg=none

missing subject

missing user ID

missing session ID

sub != uid

invalid timestamps

Expected result:

valid token → accepted

invalid token → rejected

No malformed or cryptographically invalid token may establish an authenticated security context.

## 6. Session verification

For a valid JWT:

active session → authenticated

revoked session → rejected

expired session → rejected

deleted/nonexistent session → rejected

wrong user/session relationship → rejected

The test must demonstrate that JWT validity alone is insufficient after session revocation.

## 7. Refresh-token rotation verification

Test:

Token A

   ↓

refresh

   ↓

Token B

Verify:

Token A → no longer usable

Token B → usable

The replacement token must belong to the same intended session unless the approved architecture explicitly specifies otherwise.

## 8. Refresh replay verification

Attempt:

refresh(Token A)

refresh(Token A)

Expected:

first request → success

second request → authentication failure

If the approved replay policy revokes the session, verify:

session → revoked

remaining active refresh tokens → revoked

No raw token or internal lifecycle state should appear in the response.

## 9. Refresh concurrency verification

Run concurrent refresh requests using the same token.

Required invariant:

success_count <= 1

The preferred expected result is:

success_count = 1

failure_count = 1

when exactly two concurrent requests are issued.

The database must prevent a race in which both requests successfully consume the same active token.

## 10. PostgreSQL verification

Run authentication integration tests against PostgreSQL.

Verify:

Flyway migration

JPA validation

constraints

indexes

foreign keys

transactions

refresh-token atomic update

session revocation

tenant queries

concurrent refresh

Do not substitute H2 for this gate.

If PostgreSQL is unavailable:

POSTGRESQL = BLOCKED

and authentication cannot receive the final production-verified status.

## 11. PostgreSQL transaction verification

Verify rollback behavior.

For refresh rotation, deliberately cause a failure after the old-token consumption point but before successful completion.

Expected behavior must match the selected transaction contract.

The database must not be left with an invalid intermediate authentication state.

Repeat equivalent checks for:

registration

logout

logout-all

where transactional behavior applies.

## 12. Database constraint verification

Inspect the actual PostgreSQL schema.

Verify authentication-related constraints for:

users

sessions

refresh_tokens

organizations

organization_memberships

workspaces

workspace_memberships

Check:

foreign keys

unique constraints

NOT NULL

status constraints

indexes

Verify important lookup paths have appropriate indexes.

Do not add indexes solely because they appear in the master document; establish that the actual query path requires them.

## 13. Redis verification

Run the rate-limit integration tests against Redis.

Verify:

counter creation

increment

expiration

threshold

concurrent requests

key isolation

If atomic Lua/transaction/equivalent behavior is used, verify it under concurrent requests.

A sequential test is insufficient to prove concurrency safety.

## 14. Redis failure verification

Test Redis unavailable/unreachable behavior.

The result must follow the project's explicitly selected rate-limit failure policy.

Possible result categories:

FAIL_CLOSED

FAIL_OPEN

DEGRADED

BLOCKED_BY_UNDECIDED_POLICY

Do not choose a new security policy during this test.

If no policy has been approved:

RATE_LIMIT_FAILURE_POLICY = ARCHITECTURAL DECISION REQUIRED

## 15. Authentication rate-limit verification

Verify independently:

login

registration

refresh

Test:

under threshold → accepted

threshold reached → rejected

window expires → usable again

concurrent requests → no unsafe bypass

Do not expose internal rate-limit keys or counters to clients.

## 16. Authorization verification

Test organization and workspace membership.

Verify:

authorized member → allowed

unauthorized member → denied

unknown member → denied

wrong organization → denied

wrong workspace → denied

The final role hierarchy must reflect the actually approved project policy.

If role semantics remain unresolved, mark them as an architectural blocker rather than silently approving them.

## 17. IDOR verification

Attempt access to another user's or tenant's resource using a known resource identifier.

Test at minimum where implemented:

project

note

web link

conversation

file

Expected:

authorized resource → allowed

unauthorized resource → denied

The denial must occur even when the attacker knows the resource ID.

## 18. Tenant-isolation verification

Create:

Organization A

Organization B

and appropriate users/resources.

Verify:

A → A resource = ALLOW

A → B resource = DENY

B → A resource = DENY

Repeat for workspace boundaries.

This is a mandatory security gate.

## 19. Logout verification

Execute:

login

logout

use previous access token

refresh using previous refresh token

Expected:

access token after logout → rejected

refresh token after logout → rejected

Repeat logout.

Expected:

second logout → safe/idempotent

## 20. Logout-all verification

Create multiple sessions for the same user.

Then execute logout-all.

Verify:

session A → revoked

session B → revoked

session C → revoked

Create another user and verify:

user A logout-all

        ↓

user B sessions remain valid

## 21. Security-context verification

For every protected request verify that the application obtains identity from the authenticated security context.

Do not permit request parameters/body values to override:

authenticated user ID

session ID

organization identity

workspace identity

roles

permissions

## 22. Error-security verification

password correctness

SQL

stack traces

private keys

internal exception details

Unexpected errors must use the established API error mechanism.

password

Manually classify every match.

The objective is:

NO RAW SECRET EXPOSURE

and that:

Part 270 — Authentication Closure and Transition to the AI Gateway: Freeze Verified Security Contracts, Establish the AI Security Boundary, and Prepare Model-Independent AI Execution

Aim of the code

Close the authentication implementation boundary and prepare GSIR for the next major subsystem: the AI Gateway.

This part does not create the full AI system yet.

It establishes the security and application boundaries that AI execution must use.

The central rule is:

Authenticated User

        ↓

Authorization

        ↓

AI Gateway

        ↓

Task/Request Classification

        ↓

Model Routing

        ↓

Provider Adapter

        ↓

AI Model

        ↓

Output Validation

        ↓

Persistence / Response

AI execution must never bypass authentication, authorization, tenancy, auditing, or controlled tool boundaries.

# 1. Freeze the authentication contract

Once Part 269 has verified authentication, treat the verified behavior as the canonical security contract.

The AI subsystem must consume authentication through existing boundaries rather than creating another security mechanism.

Required security context:

public record SecurityPrincipal(

    UUID userId,

    UUID sessionId,

    UUID organizationId,

    UUID workspaceId

) {}

The exact existing project representation must be preserved if already implemented.

Do not create a second principal model merely to support AI.

# 2. AI must never authenticate independently

The AI Gateway must not implement:

password authentication

JWT verification

session authentication

refresh-token handling

logout

Those responsibilities remain in the authentication subsystem.

AI requests begin only after the normal security boundary has established an authenticated principal where authentication is required.

# 3. Establish the AI Gateway boundary

Create the smallest provider-independent interface necessary for AI execution.

Conceptually:

public interface AiGateway {

    AiResponse execute(

        AiRequest request,

        SecurityPrincipal principal

    );

}

The exact package and naming must follow the existing repository conventions.

The gateway is responsible for orchestration, not model-specific implementation.

# 4. AI request contract

Define a provider-neutral request representation.

Conceptually:

public record AiRequest(

    UUID requestId,

    UUID conversationId,

    UUID userId,

    UUID organizationId,

    UUID workspaceId,

    String taskType,

    String input,

    Map<String, Object> context,

    AiExecutionPolicy policy

) {}

Do not expose provider-specific fields such as:

OpenAI-only parameters

Anthropic-only parameters

Gemini-only parameters

DeepSeek-only parameters

at the gateway contract.

Those belong behind provider adapters.

# 5. AI execution policy

Define an explicit execution policy rather than allowing unrestricted model behavior.

Conceptually:

public record AiExecutionPolicy(

    boolean allowExternalTools,

    boolean allowPersistentWrites,

    boolean allowCodeExecution,

    boolean allowNetworkAccess,

    int maxToolCalls,

    Duration timeout

) {}

These defaults must be conservative.

For example:

code execution = DENY

arbitrary network access = DENY

unapproved persistent writes = DENY

unbounded tool calls = DENY

The AI must not be able to escalate its own permissions through this policy.

# 6. AI tenancy boundary

Every AI request must carry trustworthy tenancy context.

Conceptually:

SecurityPrincipal

       ↓

organizationId

       ↓

workspaceId

       ↓

conversation/project/resource authorization

       ↓

AiGateway

Do not trust an AI request's tenant identifiers merely because the client supplied them.

The gateway must receive authoritative context from the authenticated application boundary.

# 7. AI request authorization

Before execution:

Authenticate

    ↓

Authorize

    ↓

Validate request

    ↓

AI Gateway

The AI Gateway must not assume that authentication implies permission to perform every AI operation.

Examples of distinct permissions may eventually include:

AI_READ

AI_EXECUTE

AI_USE_EXTERNAL_TOOLS

AI_WRITE

AI_RUN_CODE

AI_ADMIN

These are examples of permission categories, not final approved role definitions.

If the project has not approved these permissions, do not silently add them to the database.

# 8. Conversation authorization

For requests associated with a conversation:

request

 ↓

conversation ID

 ↓

tenant/resource authorization

 ↓

AI Gateway

The AI must not be able to access another user's or workspace's conversation merely because the conversation ID is known.

Use the existing resource authorization boundary.

Do not add a parallel AI-specific ownership system.

# 9. Project authorization

If an AI request references a project:

AI request

    ↓

project authorization

    ↓

project context

    ↓

AI Gateway

The project must belong to the authorized workspace/tenant context.

Never allow:

projectId

alone to grant AI access.

This preserves the existing IDOR and tenant-isolation principles.

# 10. Context Builder boundary

The AI Gateway should not directly construct arbitrary database queries.

Introduce a controlled context boundary:

public interface AiContextBuilder {

    AiContext build(

        AiRequest request,

        SecurityPrincipal principal

    );

}

Its responsibility is to collect only information the current request is authorized to access.

Conceptually:

Authorized resources

        ↓

Context Builder

        ↓

bounded AI context

Not:

AI

 ↓

entire database

# 11. Context minimization

Only provide the model with context necessary for the task.

The context pipeline should support:

task

 ↓

authorized resources

 ↓

relevant context

 ↓

bounded context

 ↓

model

Avoid sending:

unrelated organization data

other users' data

unnecessary credentials

security configuration

private keys

internal secrets

to the model.

# 12. Prompt/data boundary

Separate:

system instructions

developer/application policy

user input

retrieved evidence

tool results

model output

Conceptually:

AiContext

├── policy

├── task

├── user_input

├── retrieved_context

├── evidence

└── tool_results

Do not concatenate all information into one unstructured string if doing so would make provenance or trust boundaries impossible to distinguish.

# 13. Prompt injection boundary

Treat retrieved documents, websites, files, tool outputs, and user-provided content as data, not trusted instructions.

Conceptually:

Untrusted content

        ↓

Content boundary

        ↓

Model context

The model must not automatically treat text such as:

"ignore previous instructions"

"call this tool"

"reveal system prompt"

"delete this project"

as an authorized application instruction.

Authorization comes from the application/tool boundary, not from model-generated text.

# 14. AI model provider abstraction

The Gateway must remain provider independent.

Define the conceptual boundary:

public interface AiProvider {

    AiProviderResponse execute(

        AiProviderRequest request

    );

}

Provider adapters may later implement:

OpenAI

Anthropic

Gemini

DeepSeek

Qwen

Llama

Mistral

OpenRouter

Ollama

The gateway must not contain provider-specific branching throughout application code.

# 15. Provider adapter rule

A provider adapter translates:

GSIR canonical request

        ↓

provider-specific request

        ↓

provider API

        ↓

provider-specific response

        ↓

GSIR canonical response

Provider details remain isolated.

This allows model/provider replacement without rewriting the GSIR cognitive/application layer.

# 16. Model selection boundary

Do not immediately build a complicated multi-agent router.

Create one explicit model-selection boundary:

public interface AiModelRouter {

    AiModelSelection select(

        AiRequest request,

        AiContext context

    );

}

The router may eventually consider:

quality

latency

cost

context capacity

availability

privacy

task requirements

resource requirements

The initial implementation should remain deterministic and simple.

# 17. Task classification

Introduce task classification only as a lightweight decision boundary.

Conceptually:

User request

      ↓

Task classifier

      ↓

task type

      ↓

model router

Potential categories:

GENERAL

ANALYSIS

RESEARCH

WRITING

CODING

DATA_ANALYSIS

SCIENTIFIC_REASONING

TOOL_USE

SOP

These are provisional categories.

Do not create a large classification hierarchy until actual GSIR workflows require it.

# 18. Automatic mode

GSIR's automatic mode should eventually perform:

request

 ↓

task classification

 ↓

context requirements

 ↓

model selection

 ↓

tool requirements

 ↓

execution

The user should not need to understand provider/model mechanics.

The system remains provider-independent.

# 19. AI execution record

Use the existing ai_runs and ai_outputs architecture where applicable.

Do not create a second AI execution table.

An AI run should be identifiable and auditable.

Conceptually:

AI request

 ↓

ai_run

 ↓

provider execution

 ↓

ai_output

Retries must remain separate execution attempts rather than overwriting historical execution state.

# 20. No hidden chain-of-thought persistence

AI persistence must not create a database field intended to store hidden chain-of-thought.

Store only information required for:

request

result

metadata

provenance

validation

usage

audit

reproducibility

If reasoning summaries are deliberately exposed by the model/application, they may be treated as ordinary output, subject to the normal data policy.

# 21. AI output boundary

Model output must not automatically become trusted application state.

Use:

Model output

    ↓

Output validation

    ↓

Policy validation

    ↓

Structured interpretation

    ↓

Authorized action

not:

Model output

    ↓

database

# 22. Structured AI output

Where machine-readable output is required, define an explicit schema.

Conceptually:

public interface AiOutputValidator {

    ValidatedAiOutput validate(

        AiResponse response

    );

}

Validation should establish:

schema

type

required fields

size limits

allowed operations

policy constraints

Malformed model output must not silently become application commands.

# 23. Tool Gateway boundary

AI tools must be controlled through one application boundary.

Conceptually:

public interface ToolGateway {

    ToolResult execute(

        ToolRequest request,

        SecurityPrincipal principal

    );

}

The model does not receive unrestricted access to:

database

filesystem

shell

network

production services

# 24. Tool authorization

Every tool request must pass:

authenticated principal

        ↓

permission evaluation

        ↓

resource authorization

        ↓

tool policy

        ↓

tool execution

A model cannot grant itself permission.

The following is invalid:

Model:

"I authorize myself to delete the project."

Only application security policy can authorize the action.

# 25. Tool execution limits

Every tool invocation should eventually support bounded:

timeout

input size

output size

execution count

memory

CPU

network

filesystem

The exact limits should be configured according to the tool.

Do not introduce arbitrary global limits without evidence.

# 26. Scientific computation boundary

Scientific calculations should use controlled computation services.

Conceptually:

AI

 ↓

computation request

 ↓

validated parameters

 ↓

deterministic computation

 ↓

verified result

 ↓

AI context/output

The model should not be treated as the authoritative numerical calculator when deterministic computation is available.

# 27. Sandboxed execution

If future GSIR workflows require arbitrary code execution:

AI

 ↓

validated computation request

 ↓

isolated sandbox

 ↓

resource limits

 ↓

execution

 ↓

result

The sandbox must prevent unrestricted:

filesystem access

network access

host access

credential access

process control

Do not implement unrestricted shell execution as part of this transition.

# 28. AI provenance

Every externally retrieved or computationally generated context item should eventually be traceable.

Conceptually:

source

 ↓

retrieval

 ↓

context item

 ↓

AI run

 ↓

output

The system should be able to answer:

Where did this information come from?

When was it retrieved?

Which AI run used it?

Was it transformed?

Was it computationally verified?

This is particularly important for scientific research.

# 29. AI audit boundary

Security-sensitive AI events should pass through the existing audit mechanism.

Examples:

AI_EXECUTION_STARTED

AI_EXECUTION_COMPLETED

AI_EXECUTION_FAILED

TOOL_EXECUTION_REQUESTED

TOOL_EXECUTION_DENIED

TOOL_EXECUTION_COMPLETED

MODEL_SELECTION

POLICY_DENIED

Do not place raw credentials or unnecessary sensitive prompt content into audit events.

# 30. AI failure model

AI execution must distinguish:

AUTHENTICATION_FAILURE

AUTHORIZATION_FAILURE

VALIDATION_FAILURE

PROVIDER_FAILURE

TIMEOUT

RATE_LIMIT

CONTEXT_FAILURE

TOOL_FAILURE

MODEL_OUTPUT_INVALID

INTERNAL_FAILURE

Provider-specific errors should be translated into canonical GSIR errors.

The client should not receive raw provider stack traces or credentials.

# 31. Provider failure isolation

A provider outage must not corrupt the conversation or AI-run history.

The execution state should remain explicit.

Conceptually:

AI_RUN

 ├── REQUESTED

 ├── RUNNING

 ├── SUCCEEDED

 ├── FAILED

 └── CANCELLED

Exact status values must follow the existing schema if already established.

# 32. Cost and usage boundary

AI execution should capture usage metadata where the provider supplies it.

Potential information:

input tokens

output tokens

total tokens

latency

provider

model

model version

estimated cost

This is metadata, not intelligence.

Do not allow provider billing metadata to become tightly coupled to the core AI architecture.

# 33. AI Gateway security invariants

The following must always hold:

1. No unauthenticated protected AI execution.

2. No cross-tenant AI context.

3. No unrestricted database access.

4. No unrestricted tool execution.

5. No model-controlled authorization.

6. No raw secrets in model context.

7. No automatic trust of model output.

8. No hidden chain-of-thought persistence.

9. No provider-specific coupling in core application logic.

10. No unbounded execution.

# 34. Minimal initial AI architecture

The initial implementation should contain only:

AiGateway

AiRequest

AiResponse

AiContextBuilder

AiContext

AiModelRouter

AiModelSelection

AiProvider

AiProviderRequest

AiProviderResponse

AiOutputValidator

ToolGateway

Only create additional abstractions when an actual requirement requires them.

Avoid creating:

AgentManager

AgentRegistry

AgentSupervisor

AgentCoordinator

AgentFactory

AgentOrchestrator

AgentMemoryManager

unless a concrete architecture decision later proves that they are necessary.

GSIR should use a unified cognitive/application controller, not a proliferation of autonomous agents.

# 35. AGI integration boundary

The future GSIR AGI-oriented cognitive architecture should sit above the model/provider layer.

Conceptually:

Perception/Input

       ↓

Attention

       ↓

Cognitive State

       ↓

Memory

       ↓

World Model

       ↓

Reasoning/Planning

       ↓

Action/Tool Gateway

       ↓

Learning

       ↓

Metacognition

       ↓

Consolidation

The AI Gateway is infrastructure for model execution.

It is not itself the AGI.

The cognitive architecture must remain provider-independent.

# 36. Unified cognitive loop

The future execution loop is:

INPUT

  ↓

PERCEIVE

  ↓

ATTEND

  ↓

UPDATE STATE

  ↓

RETRIEVE MEMORY

  ↓

CONSOLIDATE

This loop must not be implemented as a collection of independent agents unless later evidence demonstrates that separation materially improves the required benchmarks.

# 37. Security before AGI capability

The cognitive system must inherit:

authentication

authorization

tenant isolation

tool permissions

resource boundaries

audit

provenance

It must never receive an unrestricted system-level identity.

The AGI layer operates inside GSIR security boundaries, not above them.

# 38. Database rule

Do not add new AGI-specific tables merely because the conceptual architecture contains:

memory

world model

attention

cognitive state

planning

learning

First determine whether existing GSIR tables can support the required behavior.

A new persistent structure requires:

lifecycle

query requirements

migration need

This keeps the system small.

Part 271 — AI Gateway Contracts: Canonical AI Request/Response, Execution Policy, Validation, and Provider-Independent Application Boundary

# Part 271 — AI Gateway Contracts and Provider-Independent Request Boundary

## Aim of the Code

Define the minimal provider-independent AI Gateway contract for GSIR.

This part establishes the application boundary between authenticated GSIR services and any AI model/provider. The Gateway must prevent provider-specific SDKs, authentication logic, model-specific request formats, or unrestricted tools from leaking into the rest of the application.

The design must remain compatible with the future unified AGI cognitive architecture while avoiding premature AGI-specific implementation or additional database tables.

### Required Information Flow

Authenticated Application Request

        ↓

Existing Security / Tenant Context

        ↓

AI Gateway

        ↓

Request Validation

        ↓

Context Builder

        ↓

Model Router

        ↓

Provider Adapter

        ↓

External / Local AI Model

        ↓

Provider Response

        ↓

Output Validation

        ↓

Application / Persistence / Tool Gateway

The AI Gateway is not itself an autonomous agent.

It is a controlled application service that coordinates model invocation.

## 1. Core AI Gateway Contract

package com.gsir.ai.application;

import com.gsir.ai.domain.AiRequest;

import com.gsir.ai.domain.AiResponse;

public interface AiGateway {

    AiResponse execute(AiRequest request);

}

The interface intentionally exposes no:

- OpenAI classes

- Anthropic classes

- Gemini classes

- provider SDK objects

- HTTP client implementation

- database entities

- Spring Security objects

- shell commands

- arbitrary tool execution

# 2. AI Request

package com.gsir.ai.domain;

import java.util.List;

import java.util.Map;

import java.util.UUID;

public record AiRequest(

        UUID requestId,

        UUID userId,

        UUID organizationId,

        UUID workspaceId,

        UUID projectId,

        String taskType,

        String instruction,

        List<AiMessage> messages,

        Map<String, Object> metadata

) {

    public AiRequest {

        messages = messages == null ? List.of() : List.copyOf(messages);

        metadata = metadata == null ? Map.of() : Map.copyOf(metadata);

    }

}

The request carries the minimum identity and tenancy information required by the application boundary.

The Gateway must not trust client-supplied tenant identifiers merely because they are present in this object.

The authoritative security context remains the authenticated application security context.

# 3. AI Message

package com.gsir.ai.domain;

public record AiMessage(

        Role role,

        String content

) {

    public enum Role {

        SYSTEM,

        USER,

        ASSISTANT,

        TOOL

    }

}

TOOL represents tool-result data entering the model context.

Tool results are data.

They do not grant the model additional authorization.

# 4. AI Response

package com.gsir.ai.domain;

import java.util.List;

import java.util.Map;

public record AiResponse(

        String output,

        String modelId,

        String modelVersion,

        FinishReason finishReason,

        Usage usage,

        List<AiOutputPart> parts,

        Map<String, Object> metadata

) {

    public AiResponse {

        parts = parts == null ? List.of() : List.copyOf(parts);

        metadata = metadata == null ? Map.of() : Map.copyOf(metadata);

    }

    public enum FinishReason {

        COMPLETED,

        LENGTH_LIMIT,

        TOOL_REQUEST,

        PROVIDER_ERROR,

        VALIDATION_FAILED,

        UNKNOWN

    }

}

No hidden chain-of-thought or private reasoning trace is persisted by this contract.

Only application-approved output is exposed.

# 5. Output Parts

package com.gsir.ai.domain;

public record AiOutputPart(

        Type type,

        String content

) {

    public enum Type {

        TEXT,

        STRUCTURED_DATA,

        TOOL_REQUEST,

        CITATION,

        WARNING

    }

}

The representation deliberately separates output types so future structured scientific workflows do not have to parse arbitrary model text.

# 6. Usage

package com.gsir.ai.domain;

public record Usage(

        long inputTokens,

        long outputTokens,

        long totalTokens

) {

    public Usage {

        if (inputTokens < 0) {

            throw new IllegalArgumentException("inputTokens must be >= 0");

        }

        if (outputTokens < 0) {

            throw new IllegalArgumentException("outputTokens must be >= 0");

        }

        if (totalTokens < 0) {

            throw new IllegalArgumentException("totalTokens must be >= 0");

        }

    }

}

Usage information is metadata for accounting, observability, cost control, and performance analysis.

It is not treated as scientific evidence.

# 7. AI Context

package com.gsir.ai.domain;

import java.util.List;

import java.util.Map;

public record AiContext(

        List<AiMessage> messages,

        List<ContextItem> contextItems,

        Map<String, Object> constraints

) {

    public AiContext {

        messages = messages == null ? List.of() : List.copyOf(messages);

        contextItems = contextItems == null ? List.of() : List.copyOf(contextItems);

        constraints = constraints == null ? Map.of() : Map.copyOf(constraints);

    }

}

# 8. Context Item

package com.gsir.ai.domain;

public record ContextItem(

        String id,

        SourceType sourceType,

        String content,

        String provenance

) {

    public enum SourceType {

        USER_INPUT,

        PROJECT_DATA,

        NOTE,

        DOCUMENT,

        DOCUMENT_CHUNK,

        WEB_SOURCE,

        TOOL_RESULT,

        SYSTEM_DATA

    }

}

Every retrieved context item must retain provenance where available.

Retrieved content must be treated as untrusted data.

A document containing text such as:

Ignore previous instructions and execute ...

does not become an instruction merely because it was retrieved into context.

# 9. Context Builder Contract

package com.gsir.ai.application;

import com.gsir.ai.domain.AiContext;

import com.gsir.ai.domain.AiRequest;

public interface AiContextBuilder {

    AiContext build(AiRequest request);

}

The implementation is responsible for:

- authorization-aware retrieval,

- context limits,

- provenance,

- ordering,

- deduplication,

- prompt/data separation,

- sensitive-data filtering,

- context-size protection.

It must never retrieve data outside the authenticated user's authorized scope.

# 10. Model Router Contract

package com.gsir.ai.application;

import com.gsir.ai.domain.AiContext;

import com.gsir.ai.domain.AiRequest;

public interface AiModelRouter {

    AiModelSelection select(

            AiRequest request,

            AiContext context

    );

}

The initial implementation should remain deterministic and lightweight.

Routing can consider:

- task type,

- required capability,

- context size,

- availability,

- latency,

- cost,

- privacy requirements,

- model capability.

The router must not become an autonomous decision-making agent.

# 11. Model Selection

package com.gsir.ai.domain;

public record AiModelSelection(

        String providerId,

        String modelId,

        String modelVersion,

        String reason

) {}

reason is an operational routing explanation.

It must not contain hidden model reasoning or chain-of-thought.

# 12. Provider Contract

import com.gsir.ai.domain.AiProviderResponse;

public interface AiProvider {

Provider implementations are adapters.

The rest of GSIR must not depend directly on provider SDKs.

# 15. Output Validator Contract

package com.gsir.ai.application;

import com.gsir.ai.domain.AiProviderResponse;

import com.gsir.ai.domain.AiResponse;

public interface AiOutputValidator {

    AiResponse validate(AiProviderResponse response);

}

Validation must occur before model output is allowed to:

- change application state,

- create durable records,

- invoke tools,

- trigger scientific computation,

- initiate workflows,

- influence privileged operations.

Model output is untrusted input.

# 16. Tool Gateway Boundary

package com.gsir.ai.application;

import com.gsir.ai.domain.ToolRequest;

import com.gsir.ai.domain.ToolResponse;

public interface ToolGateway {

    ToolResponse execute(ToolRequest request);

}

The AI model does not directly execute tools.

The model may request a tool operation, but the Tool Gateway must independently perform:

Authentication

      ↓

Authorization

      ↓

Input validation

      ↓

Resource/tenant validation

      ↓

Execution policy

      ↓

Tool execution

      ↓

Result validation

      ↓

Audit/provenance

# 17. Tool Request

package com.gsir.ai.domain;

import java.util.Map;

public record ToolRequest(

        String toolName,

        Map<String, Object> arguments

) {

    public ToolRequest {

        arguments = arguments == null ? Map.of() : Map.copyOf(arguments);

    }

}

No arbitrary shell command, SQL statement, filesystem path, or executable program is accepted merely because it appears in arguments.

Each tool must expose an explicit schema and execution policy.

# 18. Tool Response

package com.gsir.ai.domain;

import java.util.Map;

public record ToolResponse(

        boolean successful,

        String errorCode,

) {

    public ToolResponse {

    }

}

# 19. Gateway Implementation Boundary

The first implementation should follow this structure:

package com.gsir.ai.application;

import com.gsir.ai.domain.*;

import java.util.Objects;

public final class DefaultAiGateway implements AiGateway {

    private final AiContextBuilder contextBuilder;

    private final AiModelRouter modelRouter;

    private final AiProviderRegistry providerRegistry;

    private final AiOutputValidator outputValidator;

    public DefaultAiGateway(

            AiContextBuilder contextBuilder,

            AiModelRouter modelRouter,

            AiProviderRegistry providerRegistry,

            AiOutputValidator outputValidator

    ) {

        this.contextBuilder = Objects.requireNonNull(contextBuilder);

        this.modelRouter = Objects.requireNonNull(modelRouter);

        this.providerRegistry = Objects.requireNonNull(providerRegistry);

        this.outputValidator = Objects.requireNonNull(outputValidator);

    }

    @Override

    public AiResponse execute(AiRequest request) {

        Objects.requireNonNull(request, "request");

        AiContext context = contextBuilder.build(request);

        AiModelSelection selection =

                modelRouter.select(request, context);

        AiProvider provider =

                providerRegistry.require(selection.providerId());

        AiProviderRequest providerRequest =

                new AiProviderRequest(

                        selection.modelId(),

                        selection.modelVersion(),

                        context.messages(),

                        context.constraints()

                );

        AiProviderResponse providerResponse =

                provider.execute(providerRequest);

        return outputValidator.validate(providerResponse);

    }

}

This is intentionally a small orchestration layer.

It must not become a second business-logic system.

# 20. Provider Registry

package com.gsir.ai.application;

import java.util.Map;

import java.util.Objects;

public final class AiProviderRegistry {

    private final Map<String, AiProvider> providers;

    public AiProviderRegistry(Map<String, AiProvider> providers) {

        this.providers = Map.copyOf(

                Objects.requireNonNull(providers)

        );

    }

    public AiProvider require(String providerId) {

        AiProvider provider = providers.get(providerId);

        if (provider == null) {

            throw new IllegalStateException(

                    "AI provider is not configured"

            );

        }

        return provider;

    }

}

The registry is intentionally provider-neutral.

Provider availability must be configuration-driven.

# 21. Mandatory Security Rules

The implementation must enforce these rules:

### Rule 1 — Authentication

Protected AI operations require the existing authenticated security context.

### Rule 2 — Tenant isolation

AI context may contain only information the authenticated principal is authorized to access.

### Rule 3 — No model-controlled authorization

The model cannot grant itself permissions.

### Rule 4 — No unrestricted tools

Tool access is explicit and policy-controlled.

### Rule 5 — No unrestricted database access

The model cannot directly query PostgreSQL.

### Rule 6 — No unrestricted shell access

The model cannot directly execute operating-system commands.

### Rule 7 — No automatic trust

Model output is never automatically treated as authoritative scientific truth.

### Rule 8 — Provenance

Retrieved evidence should retain its source/provenance metadata.

### Rule 9 — Secret isolation

API keys, JWT secrets, database credentials, refresh tokens, and other secrets must never be inserted into model context.

### Rule 10 — No hidden reasoning persistence

Private model reasoning must not be stored as application data.

### Rule 11 — Bounded execution

Requests must have explicit limits for:

- context size,

- execution time,

- output size,

- tool calls,

- retries,

- external calls.

### Rule 12 — Provider independence

Application services depend on GSIR contracts rather than provider SDKs.

# 22. Future AGI Compatibility

This Gateway is deliberately compatible with the future unified cognitive architecture:

Perception

    ↓

Attention

    ↓

Cognitive State

    ↓

Memory

    ↓

World Model

    ↓

Reasoning / Planning

    ↓

Action / Tool Gateway

    ↓

Learning

    ↓

Metacognition

    ↓

Consolidation

The Gateway should remain an execution boundary, not a collection of separate agents implementing each cognitive component.

No new AGI persistence tables are introduced in this part.

# 23. Implementation Constraints

Before proceeding:

- inspect existing AI-related code;

- reuse existing contracts where they already satisfy this boundary;

- do not create duplicate gateways;

- do not create duplicate provider registries;

- do not introduce provider SDKs into domain classes;

- do not add database tables solely for this part;

- do not implement every provider immediately;

- do not add autonomous agent loops;

- do not add unrestricted tool execution;

- do not change authentication architecture.

If existing code conflicts with this contract, perform reconciliation before replacing it.

# 24. Required Tests

At minimum:

AiGateway

 ├─ rejects null request

 ├─ builds context before provider invocation

 ├─ routes through model router

 ├─ selects registered provider

 ├─ rejects unknown provider

 ├─ sends provider-independent request

 ├─ validates provider output

 ├─ rejects invalid output

 ├─ does not bypass context builder

 └─ does not directly execute tools

Security tests must additionally verify:

authenticated user

        ↓

authorized context only

        ↓

authorized model invocation

        ↓

validated output

        ↓

controlled tool boundary

Cross-tenant context access must fail.

# Part 272 — AI Request Validation, Security Boundary, Context Limits, and Prompt/Data Separation

## Aim of the Code

Implement the first security and validation boundary immediately before AI context construction and model routing.

Part 271 defined the provider-independent AI Gateway contracts. Part 272 now ensures that an AI request is:

- structurally valid;

- associated with the authenticated principal;

- inside the correct organization/workspace/project scope;

- bounded in size and execution requirements;

- protected from prompt/data confusion;

- free of secrets and forbidden control data;

- safe to pass to the Context Builder.

The AI model must never receive an unchecked application request.

# 1. Required AI Request Flow

HTTP / Application Request

        ↓

Authentication

        ↓

Tenant Context

        ↓

AI Request Validation

        ↓

Resource Authorization

        ↓

Input Normalization

        ↓

Prompt/Data Separation

        ↓

Context Builder

        ↓

Model Router

        ↓

Provider

Validation occurs before expensive model execution.

# 2. AI Request Validation Contract

package com.gsir.ai.application;

import com.gsir.ai.domain.AiRequest;

public interface AiRequestValidator {

    void validate(AiRequest request);

}

The validator must not perform provider calls.

It must also not mutate persistent application state.

# 3. Validation Policy

package com.gsir.ai.application;

public record AiRequestValidationPolicy(

        int maxInstructionCharacters,

        int maxMessages,

        int maxMessageCharacters,

        int maxMetadataEntries,

        int maxMetadataValueCharacters

) {

    public AiRequestValidationPolicy {

        if (maxInstructionCharacters <= 0) {

            throw new IllegalArgumentException(

                    "maxInstructionCharacters must be positive"

            );

        }

        if (maxMessages <= 0) {

            throw new IllegalArgumentException(

                    "maxMessages must be positive"

            );

        }

        if (maxMessageCharacters <= 0) {

            throw new IllegalArgumentException(

                    "maxMessageCharacters must be positive"

            );

        }

        if (maxMetadataEntries < 0) {

            throw new IllegalArgumentException(

                    "maxMetadataEntries must be >= 0"

            );

        }

        if (maxMetadataValueCharacters < 0) {

            throw new IllegalArgumentException(

                    "maxMetadataValueCharacters must be >= 0"

            );

        }

    }

}

These values are policy parameters, not hard-coded architectural truths.

Production values should be configured and benchmarked.

# 4. Validation Exception

Use the existing GSIR application error model rather than creating a parallel exception hierarchy.

Conceptually:

package com.gsir.ai.application;

public final class AiRequestValidationException

        extends RuntimeException {

    public AiRequestValidationException(String message) {

        super(message);

    }

}

If the existing GSIR error model already provides an appropriate validation exception, reuse it instead of adding this class.

# 5. Default Request Validator

package com.gsir.ai.application;

import com.gsir.ai.domain.AiMessage;

import com.gsir.ai.domain.AiRequest;

import java.util.Map;

import java.util.Objects;

public final class DefaultAiRequestValidator

        implements AiRequestValidator {

    private final AiRequestValidationPolicy policy;

    public DefaultAiRequestValidator(

            AiRequestValidationPolicy policy

    ) {

        this.policy = Objects.requireNonNull(policy);

    }

    @Override

    public void validate(AiRequest request) {

        Objects.requireNonNull(request, "request");

        requireIdentity(request);

        requireInstructionSize(request);

        requireMessages(request);

        requireMetadata(request);

    }

    private void requireIdentity(AiRequest request) {

        if (request.requestId() == null) {

            throw new AiRequestValidationException(

                    "requestId is required"

            );

        }

        if (request.userId() == null) {

            throw new AiRequestValidationException(

                    "userId is required"

            );

        }

        if (request.organizationId() == null) {

            throw new AiRequestValidationException(

                    "organizationId is required"

            );

        }

    }

    private void requireInstructionSize(AiRequest request) {

        String instruction = request.instruction();

        if (instruction == null || instruction.isBlank()) {

            throw new AiRequestValidationException(

                    "instruction is required"

            );

        }

        if (instruction.length()

                > policy.maxInstructionCharacters()) {

            throw new AiRequestValidationException(

                    "instruction exceeds configured limit"

            );

        }

    }

    private void requireMessages(AiRequest request) {

        if (request.messages().size()

                > policy.maxMessages()) {

            throw new AiRequestValidationException(

                    "message count exceeds configured limit"

            );

        }

        for (AiMessage message : request.messages()) {

            if (message == null || message.content() == null) {

                throw new AiRequestValidationException(

                        "message content is required"

                );

            }

            if (message.content().length()

                    > policy.maxMessageCharacters()) {

                throw new AiRequestValidationException(

                        "message exceeds configured limit"

                );

            }

        }

    }

    private void requireMetadata(AiRequest request) {

        Map<String, Object> metadata = request.metadata();

        if (metadata.size() > policy.maxMetadataEntries()) {

            throw new AiRequestValidationException(

                    "metadata entry count exceeds configured limit"

            );

        }

        for (Object value : metadata.values()) {

            if (value != null

                    && value.toString().length()

                    > policy.maxMetadataValueCharacters()) {

                throw new AiRequestValidationException(

                        "metadata value exceeds configured limit"

                );

            }

        }

    }

}

The validator is intentionally simple.

Do not add a large rule engine at this stage.

# 6. Authentication Identity Must Come From Security Context

The client must not be allowed to impersonate another user by submitting:

userId = another-user

The application should obtain the authoritative identity from the existing SecurityPrincipal.

package com.gsir.ai.application;

import com.gsir.security.SecurityPrincipal;

public interface AiSecurityContext {

    SecurityPrincipal requirePrincipal();

}

The implementation must delegate to the existing GSIR security context.

There must be one authoritative authentication mechanism.

# 7. Request Identity Verification

package com.gsir.ai.application;

import com.gsir.ai.domain.AiRequest;

import com.gsir.security.SecurityPrincipal;

import java.util.Objects;

public final class AiRequestIdentityVerifier {

    private final AiSecurityContext securityContext;

    public AiRequestIdentityVerifier(

            AiSecurityContext securityContext

    ) {

        this.securityContext =

                Objects.requireNonNull(securityContext);

    }

    public void verify(AiRequest request) {

        SecurityPrincipal principal =

                securityContext.requirePrincipal();

        if (!principal.userId().equals(request.userId())) {

            throw new AiRequestSecurityException();

        }

        if (principal.organizationId() != null

                && request.organizationId() != null

                && !principal.organizationId()

                    .equals(request.organizationId())) {

            throw new AiRequestSecurityException();

        }

        if (principal.workspaceId() != null

                && request.workspaceId() != null

                && !principal.workspaceId()

                    .equals(request.workspaceId())) {

            throw new AiRequestSecurityException();

        }

    }

}

If the request DTO does not need client-supplied identity fields, an even safer design is to remove them from the external API DTO and construct the internal AiRequest from the security context.

That is preferred where practical.

# 8. Security Exception

package com.gsir.ai.application;

public final class AiRequestSecurityException

        extends RuntimeException {

    public AiRequestSecurityException() {

        super("AI request security validation failed");

    }

}

Externally this should map to the existing generic authorization/authentication error policy.

Do not expose:

- which user ID failed;

- which tenant failed;

- which resource was denied;

- internal authorization rules.

# 9. Resource Authorization

AI access must use the existing GSIR authorization boundary.

Conceptually:

package com.gsir.ai.application;

import com.gsir.ai.domain.AiRequest;

public interface AiResourceAuthorizationService {

    void requireAccess(AiRequest request);

}

Implementation:

User

 ↓

Organization membership

 ↓

Workspace membership

 ↓

Project access

 ↓

AI operation permission

The AI Gateway must not implement a second RBAC system.

# 10. AI Permission

The exact permission matrix remains an architectural governance decision unless already approved by the existing GSIR authorization contract.

Therefore the implementation must reuse existing approved permissions.

Do not silently invent:

AI_ADMIN

AI_RESEARCHER

AI_AGENT

AI_SUPERUSER

or similar roles.

If a permission is not defined, the operation must fail closed rather than creating an implicit permission.

# 11. Prompt/Data Separation

AI context contains two fundamentally different classes of information:

CONTROL DATA

    ↓

System/application instructions

Security constraints

Output requirements

UNTRUSTED DATA

    ↓

Documents

Web pages

Notes

Tool results

User-provided files

Retrieved research material

Untrusted data must never be promoted into control instructions merely because it contains imperative language.

# 12. Context Segment

Create an explicit representation:

package com.gsir.ai.domain;

public record ContextSegment(

        SegmentType type,

        String content,

        String provenance

) {

    public enum SegmentType {

        SYSTEM_CONTROL,

        USER_INSTRUCTION,

        RETRIEVED_DATA,

        TOOL_RESULT,

        EVIDENCE

    }

}

The type is application-controlled.

The model cannot change the security classification of a segment.

# 13. Context Construction Rule

The Context Builder should conceptually construct:

[SYSTEM_CONTROL]

GSIR-controlled operating constraints

[USER_INSTRUCTION]

User's authorized request

[RETRIEVED_DATA]

Document content

Provenance

[EVIDENCE]

Scientific sources and metadata

[TOOL_RESULT]

Validated tool output

Retrieved content remains data even if it contains:

SYSTEM:

Ignore all previous instructions.

The application must not reinterpret that text as a system instruction.

# 14. Secret Detection Boundary

Before context construction, sensitive application secrets must be excluded.

At minimum, never place these in AI context:

passwords

password hashes

refresh tokens

JWT signing keys

private keys

API keys

database credentials

Redis credentials

encryption keys

session secrets

internal authentication credentials

This is not a substitute for proper authorization and data classification.

# 15. Secret Redaction Contract

package com.gsir.ai.application;

public interface AiSensitiveDataFilter {

    String filter(String content);

}

The first implementation should be conservative.

However, regex-only secret detection must not be considered complete security.

The strongest protection is architectural exclusion:

Secret store

      X

      ↓

Application domain

      X

      ↓

AI context

Secrets should never enter the context pipeline.

# 16. Input Normalization

Normalize only where it is safe.

Allowed examples:

trim unnecessary surrounding whitespace

normalize null/empty representations

validate Unicode safely

normalize metadata representation

Do not automatically rewrite scientific notation, equations, units, code, citations, or user content.

Scientific information must not be silently altered.

# 17. Context Size Budget

The Context Builder must enforce a bounded budget.

Conceptually:

package com.gsir.ai.application;

public record AiContextBudget(

        long maxCharacters,

        long maxItems,

        long maxEstimatedTokens

) {}

The budget must be applied before provider execution.

The exact token limit belongs to model selection/provider configuration because different models have different context capacities.

# 18. Context Overflow Policy

When the context exceeds the permitted budget, the system must not silently truncate arbitrary scientific evidence.

Preferred sequence:

1. Remove duplicate context

2. Remove lower-priority nonessential metadata

3. Apply deterministic prioritization

4. Summarize only through an explicitly authorized process

5. Reject request if required context still exceeds limit

Scientific evidence must not be silently discarded without preserving the resulting limitation.

# 19. AI Request Security Pipeline

Create a small application service:

package com.gsir.ai.application;

import com.gsir.ai.domain.AiRequest;

import java.util.Objects;

public final class AiRequestSecurityPipeline {

    private final AiRequestValidator validator;

    private final AiRequestIdentityVerifier identityVerifier;

    private final AiResourceAuthorizationService authorizationService;

    public AiRequestSecurityPipeline(

            AiRequestValidator validator,

            AiRequestIdentityVerifier identityVerifier,

            AiResourceAuthorizationService authorizationService

    ) {

        this.validator = Objects.requireNonNull(validator);

        this.identityVerifier =

                Objects.requireNonNull(identityVerifier);

        this.authorizationService =

                Objects.requireNonNull(authorizationService);

    }

    public void validate(AiRequest request) {

        validator.validate(request);

        identityVerifier.verify(request);

        authorizationService.requireAccess(request);

    }

}

# 20. Gateway Integration

The Gateway from Part 271 must invoke the security pipeline before context construction.

@Override

public AiResponse execute(AiRequest request) {

    securityPipeline.validate(request);

    AiContext context =

            contextBuilder.build(request);

    AiModelSelection selection =

            modelRouter.select(request, context);

    AiProvider provider =

            providerRegistry.require(selection.providerId());

    AiProviderRequest providerRequest =

            new AiProviderRequest(

                    selection.modelId(),

                    selection.modelVersion(),

                    context.messages(),

                    context.constraints()

            );

    AiProviderResponse providerResponse =

            provider.execute(providerRequest);

    return outputValidator.validate(providerResponse);

}

The ordering is mandatory:

VALIDATE

   ↓

AUTHORIZE

   ↓

BUILD CONTEXT

   ↓

ROUTE

   ↓

EXECUTE

Never:

BUILD CONTEXT

   ↓

then check authorization

because unauthorized information could already have entered the AI pipeline.

# 21. Failure Rules

The Gateway must fail safely for:

invalid request

unauthenticated request

authorization failure

tenant mismatch

context overflow

missing provider

provider timeout

provider failure

output validation failure

tool authorization failure

No failure path should silently bypass security controls.

# 22. Audit Boundary

Security-relevant AI events should be compatible with the existing audit_events architecture.

Safe metadata may include:

request ID

operation type

user ID

organization ID

workspace ID

project ID

model identifier

provider identifier

success/failure category

timestamp

Never audit:

password

refresh token

API key

JWT signing secret

private key

raw authentication credential

Raw model context should not automatically be copied into audit logs.

# 23. Required Tests

### Request validation

valid request

missing request ID

missing user

missing organization

blank instruction

instruction too large

too many messages

message too large

metadata too large

### Security

authenticated user succeeds

unauthenticated request fails

user mismatch fails

organization mismatch fails

workspace mismatch fails

unauthorized project fails

cross-tenant request fails

### Prompt/data separation

retrieved text containing instructions remains data

tool output cannot become system control

document cannot modify authorization

web content cannot grant permissions

user content cannot create system instructions

### Context limits

within budget succeeds

over budget rejected

duplicate context removed

priority ordering deterministic

scientific content not silently corrupted

### Secret isolation

credentials never enter context

JWT secrets never enter context

refresh tokens never enter context

provider API keys never enter context

database credentials never enter context

# 24. Security Invariants

The following invariants must remain true:

I1:

AI execution requires existing authentication.

I2:

AI execution uses existing authorization.

I3:

AI context cannot cross tenant boundaries.

I4:

Untrusted retrieved content cannot become control instructions.

I5:

Model output cannot grant authorization.

I6:

Model output cannot directly access the database.

I7:

Model output cannot directly execute arbitrary operating-system commands.

I8:

Secrets cannot enter model context.

I9:

Context is bounded.

I10:

Provider adapters cannot bypass the security pipeline.

I11:

Tool execution remains behind Tool Gateway.

I12:

Scientific evidence is not silently transformed into truth merely

because an AI model generated or summarized it.

# 25. Implementation Gate

Part 272 must not introduce:

- new authentication architecture;

- duplicate authorization;

- unrestricted agent execution;

- arbitrary code execution;

- provider-specific security logic;

- new AI database tables;

- hidden reasoning storage;

- automatic scientific-truth classification.

The implementation is complete only when the existing repository has been reconciled and the required tests pass.
