# Part 273 — AI Provider Abstraction, Provider Adapters, and External/Local Model Isolation

## Aim of the Code

Implement the provider-independent AI infrastructure boundary defined in Parts 271–272.

GSIR must be able to use external cloud providers, self-hosted models, and local inference without allowing provider-specific APIs to leak into the application, domain, research, or frontend layers.

The existing master architecture explicitly requires all providers to communicate through a common abstraction and requires provider-specific responses to be normalized before reaching the rest of GSIR.

The target architecture is:

AI Gateway

    ↓

Model Router

    ↓

Provider Registry

    ↓

AI Provider Interface

    ↓

Provider Adapter

    ↓

┌───────────────────────────────┐

│ Cloud Provider                │

│ Self-hosted Provider          │

│ Local Inference Engine        │

│ Specialized Scientific Model │

└───────────────────────────────┘

    ↓

Normalized Provider Response

    ↓

AI Gateway

# 1. Provider Independence Rule

No application feature may contain code such as:

OpenAiClient client;

AnthropicClient client;

GeminiClient client;

outside its corresponding provider adapter.

The correct dependency direction is:

ConversationService

        ↓

AiGateway

        ↓

AiModelRouter

        ↓

AiProvider

        ↓

ProviderAdapter

        ↓

Provider SDK / HTTP Client

The existing GSIR source likewise requires provider SDK isolation and prohibits application controllers from directly calling provider SDKs.

# 2. Common Provider Interface

package com.gsir.ai.application;

import com.gsir.ai.domain.AiProviderRequest;

import com.gsir.ai.domain.AiProviderResponse;

public interface AiProvider {

    String providerId();

    AiProviderResponse execute(

            AiProviderRequest request

    );

}

This is the minimum synchronous generation contract.

Do not add provider-specific parameters here.

# 3. Provider Capability Model

Provider selection must depend on capabilities rather than vendor names.

package com.gsir.ai.domain;

import java.util.Set;

public record AiProviderCapabilities(

        Set<Capability> capabilities

) {

    public AiProviderCapabilities {

        capabilities = Set.copyOf(capabilities);

    }

    public boolean supports(Capability capability) {

        return capabilities.contains(capability);

    }

    public enum Capability {

        TEXT_GENERATION,

        STRUCTURED_OUTPUT,

        STREAMING,

        TOOL_CALLING,

        VISION,

        AUDIO_INPUT,

        AUDIO_OUTPUT,

        EMBEDDING,

        RERANKING,

        LONG_CONTEXT,

        LOCAL_EXECUTION

    }

}

A provider must not be selected simply because it is considered “better”.

The selected provider must satisfy the actual task requirements.

The existing GSIR design specifies routing by task, capability, context, latency, cost, availability, privacy, and related constraints.

# 4. Provider Descriptor

package com.gsir.ai.domain;

public record AiProviderDescriptor(

        String providerId,

        String displayName,

        AiProviderCapabilities capabilities,

        boolean enabled

) {}

This is operational metadata.

It must not contain provider secrets.

# 5. Provider Registry

package com.gsir.ai.application;

import com.gsir.ai.domain.AiProviderDescriptor;

import java.util.List;

public interface AiProviderRegistry {

    AiProvider require(String providerId);

    AiProviderDescriptor descriptor(String providerId);

    List<AiProviderDescriptor> available();

}

The registry provides the canonical provider lookup boundary.

# 6. Registry Implementation

package com.gsir.ai.application;

import com.gsir.ai.domain.AiProviderDescriptor;

import java.util.List;

import java.util.Map;

import java.util.Objects;

public final class DefaultAiProviderRegistry

        implements AiProviderRegistry {

    private final Map<String, AiProvider> providers;

    private final Map<String, AiProviderDescriptor> descriptors;

    public DefaultAiProviderRegistry(

            Map<String, AiProvider> providers,

            Map<String, AiProviderDescriptor> descriptors

    ) {

        this.providers = Map.copyOf(

                Objects.requireNonNull(providers)

        );

        this.descriptors = Map.copyOf(

                Objects.requireNonNull(descriptors)

        );

    }

    @Override

    public AiProvider require(String providerId) {

        AiProvider provider = providers.get(providerId);

        if (provider == null) {

            throw new IllegalStateException(

                    "AI provider unavailable"

            );

        }

        AiProviderDescriptor descriptor =

                descriptors.get(providerId);

        if (descriptor == null || !descriptor.enabled()) {

            throw new IllegalStateException(

                    "AI provider disabled"

            );

        }

        return provider;

    }

    @Override

    public AiProviderDescriptor descriptor(

            String providerId

    ) {

        AiProviderDescriptor descriptor =

                descriptors.get(providerId);

        if (descriptor == null) {

            throw new IllegalStateException(

                    "AI provider metadata unavailable"

            );

        }

        return descriptor;

    }

    @Override

    public List<AiProviderDescriptor> available() {

        return descriptors.values()

                .stream()

                .filter(AiProviderDescriptor::enabled)

                .toList();

    }

}

# 7. Provider Adapter Principle

Every external provider must have an adapter.

GSIR Request

     ↓

Provider Adapter

     ↓

Provider Request

     ↓

External Model

     ↓

Provider Response

     ↓

Provider Adapter

     ↓

GSIR Response

The adapter performs translation.

It must not contain GSIR business logic.

# 8. Example Provider Adapter

Use a generic adapter pattern rather than coupling the architecture to a particular vendor.

package com.gsir.ai.infrastructure.provider;

import com.gsir.ai.application.AiProvider;

import com.gsir.ai.domain.*;

public final class HttpAiProviderAdapter

        implements AiProvider {

    private final String providerId;

    private final AiProviderClient client;

    public HttpAiProviderAdapter(

            String providerId,

            AiProviderClient client

    ) {

        this.providerId = providerId;

        this.client = client;

    }

    @Override

    public String providerId() {

        return providerId;

    }

    @Override

    public AiProviderResponse execute(

            AiProviderRequest request

    ) {

        ProviderNativeRequest nativeRequest =

                ProviderNativeRequest.from(request);

        ProviderNativeResponse nativeResponse =

                client.execute(nativeRequest);

        return ProviderResponseMapper.normalize(

                nativeResponse

        );

    }

}

The exact provider-specific implementation belongs inside the infrastructure package.

# 9. Provider Client Boundary

package com.gsir.ai.infrastructure.provider;

public interface AiProviderClient {

    ProviderNativeResponse execute(

            ProviderNativeRequest request

    );

}

A provider SDK or HTTP implementation may implement this interface.

The provider SDK must remain below this boundary.

# 10. Native Request Isolation

Provider-specific request structures must never escape the adapter.

Conceptually:

GSIR AiProviderRequest

        ↓

Provider Adapter

        ↓

ProviderNativeRequest

        ↓

Provider SDK

Never:

GSIR Domain

    ↓

ProviderNativeRequest

because this creates vendor coupling.

# 11. Response Normalization

Every provider response must be converted into:

AiProviderResponse

The normalized response must represent common concepts such as:

output

model

model version

finish reason

usage

structured output

tool request

metadata

Provider-specific fields may be preserved only when there is a clear application need.

# 12. Error Normalization

Provider-specific exceptions must not propagate through the application.

Create a common error classification:

package com.gsir.ai.domain;

public enum AiProviderErrorType {

    AUTHENTICATION,

    AUTHORIZATION,

    RATE_LIMIT,

    TIMEOUT,

    NETWORK,

    INVALID_REQUEST,

    CONTEXT_LIMIT,

    MODEL_UNAVAILABLE,

    PROVIDER_UNAVAILABLE,

    SAFETY_REJECTION,

    UNKNOWN

}

Then:

package com.gsir.ai.domain;

public record AiProviderFailure(

        AiProviderErrorType type,

        boolean retryable,

        String providerId

) {}

Do not expose raw provider exception messages to users.

# 13. Retry Classification

The adapter or provider infrastructure must classify failures.

Retryable examples:

temporary network failure

temporary upstream outage

temporary timeout

rate limit with retry-after

Non-retryable examples:

invalid request

invalid credentials

unsupported model

unsupported capability

permanent policy rejection

The existing GSIR architecture explicitly requires error-aware, bounded retries with backoff and jitter.

Retry orchestration should remain outside individual feature modules.

# 14. Provider Timeouts

Every provider call must have a bounded timeout.

package com.gsir.ai.domain;

import java.time.Duration;

public record AiProviderTimeoutPolicy(

        Duration connectTimeout,

        Duration requestTimeout

) {

    public AiProviderTimeoutPolicy {

        if (connectTimeout.isNegative()

                || connectTimeout.isZero()) {

            throw new IllegalArgumentException(

                    "connectTimeout must be positive"

            );

        }

        if (requestTimeout.isNegative()

                || requestTimeout.isZero()) {

            throw new IllegalArgumentException(

                    "requestTimeout must be positive"

            );

        }

    }

}

Infinite provider waits are prohibited.

# 15. Local Model Adapter

Local inference uses the same provider contract.

AI Gateway

    ↓

Model Router

    ↓

AiProvider

    ↓

LocalModelAdapter

    ↓

LocalInferenceClient

    ↓

Local Model

This allows local models to participate in normal routing without creating a second AI architecture.

The existing GSIR specification explicitly requires support for self-hosted/private/local inference and capability detection before routing.

# 16. Local Inference Client

package com.gsir.ai.infrastructure.local;

import com.gsir.ai.infrastructure.provider.*;

public interface LocalInferenceClient {

    ProviderNativeResponse execute(

            ProviderNativeRequest request

    );

}

The client may later connect to:

local runtime

self-hosted inference server

GPU inference server

CPU inference engine

specialized inference service

No particular runtime is made mandatory here.

# 17. Local Capability Detection

A local model must not be assumed to support a capability.

The system should inspect:

model

context capacity

quantization

available RAM

GPU/NPU availability

supported operations

throughput

health

current resource availability

Routing must reject a local model when its required capabilities are unavailable.

This is consistent with the existing GSIR requirement that local-model capability be detected before routing.

# 18. Model Abstraction

Provider and model are separate concepts.

package com.gsir.ai.domain;

import java.util.Set;

public record AiModelDescriptor(

        String modelId,

        String providerId,

        String version,

        AiProviderCapabilities capabilities,

        boolean enabled,

        Set<String> modalities

) {}

This permits:

Provider

 ├── Model A

 │    ├── Version 1

 │    └── Version 2

 │

 └── Model B

      └── Version 1

The application should route against model capabilities rather than hard-coded model names.

# 19. Provider Credentials

Credentials are infrastructure configuration.

They must never appear in:

AiRequest

AiContext

AiProviderRequest

AiModelSelection

AiProviderDescriptor

logs

audit events

frontend responses

The provider adapter obtains credentials through a secure server-side configuration mechanism.

# 20. Provider Credential Interface

package com.gsir.ai.infrastructure.provider;

public interface AiProviderCredentialResolver {

    String resolve(String providerId);

}

The concrete implementation must integrate with the deployment's secret-management mechanism.

Do not hard-code secrets in Java source.

# 21. Credential Boundary

The correct flow is:

Secure Configuration

       ↓

Credential Resolver

       ↓

Provider Adapter

       ↓

Provider Client

       ↓

Provider

Not:

Frontend

   ↓

API

   ↓

AiRequest

   ↓

Provider API key

The existing GSIR source explicitly requires provider credentials to remain server-side and requires secret management.

# 22. No Credential Exposure Through Errors

Provider failures must not return:

Authorization: Bearer ...

x-api-key: ...

API key ...

request signing data ...

Even when provider libraries include these values in exceptions, the adapter must normalize the error before it reaches application logging or API responses.

# 23. Provider Health Contract

package com.gsir.ai.application;

public interface AiProviderHealthService {

    ProviderHealthStatus check(String providerId);

}

package com.gsir.ai.domain;

public record ProviderHealthStatus(

        String providerId,

        Status status,

        long latencyMillis

) {

    public enum Status {

        HEALTHY,

        DEGRADED,

        UNAVAILABLE,

        UNKNOWN

    }

}

Health information can influence routing.

It must not bypass authorization or request validation.

# 24. Circuit Breaker Boundary

Circuit breaking belongs around unreliable external dependencies.

Provider Request

      ↓

Circuit Breaker

      ↓

Provider Adapter

      ↓

Provider

States:

CLOSED

  ↓ failure threshold

OPEN

  ↓ recovery interval

HALF_OPEN

  ↓ success

CLOSED

The existing GSIR architecture already specifies this model for provider reliability.

Do not implement a custom distributed circuit breaker until actual deployment requirements justify it.

# 25. Provider Isolation

A provider outage must not crash unrelated GSIR functionality.

Example:

Provider A DOWN

      ↓

Router excludes A

      ↓

Provider B

      ↓

Response

If no permitted provider remains:

Controlled AI failure

        ↓

AI run failure

        ↓

Telemetry

        ↓

Optional asynchronous retry

Do not silently change to an unsuitable model merely to avoid reporting failure.

# 26. Provider-Specific Feature Handling

Not every provider supports every feature.

For example:

Provider A

  TEXT

  STREAMING

  TOOLS

Provider B

  TEXT

  VISION

Local Model

  TEXT

  STRUCTURED_OUTPUT

The router must evaluate capabilities before selection.

Unsupported capabilities must fail deterministically.

# 27. Embedding and Reranking Isolation

Embedding and reranking are related AI infrastructure but should not be forced into text-generation semantics.

Use separate logical interfaces:

public interface EmbeddingProvider {

    float[] embed(String input);

}

public interface RerankingProvider {

    java.util.List<Integer> rerank(

            String query,

            java.util.List<String> documents

    );

}

These may share provider infrastructure but must retain distinct contracts.

The existing GSIR source explicitly describes a separate embedding pipeline and a retrieval → reranker → context-builder flow.

Recommended backend organization:

backend/src/main/java/com/gsir/ai/

│   ├── AiGateway.java

│   ├── AiProvider.java

│   ├── AiProviderRegistry.java

│

│

└── infrastructure/

    │   └── adapters/

    │

    │   └── LocalInferenceClient.java

    │

    └── embedding/

        └── ...

Adjust paths to the repository's actual established package structure during implementation.

Do not create duplicate AI directories if an existing canonical structure already exists.

# 29. Provider Adapter Tests

Every adapter must have contract tests covering:

normal request

response normalization

usage normalization

finish reason normalization

structured output

tool request normalization

timeout

network failure

rate limit

invalid request

authentication failure

provider unavailable

malformed response

secret isolation

# 30. Provider Contract Test

All providers should satisfy the same test contract.

Conceptually:

abstract class AiProviderContractTest {

    protected abstract AiProvider provider();

    @Test

    void exposesProviderId() {}

    @Test

    void executesValidRequest() {}

    @Test

    void normalizesResponse() {}

    @Test

    void normalizesFailures() {}

    @Test

    void doesNotExposeCredentials() {}

}

Each concrete provider adapter extends the contract test.

This prevents one provider from silently violating the common abstraction.

# 31. Provider Independence Acceptance Test

The architecture must permit:

Provider A

    ↓

remove adapter

    ↓

Provider B

    ↓

same AI application workflow

without rewriting:

projects

conversations

research

notes

files

knowledge

frontend

authorization

scientific validation

This is the practical definition of provider independence.

# 32. Security Invariants

The following must remain true:

P1:

Provider SDKs exist only in provider infrastructure.

P2:

Provider credentials remain server-side.

P3:

Provider responses are normalized.

P4:

Provider errors are normalized.

P5:

Provider capability must be known before routing.

P6:

Local models use the same controlled abstraction.

P7:

Provider failure cannot bypass authorization.

P8:

Provider failure cannot expose credentials.

P9:

Unsupported capabilities fail safely.

P10:

No provider becomes a permanent application dependency.

# 33. Implementation Rule

Before creating concrete provider adapters:

- inspect existing AI dependencies;

- identify existing provider integrations;

- identify duplicate provider clients;

- identify existing HTTP clients;

- inspect configuration and secret handling;

- inspect existing AI database metadata;

- reuse existing abstractions where compatible;

- remove duplication only after evidence;

- implement the common contract;

- add adapters incrementally.

Do not add every provider at once.

The first production adapter should be selected based on the actual deployment requirement.

# 34. No Premature Vendor Lock-In

The following are prohibited in core AI code:

if (provider.equals("specific-vendor")) {

    ...

}

unless the logic is explicitly confined to the provider adapter or a capability policy.

Prefer:

if (capabilities.supports(

        AiProviderCapabilities.Capability.TOOL_CALLING

)) {

    ...

}

The router should reason about capabilities and constraints, not vendor branding.

# Part 274 — AI Provider Configuration, Secret Isolation, Model Registry Metadata, and Secure Runtime Configuration

## Aim of the Code

Define the secure runtime configuration boundary for AI providers and models.

This part ensures that:

- provider credentials remain outside application source code;

- secrets never enter AI requests or model context;

- provider configuration is environment/deployment controlled;

- models are represented independently from providers;

- capabilities and operational limits are explicit;

- disabled or unavailable providers cannot be selected;

- configuration errors fail safely;

- local and cloud providers use the same configuration boundary.

No provider-specific secret or model credential is stored in Java source, frontend code, Git, AI context, logs, or ordinary application DTOs.

# 1. Configuration Architecture

Deployment / Secret Store

          ↓

Spring Configuration

          ↓

Provider Configuration

          ↓

Provider Registry

          ↓

Model Registry

          ↓

AI Model Router

          ↓

Provider Adapter

The frontend never receives provider credentials.

# 2. Provider Configuration

package com.gsir.ai.infrastructure.config;

import java.time.Duration;

public record AiProviderConfiguration(

        String providerId,

        String endpoint,

        boolean enabled,

        Duration connectTimeout,

        Duration requestTimeout

) {}

Credentials are deliberately absent.

The configuration object contains operational configuration only.

# 3. Provider Secret Reference

package com.gsir.ai.infrastructure.config;

public record AiProviderSecretReference(

        String providerId,

        String secretReference

) {}

The reference identifies where the credential is stored.

It must not contain the actual credential in logs, API responses, or domain objects.

# 4. Credential Resolver

package com.gsir.ai.infrastructure.provider;

public interface AiProviderCredentialResolver {

    String resolve(String providerId);

}

The resolver is the only infrastructure boundary responsible for obtaining a provider credential.

Provider adapters consume credentials through this interface.

# 5. Environment-Based Initial Implementation

For a simple MVP deployment, credentials may initially come from environment-backed configuration.

package com.gsir.ai.infrastructure.provider;

import java.util.Map;

import java.util.Objects;

public final class EnvironmentAiProviderCredentialResolver

        implements AiProviderCredentialResolver {

    private final Map<String, String> credentials;

    public EnvironmentAiProviderCredentialResolver(

            Map<String, String> credentials

    ) {

        this.credentials = Map.copyOf(

                Objects.requireNonNull(credentials)

        );

    }

    @Override

    public String resolve(String providerId) {

        String credential = credentials.get(providerId);

        if (credential == null || credential.isBlank()) {

            throw new IllegalStateException(

                    "AI provider credential unavailable"

            );

        }

        return credential;

    }

}

The implementation may later be replaced with a dedicated secret manager without changing the AI Gateway.

# 6. Secret Isolation Rule

The following objects must never contain provider secrets:

AiRequest

AiContext

AiResponse

AiModelSelection

AiModelDescriptor

AiProviderDescriptor

Conversation DTOs

Message DTOs

Frontend state

Audit events

Normal application logs

Database entities unrelated to secret storage

Only the provider infrastructure boundary may handle the credential.

# 7. Configuration Validation

package com.gsir.ai.infrastructure.config;

public interface AiConfigurationValidator {

    void validate();

}

Validation should occur during application startup where possible.

A deployment with an enabled provider but missing mandatory configuration should fail clearly rather than discovering the problem during a user's AI request.

# 8. Configuration Validation Rules

For each enabled provider:

provider ID                  required

endpoint                     required where applicable

credential                   required where applicable

connect timeout              positive

request timeout              positive

provider identifier          unique

For each enabled model:

model ID                     required

provider ID                  required

version                      required where versioned

capabilities                 required

context limit                valid

output limit                 valid

enabled state                valid

# 9. Model Runtime Configuration

package com.gsir.ai.infrastructure.config;

import com.gsir.ai.domain.AiProviderCapabilities;

public record AiModelRuntimeConfiguration(

        String modelId,

        String providerId,

        String version,

        AiProviderCapabilities capabilities,

        long maxContextTokens,

        long maxOutputTokens,

        boolean enabled

) {

    public AiModelRuntimeConfiguration {

        if (maxContextTokens <= 0) {

            throw new IllegalArgumentException(

                    "maxContextTokens must be positive"

            );

        }

        if (maxOutputTokens <= 0) {

            throw new IllegalArgumentException(

                    "maxOutputTokens must be positive"

            );

        }

    }

}

These values are routing constraints.

They are not guarantees of actual provider behavior.

Provider responses must still be validated.

# 10. Model Registry Contract

package com.gsir.ai.application;

import com.gsir.ai.domain.AiModelDescriptor;

import java.util.List;

public interface AiModelRegistry {

    AiModelDescriptor require(

            String providerId,

            String modelId,

            String version

    );

    List<AiModelDescriptor> available();

}

The registry provides a single application-level model metadata boundary.

# 11. Model Registry Implementation

package com.gsir.ai.application;

import com.gsir.ai.domain.AiModelDescriptor;

import java.util.List;

import java.util.Map;

import java.util.Objects;

public final class DefaultAiModelRegistry

        implements AiModelRegistry {

    private final Map<String, AiModelDescriptor> models;

    public DefaultAiModelRegistry(

            Map<String, AiModelDescriptor> models

    ) {

        this.models = Map.copyOf(

                Objects.requireNonNull(models)

        );

    }

    @Override

    public AiModelDescriptor require(

            String providerId,

            String modelId,

            String version

    ) {

        String key = key(providerId, modelId, version);

        AiModelDescriptor descriptor = models.get(key);

        if (descriptor == null || !descriptor.enabled()) {

            throw new IllegalStateException(

                    "AI model unavailable"

            );

        }

        return descriptor;

    }

    @Override

    public List<AiModelDescriptor> available() {

        return models.values()

                .stream()

                .filter(AiModelDescriptor::enabled)

                .toList();

    }

    private String key(

            String providerId,

            String modelId,

            String version

    ) {

        return providerId

                + ":"

                + modelId

                + ":"

                + version;

    }

}

# 12. Provider–Model Integrity

A model must never be routed through an unrelated provider.

The following relationship must hold:

AiModelDescriptor.providerId

            ==

AiModelSelection.providerId

and:

AiModelDescriptor.modelId

            ==

AiModelSelection.modelId

and, where versioned:

AiModelDescriptor.version

            ==

AiModelSelection.modelVersion

# 13. Capability Validation

Before execution:

package com.gsir.ai.application;

import com.gsir.ai.domain.AiModelDescriptor;

public interface AiCapabilityValidator {

    void requireSupported(

            AiModelDescriptor model,

            RequiredAiCapabilities requirements

    );

}

Example requirement object:

package com.gsir.ai.domain;

import java.util.Set;

public record RequiredAiCapabilities(

        Set<AiProviderCapabilities.Capability> capabilities

) {

    public RequiredAiCapabilities {

        capabilities = Set.copyOf(capabilities);

    }

}

A model lacking a required capability must not be selected.

# 14. Configuration Must Not Grant Capability

Configuration claiming:

TOOL_CALLING=true

does not prove that the upstream model actually supports tool calling correctly.

Configuration describes the expected contract.

Runtime responses remain subject to validation.

# 15. Provider Endpoint Validation

For remote providers, endpoints must be explicitly configured.

The system must reject unsafe or malformed configuration.

At minimum:

missing scheme

missing host

malformed URI

unsupported protocol

For production remote providers, HTTPS should be required unless a deliberately configured trusted internal/local endpoint is being used.

Do not silently convert an insecure endpoint into a secure one.

# 16. Local Provider Configuration

Local inference may use:

http://localhost/...

or an internal network endpoint where explicitly configured.

Local execution must still pass through:

authentication

authorization

AI Gateway

model routing

provider adapter

output validation

“Local” does not mean “trusted”.

# 17. Provider Configuration Example

Illustrative configuration:

gsir:

  ai:

    providers:

      primary:

        enabled: true

        endpoint: ${GSIR_AI_PRIMARY_ENDPOINT}

        connect-timeout: 5s

        request-timeout: 60s

      secondary:

        enabled: false

        endpoint: ${GSIR_AI_SECONDARY_ENDPOINT}

        connect-timeout: 5s

        request-timeout: 60s

      local:

        enabled: false

        endpoint: ${GSIR_AI_LOCAL_ENDPOINT}

        connect-timeout: 2s

        request-timeout: 120s

No API key appears in this configuration.

# 18. Secret Configuration

A deployment may provide:

GSIR_AI_PRIMARY_API_KEY

GSIR_AI_SECONDARY_API_KEY

but the exact secret names should be selected according to the deployment environment.

Secrets must not be committed to:

application.yml

application.properties

source code

tests

Docker images

frontend bundles

Git repository

# 19. Test Secret Isolation

Tests must never contain real credentials.

Use:

dummy credentials

mock credential resolver

test secret store

Example:

package com.gsir.ai.infrastructure.provider;

import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

import static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.*;

class CredentialResolverTest {

    @Test

    void resolvesConfiguredCredential() {

        var resolver =

                new EnvironmentAiProviderCredentialResolver(

                        java.util.Map.of(

                                "test-provider",

                                "test-secret"

                        )

                );

        assertEquals(

                "test-secret",

                resolver.resolve("test-provider")

        );

    }

    @Test

    void rejectsMissingCredential() {

        var resolver =

                new EnvironmentAiProviderCredentialResolver(

                        java.util.Map.of()

                );

        assertThrows(

                IllegalStateException.class,

                () -> resolver.resolve("missing")

        );

    }

}

# 20. Logging Rule

Never log:

logger.info("provider key={}", apiKey);

or:

logger.debug("provider request={}", requestContainingSecret);

Instead log safe metadata:

provider ID

model ID

request ID

latency

success/failure category

usage

retry count

The complete provider request should not automatically be logged.

# 21. Configuration Error Model

Configuration errors should be distinguishable from runtime provider failures.

Examples:

AI_PROVIDER_CONFIGURATION_INVALID

AI_PROVIDER_CREDENTIAL_MISSING

AI_MODEL_CONFIGURATION_INVALID

AI_MODEL_DISABLED

AI_PROVIDER_DISABLED

AI_PROVIDER_UNAVAILABLE

These codes are internal/application classifications.

External API responses should use the established GSIR error model rather than exposing infrastructure details.

# 22. Dynamic Configuration Rule

Do not introduce a distributed dynamic configuration system in the MVP unless required.

For the initial implementation:

deployment configuration

        ↓

application startup

        ↓

validated immutable runtime configuration

This is simpler and safer.

Dynamic provider/model management can be introduced later if a concrete operational requirement exists.

# 23. Database Model Metadata

The existing GSIR architecture already contains AI model/provider persistence structures.

Therefore:

Do not create another provider table or model table merely for runtime configuration.

The implementation must first reconcile:

ai_providers

ai_models

ai_model_versions

with the runtime configuration model.

Use persistence for approved application metadata and configuration where appropriate.

Use deployment secrets for credentials.

Do not mix these responsibilities.

# 24. Separation of Responsibilities

DATABASE

 ├── provider metadata

 ├── model metadata

 ├── versions

 ├── capabilities

 └── lifecycle state

DEPLOYMENT / SECRET STORE

 └── credentials

RUNTIME CONFIGURATION

 ├── endpoint

 ├── timeout

 ├── limits

 └── enabled state

AI GATEWAY

 └── execution policy

MODEL ROUTER

 └── model selection

PROVIDER ADAPTER

 └── provider translation

This prevents configuration responsibilities from becoming duplicated.

# 25. Provider Startup Verification

Startup should validate configuration.

It should not necessarily make expensive generation calls to every provider.

A lightweight sequence is preferred:

configuration validation

       ↓

credential presence validation

       ↓

model metadata validation

       ↓

optional provider health check

Expensive model-generation tests should remain separate from ordinary startup.

# 26. Provider Health and Configuration

A provider can be:

CONFIGURED

HEALTHY

DEGRADED

UNAVAILABLE

DISABLED

MISCONFIGURED

These states must not be conflated.

For example:

configured ≠ healthy

enabled ≠ available

available ≠ suitable

The router must consider all relevant conditions.

# 27. Secure Fallback

If the primary model becomes unavailable:

Primary unavailable

       ↓

Find alternative

       ↓

Check capability

       ↓

Check policy

       ↓

Check tenant/privacy constraints

       ↓

Select fallback

Never automatically fall back to a model that violates:

- privacy policy;

- required capability;

- context requirement;

- organizational policy;

- task constraints.

A failed request is preferable to an unsafe fallback.

# 28. Configuration Tests

Required tests:

valid provider configuration

missing endpoint

invalid endpoint

invalid timeout

disabled provider

missing credential

provider/model mismatch

unknown model

disabled model

invalid capability configuration

invalid context limit

invalid output limit

duplicate provider ID

duplicate model identity

secret isolation

local provider configuration

secure remote endpoint

# 29. Integration Tests

Provider integration tests must use controlled environments.

They should verify:

GSIR request

    ↓

AI Gateway

    ↓

router

    ↓

provider registry

    ↓

credential resolver

    ↓

provider adapter

    ↓

test provider

    ↓

normalized response

Real production credentials must never be required for ordinary CI.

Optional live-provider tests must be isolated and explicitly enabled.

# 30. Security Invariants

The following invariants are mandatory:

C1:

No provider credential exists in source code.

C2:

No provider credential is returned to the frontend.

C3:

No provider credential enters AiRequest.

C4:

No provider credential enters AiContext.

C5:

No provider credential enters AiResponse.

C6:

Provider SDKs cannot access arbitrary application services.

C7:

Disabled providers cannot be selected.

C8:

Disabled models cannot be selected.

C9:

A model cannot be executed through the wrong provider.

C10:

Missing credentials fail closed.

C11:

Invalid configuration fails safely.

C12:

Provider fallback must respect capability and security policy.

C13:

Local providers remain behind the same Gateway.

C14:

Runtime configuration does not replace authorization.

C15:

Database metadata and deployment secrets remain separate concerns.

# 31. Implementation Reconciliation Rule

Before implementation, inspect the actual repository for:

provider configuration classes

AI properties

environment variables

secret handling

provider clients

model configuration

ai_providers

ai_models

ai_model_versions

existing provider adapters

existing HTTP clients

existing health checks

If equivalent infrastructure already exists, modify or extend the canonical implementation.

Do not create parallel configuration systems.

Model configuration boundary          DEFINED

Model registry                        DEFINED

Capability validation                 DEFINED

# Part 275 — AI Model Router: Capability Matching, Cost, Latency, Quality, Privacy, and Deterministic Fallback

## Aim of the Code

Implement the GSIR AI Model Router.

The router converts an AI task and its constraints into a permitted model selection.

The router must optimize practical execution without becoming an autonomous reasoning agent.

It should consider:

- required capabilities;

- task type;

- context requirements;

- privacy constraints;

- availability;

- latency;

- cost;

- quality requirements;

- resource constraints;

- organizational policy.

The existing GSIR architecture specifies this routing responsibility and requires routing to consider task, capability, context, latency, cost, availability, privacy, and related constraints.

# 1. Router Position

AI Request

    ↓

Request Validation

    ↓

Context Builder

    ↓

Model Router

    ↓

Model Selection

    ↓

Provider Registry

    ↓

Provider Adapter

The router does not:

- authenticate users;

- authorize resources;

- execute tools;

- access the database directly;

- call providers directly;

- generate scientific conclusions;

- modify application state.

# 2. Router Contract

package com.gsir.ai.application;

import com.gsir.ai.domain.AiContext;

import com.gsir.ai.domain.AiModelSelection;

import com.gsir.ai.domain.AiRequest;

public interface AiModelRouter {

    AiModelSelection select(

            AiRequest request,

            AiContext context

    );

}

The interface remains intentionally small.

# 3. Routing Requirements

package com.gsir.ai.domain;

import java.util.Set;

public record AiRoutingRequirements(

        String taskType,

        Set<AiProviderCapabilities.Capability> capabilities,

        PrivacyLevel privacyLevel,

        QualityLevel qualityLevel,

        LatencyLevel latencyLevel,

        CostLevel costLevel

) {

    public AiRoutingRequirements {

        capabilities = Set.copyOf(capabilities);

    }

    public enum PrivacyLevel {

        STANDARD,

        SENSITIVE,

        PRIVATE_ONLY

    }

    public enum QualityLevel {

        STANDARD,

        HIGH,

        MAXIMUM

    }

    public enum LatencyLevel {

        STANDARD,

        LOW,

        MINIMUM

    }

    public enum CostLevel {

        STANDARD,

        LOW,

        MINIMUM

    }

}

These are routing constraints, not model intelligence labels.

# 4. Routing Context

The router should not require the entire application database.

It should receive a bounded routing representation.

package com.gsir.ai.domain;

public record AiRoutingContext(

        long estimatedInputTokens,

        long requestedOutputTokens,

        boolean requiresTools,

        boolean requiresStructuredOutput,

        boolean requiresLocalExecution

) {}

This keeps the router lightweight.

# 5. Candidate Model

package com.gsir.ai.domain;

public record AiModelCandidate(

        AiModelDescriptor model,

        double estimatedCost,

        long estimatedLatencyMillis,

        double qualityScore,

        boolean available

) {}

Operational scores must be based on measurable information where possible.

# 6. Model Eligibility

A candidate must first pass hard constraints.

Model

 ↓

Enabled?

 ↓

Provider enabled?

 ↓

Available?

 ↓

Required capabilities?

 ↓

Privacy requirement?

 ↓

Context capacity?

 ↓

Output capacity?

 ↓

Eligible

Only eligible models proceed to scoring.

# 7. Hard Constraints Before Optimization

This distinction is mandatory.

HARD CONSTRAINT

    ↓

must pass

SOFT OBJECTIVE

    ↓

used for ranking

For example:

PRIVATE_ONLY

must not become a small negative score.

It is a hard exclusion for a cloud model if policy requires local/private execution.

# 8. Eligibility Contract

package com.gsir.ai.application;

import com.gsir.ai.domain.AiModelDescriptor;

import com.gsir.ai.domain.AiRoutingRequirements;

import com.gsir.ai.domain.AiRoutingContext;

public interface AiModelEligibilityPolicy {

    boolean isEligible(

            AiModelDescriptor model,

            AiRoutingRequirements requirements,

            AiRoutingContext context

    );

}

# 9. Capability Matching

package com.gsir.ai.application;

import com.gsir.ai.domain.AiModelDescriptor;

import com.gsir.ai.domain.AiRoutingRequirements;

public final class CapabilityEligibilityPolicy

        implements AiModelEligibilityPolicy {

    @Override

    public boolean isEligible(

            AiModelDescriptor model,

            AiRoutingRequirements requirements,

            com.gsir.ai.domain.AiRoutingContext context

    ) {

        if (!model.enabled()) {

            return false;

        }

        return requirements.capabilities()

                .stream()

                .allMatch(

                        model.capabilities()::supports

                );

    }

}

Additional policies should remain composable rather than producing a large monolithic router.

# 10. Context Capacity

A model cannot be selected when the estimated context exceeds its configured capacity.

package com.gsir.ai.application;

import com.gsir.ai.domain.AiModelDescriptor;

import com.gsir.ai.domain.AiRoutingContext;

import com.gsir.ai.domain.AiRoutingRequirements;

public final class ContextCapacityPolicy

        implements AiModelEligibilityPolicy {

    @Override

    public boolean isEligible(

            AiModelDescriptor model,

            AiRoutingRequirements requirements,

            AiRoutingContext context

    ) {

        /*

         * Actual context-capacity metadata should come from

         * the canonical model registry/configuration.

         *

         * This policy must never assume unlimited context.

         */

        return true;

    }

}

The actual implementation must use the model's authoritative configured capacity.

This placeholder is intentionally not a fabricated capacity value.

# 11. Privacy Policy

package com.gsir.ai.application;

import com.gsir.ai.domain.AiModelDescriptor;

import com.gsir.ai.domain.AiRoutingContext;

import com.gsir.ai.domain.AiRoutingRequirements;

public interface AiModelPrivacyPolicy {

    boolean permitted(

            AiModelDescriptor model,

            AiRoutingRequirements requirements

    );

}

Privacy policy must be evaluated before model ranking.

# 12. Local-Only Routing

For a private-only request:

Cloud model

    ↓

REJECT

Private/self-hosted model

    ↓

ELIGIBLE

This must be determined by explicit policy.

The router must not infer privacy requirements from vague model descriptions.

# 13. Routing Score

After hard constraints, eligible models may be ranked.

A general normalized score can be represented as:

[ S(m)= w_qQ(m) +w_lL(m) +w_cC(m) +w_aA(m) +w_rR(m) ]

where:

- (Q) = quality suitability;

- (L) = latency suitability;

- (C) = cost suitability;

- (A) = availability;

- (R) = resource suitability.

The weights must be configured and validated.

They are not universal scientific constants.

# 14. Normalization

Raw values must not be compared directly when their scales differ.

For example:

cost:        currency/request

latency:     milliseconds

quality:     normalized score

availability: probability/health metric

Each metric must be normalized before weighted scoring.

# 15. Cost Score

For minimization:

[ C(m)=1-\operatorname{normalize}(cost_m) ]

A cheaper eligible model therefore receives a higher cost score.

However, cost must never override a mandatory quality or capability requirement.

# 16. Latency Score

For minimization:

[ L(m)=1-\operatorname{normalize}(latency_m) ]

Latency measurements should preferably come from observed telemetry rather than assumptions.

The router must distinguish:

configured latency

observed latency

temporary latency spike

provider unavailable

# 17. Quality Score

Quality should be represented as an empirically supported model/task suitability metric where possible.

package com.gsir.ai.domain;

public record AiModelQualityProfile(

        double taskSuitabilityScore,

        long evaluationCount

) {

    public AiModelQualityProfile {

        if (taskSuitabilityScore < 0

                || taskSuitabilityScore > 1) {

            throw new IllegalArgumentException(

                    "quality score must be between 0 and 1"

            );

        }

        if (evaluationCount < 0) {

            throw new IllegalArgumentException(

                    "evaluationCount must be >= 0"

            );

        }

    }

}

A score with insufficient evaluation data should not be presented as established fact.

# 18. Quality Uncertainty

A model quality score should carry evidence quality.

package com.gsir.ai.domain;

public enum AiMetricEvidenceLevel {

    VERIFIED,

    EXPERIMENTALLY_SUPPORTED,

    ESTIMATED,

    UNKNOWN

}

Routing can use only sufficiently reliable metrics for production-critical decisions.

# 19. Avoid False Precision

Do not claim:

Model A = 0.873421 quality

unless the measurement process genuinely supports that precision.

The router should preserve meaningful precision.

# 20. Composite Score

package com.gsir.ai.domain;

public record AiRoutingScore(

        double total,

        double quality,

        double latency,

        double cost,

        double availability,

        double resource

) {}

All values should be normalized consistently.

# 21. Scoring Contract

package com.gsir.ai.application;

import com.gsir.ai.domain.*;

public interface AiModelScorer {

    AiRoutingScore score(

            AiModelCandidate candidate,

            AiRoutingRequirements requirements

    );

}

# 22. Deterministic Tie Breaking

The router must produce deterministic results.

If two models have equivalent scores:

1. higher required-task suitability

2. higher availability

3. lower estimated cost

4. lower estimated latency

5. stable model identifier

The final stable identifier prevents nondeterministic selection.

Do not randomly select between equivalent models in the initial implementation.

# 23. Routing Decision

package com.gsir.ai.domain;

public record AiRoutingDecision(

        String providerId,

        String modelId,

        String modelVersion,

        String reason,

        AiRoutingScore score

) {}

The reason should contain operational selection information, for example:

required capability satisfied;

private execution required;

lowest-cost eligible model;

It must not expose hidden model reasoning.

# 24. Router Implementation

package com.gsir.ai.application;

import com.gsir.ai.domain.*;

import java.util.Comparator;

import java.util.List;

import java.util.Objects;

public final class DefaultAiModelRouter

        implements AiModelRouter {

    private final AiModelRegistry modelRegistry;

    private final AiModelEligibilityPolicy eligibilityPolicy;

    private final AiModelScorer scorer;

    public DefaultAiModelRouter(

            AiModelRegistry modelRegistry,

            AiModelEligibilityPolicy eligibilityPolicy,

            AiModelScorer scorer

    ) {

        this.modelRegistry =

                Objects.requireNonNull(modelRegistry);

        this.eligibilityPolicy =

                Objects.requireNonNull(eligibilityPolicy);

        this.scorer =

                Objects.requireNonNull(scorer);

    }

    @Override

    public AiModelSelection select(

            AiRequest request,

            AiContext context

    ) {

        Objects.requireNonNull(request);

        Objects.requireNonNull(context);

        AiRoutingRequirements requirements =

                buildRequirements(request);

        AiRoutingContext routingContext =

                buildRoutingContext(request, context);

        List<AiModelCandidate> candidates =

                modelRegistry.available()

                        .stream()

                        .filter(model ->

                                eligibilityPolicy.isEligible(

                                        model,

                                        requirements,

                                        routingContext

                                ))

                        .map(model ->

                                new AiModelCandidate(

                                        model,

                                        0.0,

                                        Long.MAX_VALUE,

                                        0.0,

                                        true

                                ))

                        .toList();

        if (candidates.isEmpty()) {

            throw new IllegalStateException(

                    "No eligible AI model available"

            );

        }

        AiModelCandidate selected =

                candidates.stream()

                        .max(

                                Comparator

                                    .comparingDouble(

                                        c -> scorer.score(

                                                c,

                                                requirements

                                        ).total()

                                    )

                                    .thenComparing(

                                        c -> c.model().modelId()

                                    )

                        )

                        .orElseThrow();

        return new AiModelSelection(

                selected.model().providerId(),

                selected.model().modelId(),

                selected.model().version(),

                "highest-scoring eligible model"

        );

    }

    private AiRoutingRequirements buildRequirements(

            AiRequest request

    ) {

        return new AiRoutingRequirements(

                request.taskType(),

                java.util.Set.of(),

                AiRoutingRequirements.PrivacyLevel.STANDARD,

                AiRoutingRequirements.QualityLevel.STANDARD,

                AiRoutingRequirements.LatencyLevel.STANDARD,

                AiRoutingRequirements.CostLevel.STANDARD

        );

    }

    private AiRoutingContext buildRoutingContext(

            AiRequest request,

            AiContext context

    ) {

        long characters = context.messages()

                .stream()

                .mapToLong(message ->

                        message.content() == null

                                ? 0

                                : message.content().length())

                .sum();

        return new AiRoutingContext(

                Math.max(1, characters / 4),

                0,

                false,

                false,

                false

        );

    }

}

### Important implementation note

The default values above are initial structural defaults only.

They must not be treated as the final GSIR routing policy.

The actual repository implementation must obtain task/capability/privacy/quality/latency/cost requirements from the approved application contract.

# 25. No Random Routing

Do not implement:

Random random = new Random();

to choose providers.

Random exploration may become useful for controlled experiments later, but production routing must initially be reproducible.

# 26. No Unbounded Fallback

Fallback must be bounded:

Primary

 ↓

Fallback 1

 ↓

Fallback 2

 ↓

FAIL

Not:

try every provider forever

A maximum routing-attempt count must exist.

# 27. Fallback Eligibility

Every fallback must pass the same hard constraints.

Primary fails

     ↓

Candidate fallback

     ↓

Capabilities?

Privacy?

Context?

Availability?

Policy?

     ↓

YES → eligible

NO  → reject

A fallback is not allowed to bypass policy merely because the primary provider failed.

# 28. Provider Health

The router should consume provider/model health information through an existing health abstraction.

package com.gsir.ai.application;

public interface AiAvailabilityService {

    boolean isAvailable(

            String providerId,

            String modelId,

            String version

    );

}

The router should not directly inspect network connectivity.

# 29. Routing Telemetry

Record safe routing metrics such as:

request ID

task type

selected provider

selected model

selection latency

fallback count

routing failure

Do not record:

API keys

passwords

refresh tokens

private keys

hidden reasoning

unbounded raw context

# 30. Routing Cost Control

The router should prefer a cheaper model when:

capabilities are equivalent

quality requirement is satisfied

privacy requirement is satisfied

latency requirement is satisfied

Conceptually:

[ \min Cost(m) ]

subject to:

[ Capability(m)=required ]

[ Privacy(m)\ge required ]

[ Quality(m)\ge required ]

[ Latency(m)\le required ]

This constrained optimization formulation is preferable to simply selecting the cheapest model.

# 31. Quality-Cost Tradeoff

For suitable tasks:

High-quality expensive model

             vs

Lower-cost sufficiently capable model

The router should choose according to the declared task requirements.

This prevents using the most expensive model for every request.

# 32. Scientific Task Routing

Scientific workflows may later require stronger routing constraints.

Example:

literature summarization

      ↓

standard generation model

numerical calculation

      ↓

deterministic computation tool

statistical analysis

      ↓

scientific computation engine

research evidence synthesis

      ↓

retrieval + evidence-aware model workflow

experiment execution

      ↓

controlled tool/action pathway

The router must not assume that an LLM is the correct executor for every scientific task.

# 33. Tool-Aware Routing

If a task requires a capability unavailable to the selected model:

Model A

  TEXT only

Task

  requires TOOL_CALLING

→ Model A rejected

The router may select another eligible model.

If none exists:

No eligible model

      ↓

controlled failure

Do not silently remove the required capability.

# 34. Local Resource Constraints

For local inference, routing may eventually incorporate:

[ R(m)=f( RAM, VRAM, CPU, GPU/NPU, queue, thermal/resource state ) ]

However, resource metrics must be measured rather than invented.

A local model should be excluded if current resource availability makes execution unsafe or infeasible.

# 35. Routing Explainability

Every routing decision should have a compact machine-readable explanation:

provider=...

model=...

requiredCapabilities=...

privacy=...

eligibleCandidates=...

selectedBecause=...

fallbackCount=...

This supports debugging and reproducibility.

It is not hidden reasoning.

# 36. Routing Reproducibility

Given identical:

request requirements

model registry

provider health state

routing policy

metrics

the router should produce the same selection.

This property is important for:

- testing;

- scientific reproducibility;

- debugging;

- cost analysis;

- regression detection.

# 37. Required Tests

### Eligibility

disabled model rejected

disabled provider rejected

missing capability rejected

insufficient context rejected

privacy violation rejected

unavailable provider rejected

### Scoring

quality normalization

cost normalization

latency normalization

availability

weighted scoring

### Selection

highest eligible score selected

stable tie-break

no random selection

### Fallback

primary failure

eligible fallback selected

ineligible fallback rejected

privacy-incompatible fallback rejected

capability-incompatible fallback rejected

bounded fallback count

all providers unavailable

### Reproducibility

same inputs → same selection

# 38. Security Tests

Verify that routing cannot:

cross tenant boundaries

bypass authorization

select a forbidden private/cloud model

access provider credentials

invoke a provider directly outside Gateway

execute tools

modify database state

The router remains a selection component, not an authority component.

# 39. Performance Requirements

Routing should be cheap relative to model execution.

Avoid:

large LLM call for routing

recursive agent planning

unbounded provider probing

database scans over unrelated tenants

large context duplication

Initial routing should be ordinary deterministic application code.

This preserves the GSIR goal of minimizing unnecessary token and computational cost.

# 40. Architecture Boundary

The final relationship is:

Security

   ↓

AI Request Validator

   ↓

Authorization

   ↓

Context Builder

   ↓

Model Router

   ↓

Provider Registry

   ↓

Provider Adapter

   ↓

Model

Each layer has one primary responsibility.

# Part 275 — AI Model Router: Capability Matching, Cost, Latency, Quality, Privacy, and Deterministic Fallback

## Aim of the Code

Implement the GSIR AI Model Router.

The router converts an AI task and its constraints into a permitted model selection.

The router must optimize practical execution without becoming an autonomous reasoning agent.

It should consider:

- required capabilities;

- task type;

- context requirements;

- privacy constraints;

- availability;

- latency;

- cost;

- quality requirements;

- resource constraints;

- organizational policy.

The existing GSIR architecture specifies this routing responsibility and requires routing to consider task, capability, context, latency, cost, availability, privacy, and related constraints.

# 1. Router Position

AI Request

    ↓

Request Validation

    ↓

Context Builder

    ↓

Model Router

    ↓

Model Selection

    ↓

Provider Registry

    ↓

Provider Adapter

The router does not:

- authenticate users;

- authorize resources;

- execute tools;

- access the database directly;

- call providers directly;

- generate scientific conclusions;

- modify application state.

# 2. Router Contract

package com.gsir.ai.application;

import com.gsir.ai.domain.AiContext;

import com.gsir.ai.domain.AiModelSelection;

import com.gsir.ai.domain.AiRequest;

public interface AiModelRouter {

    AiModelSelection select(

            AiRequest request,

            AiContext context

    );

}

The interface remains intentionally small.

# 3. Routing Requirements

package com.gsir.ai.domain;

import java.util.Set;

public record AiRoutingRequirements(

        String taskType,

        Set<AiProviderCapabilities.Capability> capabilities,

        PrivacyLevel privacyLevel,

        QualityLevel qualityLevel,

        LatencyLevel latencyLevel,

        CostLevel costLevel

) {

    public AiRoutingRequirements {

        capabilities = Set.copyOf(capabilities);

    }

    public enum PrivacyLevel {

        STANDARD,

        SENSITIVE,

        PRIVATE_ONLY

    }

    public enum QualityLevel {

        STANDARD,

        HIGH,

        MAXIMUM

    }

    public enum LatencyLevel {

        STANDARD,

        LOW,

        MINIMUM

    }

    public enum CostLevel {

        STANDARD,

        LOW,

        MINIMUM

    }

}

These are routing constraints, not model intelligence labels.

# 4. Routing Context

The router should not require the entire application database.

It should receive a bounded routing representation.

package com.gsir.ai.domain;

public record AiRoutingContext(

        long estimatedInputTokens,

        long requestedOutputTokens,

        boolean requiresTools,

        boolean requiresStructuredOutput,

        boolean requiresLocalExecution

) {}

This keeps the router lightweight.

# 5. Candidate Model

package com.gsir.ai.domain;

public record AiModelCandidate(

        AiModelDescriptor model,

        double estimatedCost,

        long estimatedLatencyMillis,

        double qualityScore,

        boolean available

) {}

Operational scores must be based on measurable information where possible.

# 6. Model Eligibility

A candidate must first pass hard constraints.

Model

 ↓

Enabled?

 ↓

Provider enabled?

 ↓

Available?

 ↓

Required capabilities?

 ↓

Privacy requirement?

 ↓

Context capacity?

 ↓

Output capacity?

 ↓

Eligible

Only eligible models proceed to scoring.

# 7. Hard Constraints Before Optimization

This distinction is mandatory.

HARD CONSTRAINT

    ↓

must pass

SOFT OBJECTIVE

    ↓

used for ranking

For example:

PRIVATE_ONLY

must not become a small negative score.

It is a hard exclusion for a cloud model if policy requires local/private execution.

# 8. Eligibility Contract

package com.gsir.ai.application;

import com.gsir.ai.domain.AiModelDescriptor;

import com.gsir.ai.domain.AiRoutingRequirements;

import com.gsir.ai.domain.AiRoutingContext;

public interface AiModelEligibilityPolicy {

    boolean isEligible(

            AiModelDescriptor model,

            AiRoutingRequirements requirements,

            AiRoutingContext context

    );

}

# 9. Capability Matching

package com.gsir.ai.application;

import com.gsir.ai.domain.AiModelDescriptor;

import com.gsir.ai.domain.AiRoutingRequirements;

public final class CapabilityEligibilityPolicy

        implements AiModelEligibilityPolicy {

    @Override

    public boolean isEligible(

            AiModelDescriptor model,

            AiRoutingRequirements requirements,

            com.gsir.ai.domain.AiRoutingContext context

    ) {

        if (!model.enabled()) {

            return false;

        }

        return requirements.capabilities()

                .stream()

                .allMatch(

                        model.capabilities()::supports

                );

    }

}

Additional policies should remain composable rather than producing a large monolithic router.

# 10. Context Capacity

A model cannot be selected when the estimated context exceeds its configured capacity.

package com.gsir.ai.application;

import com.gsir.ai.domain.AiModelDescriptor;

import com.gsir.ai.domain.AiRoutingContext;

import com.gsir.ai.domain.AiRoutingRequirements;

public final class ContextCapacityPolicy

        implements AiModelEligibilityPolicy {

    @Override

    public boolean isEligible(

            AiModelDescriptor model,

            AiRoutingRequirements requirements,

            AiRoutingContext context

    ) {

        /*

         * Actual context-capacity metadata should come from

         * the canonical model registry/configuration.

         *

         * This policy must never assume unlimited context.

         */

        return true;

    }

}

The actual implementation must use the model's authoritative configured capacity.

This placeholder is intentionally not a fabricated capacity value.

# 11. Privacy Policy

package com.gsir.ai.application;

import com.gsir.ai.domain.AiModelDescriptor;

import com.gsir.ai.domain.AiRoutingContext;

import com.gsir.ai.domain.AiRoutingRequirements;

public interface AiModelPrivacyPolicy {

    boolean permitted(

            AiModelDescriptor model,

            AiRoutingRequirements requirements

    );

}

Privacy policy must be evaluated before model ranking.

# 12. Local-Only Routing

For a private-only request:

Cloud model

    ↓

REJECT

Private/self-hosted model

    ↓

ELIGIBLE

This must be determined by explicit policy.

The router must not infer privacy requirements from vague model descriptions.

# 13. Routing Score

After hard constraints, eligible models may be ranked.

A general normalized score can be represented as:

[ S(m)= w_qQ(m) +w_lL(m) +w_cC(m) +w_aA(m) +w_rR(m) ]

where:

- (Q) = quality suitability;

- (L) = latency suitability;

- (C) = cost suitability;

- (A) = availability;

- (R) = resource suitability.

The weights must be configured and validated.

They are not universal scientific constants.

# 14. Normalization

Raw values must not be compared directly when their scales differ.

For example:

cost:        currency/request

latency:     milliseconds

quality:     normalized score

availability: probability/health metric

Each metric must be normalized before weighted scoring.

# 15. Cost Score

For minimization:

[ C(m)=1-\operatorname{normalize}(cost_m) ]

A cheaper eligible model therefore receives a higher cost score.

However, cost must never override a mandatory quality or capability requirement.

# 16. Latency Score

For minimization:

[ L(m)=1-\operatorname{normalize}(latency_m) ]

Latency measurements should preferably come from observed telemetry rather than assumptions.

The router must distinguish:

configured latency

observed latency

temporary latency spike

provider unavailable

# 17. Quality Score

Quality should be represented as an empirically supported model/task suitability metric where possible.

package com.gsir.ai.domain;

public record AiModelQualityProfile(

        double taskSuitabilityScore,

        long evaluationCount

) {

    public AiModelQualityProfile {

        if (taskSuitabilityScore < 0

                || taskSuitabilityScore > 1) {

            throw new IllegalArgumentException(

                    "quality score must be between 0 and 1"

            );

        }

        if (evaluationCount < 0) {

            throw new IllegalArgumentException(

                    "evaluationCount must be >= 0"

            );

        }

    }

}

A score with insufficient evaluation data should not be presented as established fact.

# 18. Quality Uncertainty

A model quality score should carry evidence quality.

package com.gsir.ai.domain;

public enum AiMetricEvidenceLevel {

    VERIFIED,

    EXPERIMENTALLY_SUPPORTED,

    ESTIMATED,

    UNKNOWN

}

Routing can use only sufficiently reliable metrics for production-critical decisions.

# 19. Avoid False Precision

Do not claim:

Model A = 0.873421 quality

unless the measurement process genuinely supports that precision.

The router should preserve meaningful precision.

# 20. Composite Score

package com.gsir.ai.domain;

public record AiRoutingScore(

        double total,

        double quality,

        double latency,

        double cost,

        double availability,

        double resource

) {}

All values should be normalized consistently.

# 21. Scoring Contract

package com.gsir.ai.application;

import com.gsir.ai.domain.*;

public interface AiModelScorer {

    AiRoutingScore score(

            AiModelCandidate candidate,

            AiRoutingRequirements requirements

    );

}

# 22. Deterministic Tie Breaking

The router must produce deterministic results.

If two models have equivalent scores:

1. higher required-task suitability

2. higher availability

3. lower estimated cost

4. lower estimated latency

5. stable model identifier

The final stable identifier prevents nondeterministic selection.

Do not randomly select between equivalent models in the initial implementation.

# 23. Routing Decision

package com.gsir.ai.domain;

public record AiRoutingDecision(

        String providerId,

        String modelId,

        String modelVersion,

        String reason,

        AiRoutingScore score

) {}

The reason should contain operational selection information, for example:

required capability satisfied;

private execution required;

lowest-cost eligible model;

It must not expose hidden model reasoning.

# 24. Router Implementation

package com.gsir.ai.application;

import com.gsir.ai.domain.*;

import java.util.Comparator;

import java.util.List;

import java.util.Objects;

public final class DefaultAiModelRouter

        implements AiModelRouter {

    private final AiModelRegistry modelRegistry;

    private final AiModelEligibilityPolicy eligibilityPolicy;

    private final AiModelScorer scorer;

    public DefaultAiModelRouter(

            AiModelRegistry modelRegistry,

            AiModelEligibilityPolicy eligibilityPolicy,

            AiModelScorer scorer

    ) {

        this.modelRegistry =

                Objects.requireNonNull(modelRegistry);

        this.eligibilityPolicy =

                Objects.requireNonNull(eligibilityPolicy);

        this.scorer =

                Objects.requireNonNull(scorer);

    }

    @Override

    public AiModelSelection select(

            AiRequest request,

            AiContext context

    ) {

        Objects.requireNonNull(request);

        Objects.requireNonNull(context);

        AiRoutingRequirements requirements =

                buildRequirements(request);

        AiRoutingContext routingContext =

                buildRoutingContext(request, context);

        List<AiModelCandidate> candidates =

                modelRegistry.available()

                        .stream()

                        .filter(model ->

                                eligibilityPolicy.isEligible(

                                        model,

                                        requirements,

                                        routingContext

                                ))

                        .map(model ->

                                new AiModelCandidate(

                                        model,

                                        0.0,

                                        Long.MAX_VALUE,

                                        0.0,

                                        true

                                ))

                        .toList();

        if (candidates.isEmpty()) {

            throw new IllegalStateException(

                    "No eligible AI model available"

            );

        }

        AiModelCandidate selected =

                candidates.stream()

                        .max(

                                Comparator

                                    .comparingDouble(

                                        c -> scorer.score(

                                                c,

                                                requirements

                                        ).total()

                                    )

                                    .thenComparing(

                                        c -> c.model().modelId()

                                    )

                        )

                        .orElseThrow();

        return new AiModelSelection(

                selected.model().providerId(),

                selected.model().modelId(),

                selected.model().version(),

                "highest-scoring eligible model"

        );

    }

    private AiRoutingRequirements buildRequirements(

            AiRequest request

    ) {

        return new AiRoutingRequirements(

                request.taskType(),

                java.util.Set.of(),

                AiRoutingRequirements.PrivacyLevel.STANDARD,

                AiRoutingRequirements.QualityLevel.STANDARD,

                AiRoutingRequirements.LatencyLevel.STANDARD,

                AiRoutingRequirements.CostLevel.STANDARD

        );

    }

    private AiRoutingContext buildRoutingContext(

            AiRequest request,

            AiContext context

    ) {

        long characters = context.messages()

                .stream()

                .mapToLong(message ->

                        message.content() == null

                                ? 0

                                : message.content().length())

                .sum();

        return new AiRoutingContext(

                Math.max(1, characters / 4),

                0,

                false,

                false,

                false

        );

    }

}
