### 35.72 FRONTEND ARCHITECTURAL INVARIANTS

The following rules are mandatory:

- Components do not directly access databases.

- Components do not directly call AI providers.

- Components do not contain domain business logic.

- Feature services own feature API communication.

- API clients own HTTP transport concerns.

- Server state is separated from UI state.

- Authentication is centralized.

- Authorization is enforced by the backend.

- API contracts are versioned.

- API schemas are strongly typed.

- Real-time events are schema validated.

- External data is treated as untrusted.

- Plugin data is treated as untrusted.

- AI output is treated as untrusted.

- Large datasets use incremental loading.

- Search requests are debounced and cancellable.

- Destructive actions require confirmation.

- Sensitive data is not unnecessarily stored in the browser.

- Feature modules expose controlled public APIs.

- Circular dependencies are prohibited.

- UI components remain reusable.

- Backend implementation details remain hidden from the frontend.

- BFF logic remains client-oriented and does not become domain logic.

- API Gateway remains focused on edge concerns.

- Every important frontend operation has defined loading, success, failure, and cancellation behavior.

END OF 35.72

### 35.73 PART 35 ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA

Part 35 shall be considered complete only when:

- The application shell is implemented.

- Primary navigation is implemented.

- Top navigation is implemented.

- Responsive navigation is implemented.

- Route configuration is centralized.

- Protected routes are implemented.

- Public routes are implemented.

- Route guards are implemented.

- Lazy loading is implemented for large features.

- Page modules are separated from feature modules.

- Feature modules follow the defined structure.

- State ownership is clearly defined.

- Server state is separated from client state.

- Global UI state is minimized.

- API communication is centralized.

- Raw API calls are prohibited inside components.

- API contracts are version-controlled.

- API request and response types are defined.

- Request correlation is supported.

- Idempotency is supported where required.

- Retry behavior is controlled.

- Timeout behavior is defined.

- Long-running operations use asynchronous job patterns where required.

- Real-time communication is typed.

- AI streaming is supported.

- AI cancellation is supported.

- Network failure is handled.

- Search debouncing is implemented.

- Request cancellation is implemented.

- Cache invalidation is defined.

- Large datasets use efficient loading.

- Authentication state is centralized.

- Session expiration is handled.

- Permission-aware UI is implemented.

- Backend authorization remains authoritative.

- Plugin installation has a defined frontend flow.

- Plugin permissions are displayed.

- Installed plugins appear in Connections/Links.

- Connection states are represented.

- Security boundaries are enforced.

- API Gateway responsibilities are defined.

- BFF responsibilities are defined where required.

- Domain logic remains outside the gateway/BFF.

- Frontend architecture remains modular.

- Frontend-to-backend data flow is explicitly documented.

- All major GSIR features can connect through the same architecture.

- The architecture supports future web, mobile, and desktop clients without coupling domain services to one UI.

- The frontend can scale to the larger GSIR AI Scientist and Scientific Research Operating System architecture without requiring a complete rewrite.

END OF PART 35

PART 35 COMPLETED.

## PART 36 — COMPLETE API CONTRACT, TYPE SYSTEM, REQUEST/RESPONSE SCHEMAS AND FRONTEND–BACKEND DATA CONTRACT

### 36.1 PURPOSE

GSIR shall use a strict, typed, versioned API contract between the frontend and backend.

The API contract is the formal agreement that defines:

Request

↓

Validation

↓

Authentication

↓

Authorization

↓

Business Processing

↓

Response

Every feature must have clearly defined request types, response types, error types, pagination types, identifiers, timestamps, status values, and validation rules.

The frontend and backend must not independently invent different representations of the same data.

The API contract shall become the single source of truth for communication between application layers.

OpenAPI supports explicit request and response schemas, reusable schema references, media types, and documented error responses; GSIR shall use these capabilities to keep its contracts strongly defined and machine-readable. 

END OF 36.1

### 36.2 CONTRACT-FIRST ARCHITECTURE

GSIR shall follow:

API Contract

      ↓

Schema Definition

      ↓

Backend Validation

      ↓

Backend Implementation

      ↓

Frontend Types

      ↓

Frontend API Client

      ↓

UI

The API contract must be defined before implementing a new cross-layer feature.

The implementation must conform to the contract.

END OF 36.2

### 36.3 CONTRACT DIRECTORY

The root contract structure shall be:

contracts/

├── openapi/

│   ├── openapi.yaml

│   ├── common.yaml

│   ├── auth.yaml

│   ├── users.yaml

│   ├── settings.yaml

│   ├── administration.yaml

│   └── health.yaml

│

└── schemas/

    ├── common/

    ├── auth/

    ├── user/

    ├── chat/

    ├── ai/

### 36.4 API VERSION

The first production API version shall be:

/api/v1/

Examples:

/api/v1/auth/login

/api/v1/chats

/api/v1/projects

/api/v1/research/jobs

/api/v1/ai/runs

/api/v1/plugins

Breaking API changes shall require a new API version.

END OF 36.4

### 36.5 API NAMING STANDARD

Endpoints shall use resource-oriented naming.

Preferred:

GET    /api/v1/projects

POST   /api/v1/projects

GET    /api/v1/projects/{projectId}

PATCH  /api/v1/projects/{projectId}

DELETE /api/v1/projects/{projectId}

Avoid unnecessary action-style endpoints.

Action endpoints may be used where the operation represents a command rather than ordinary CRUD.

Example:

POST /api/v1/ai/runs/{runId}/cancel

POST /api/v1/files/{fileId}/process

POST /api/v1/plugins/{pluginId}/enable

END OF 36.5

### 36.6 UNIVERSAL IDENTIFIER TYPE

All major persistent entities shall use a globally unique identifier.

The API representation shall use:

id: string

The actual backend identifier strategy shall be defined by the database architecture.

Frontend code must not depend on the database's internal numeric sequence.

END OF 36.6

### 36.7 ENTITY IDENTIFIER NAMING

Identifiers shall use explicit names.

Examples:

userId

organizationId

projectId

conversationId

messageId

runId

fileId

noteId

pluginId

connectionId

researchJobId

notificationId

Generic ambiguous names shall be avoided in nested structures when multiple entity types are present.

END OF 36.7

### 36.8 TIMESTAMP STANDARD

All API timestamps shall use ISO 8601-compatible UTC timestamps.

Example:

2026-08-31T10:30:00Z

The backend shall store authoritative timestamps.

The frontend may convert them to the user's selected timezone for display.

END OF 36.8

### 36.9 BASE ENTITY METADATA

Common persistent entities may contain:

id

createdAt

updatedAt

Where applicable:

createdBy

updatedBy

deletedAt

version

These fields shall not be added blindly to every response. They must be included when useful for the specific entity.

END OF 36.9

### 36.10 API RESPONSE ENVELOPE

GSIR shall use a consistent response structure.

Successful single-resource response:

{

  "data": {...},

  "meta": {...}

}

Successful collection response:

{

  "data": [...],

  "meta": {

    "nextCursor": "...",

    "hasMore": true

  }

}

Error response:

{

  "error": {

    "code": "ERROR_CODE",

    "message": "Safe human-readable message",

    "details": {},

    "requestId": "..."

  }

}

The exact schema shall be centrally defined.

END OF 36.10

### 36.11 RESPONSE METADATA

Common metadata may include:

requestId

timestamp

nextCursor

hasMore

total

version

Only relevant metadata shall be returned.

Large or expensive aggregate values such as total shall not be calculated unnecessarily.

END OF 36.11

### 36.12 COMMON API SCHEMAS

Exact schema directory:

contracts/schemas/common/

Required schemas:

ApiResponse

ApiError

ApiErrorDetail

PaginationMeta

CursorPagination

RequestContext

AuditMetadata

Timestamp

EntityId

ValidationError

END OF 36.12

### 36.13 ERROR TYPE SYSTEM

Errors shall be machine-readable.

Required categories include:

VALIDATION_ERROR

AUTHENTICATION_REQUIRED

AUTHENTICATION_FAILED

AUTHORIZATION_DENIED

RESOURCE_NOT_FOUND

CONFLICT

RATE_LIMITED

PAYLOAD_TOO_LARGE

UNSUPPORTED_OPERATION

DEPENDENCY_UNAVAILABLE

TIMEOUT

INTERNAL_ERROR

SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE

Feature-specific errors may extend this list.

END OF 36.13

### 36.14 ERROR RESPONSE RULE

Error messages returned to users must not expose:

Database queries

Internal stack traces

API secrets

Access tokens

Provider credentials

Internal network topology

Private file paths

Security configuration

Detailed diagnostics shall remain in protected server-side logs.

END OF 36.14

### 36.15 VALIDATION ERROR STRUCTURE

Validation failures shall identify the affected field when possible.

Example:

{

  "error": {

    "code": "VALIDATION_ERROR",

    "message": "One or more fields are invalid.",

    "details": {

      "fields": [

        {

          "field": "title",

          "code": "REQUIRED",

          "message": "Title is required."

        }

      ]

    }

  }

}

END OF 36.15

### 36.16 HTTP STATUS STANDARD

GSIR shall use HTTP status codes consistently.

Primary mapping:

200 → Successful request

201 → Resource created

202 → Accepted asynchronous operation

204 → Successful operation with no response body

400 → Invalid request

401 → Authentication required/failed

403 → Permission denied

404 → Resource not found

409 → Resource conflict

413 → Payload too large

422 → Validation failure where applicable

429 → Rate limit exceeded

500 → Internal server error

502 → Upstream dependency error

503 → Service unavailable

504 → Upstream timeout

The exact use of 400 versus 422 shall be standardized across the backend and not vary between services.

END OF 36.16

### 36.17 REQUEST CONTEXT

Every authenticated request shall internally carry a request context.

Conceptually:

RequestContext

├── requestId

├── userId

├── organizationId

├── sessionId

├── permissions

├── locale

├── timezone

├── clientType

└── authenticationMethod

Not every field must be transmitted directly by the browser.

Trusted security-related values must be derived or validated by the backend.

END OF 36.17

### 36.18 CLIENT INFORMATION

The frontend may provide:

clientType

clientVersion

platform

locale

timezone

The backend must treat these as informational unless independently verified.

They must never be used as security credentials.

END OF 36.18

### 36.57 STRUCTURED DATA TYPES

GSIR shall prefer explicit structured objects rather than ambiguous dictionaries.

Poor:

metadata: {}

Preferred:

metadata:

  sourceType

  sourceId

  createdAt

  confidence

Free-form metadata may exist where required, but important business fields must have defined schemas.

### 36.58 ENUMERATION RULE

Finite states shall use enumerated values.

Example:

status:

  - active

  - paused

  - disabled

Arbitrary user-generated strings shall not replace controlled state values.

END OF 36.58

### 36.59 NULLABILITY RULE

Every nullable field must explicitly define whether null is meaningful.

The following must not be treated as equivalent automatically:

missing

null

empty string

empty array

false

Each field's contract shall define the expected behavior.

END OF 36.59

### 36.60 PATCH SEMANTICS

PATCH operations must clearly define:

Field omitted

→ Keep existing value

Field supplied with value

→ Replace value

Field explicitly set to null

→ Clear value, only when nullable

This behavior must be consistent across all APIs.

END OF 36.60

↓

↓

Review

↓

Schema Validation

↓

↓

### 36.73 BACKWARD COMPATIBILITY

Adding optional response fields

Adding optional request fields

Adding new endpoints

Adding new enum values only where clients are designed to tolerate them

Potential breaking changes include:

Removing fields

Renaming fields

Changing field types

Changing required fields

Changing semantic meaning

Removing endpoints

Changing authentication behavior

END OF 36.73

### 36.74 API SECURITY CONTRACT

Every protected API endpoint shall define:

Authentication requirement

Authorization requirement

Resource ownership requirement

Input validation

Rate limit

Payload limit

Audit requirement

Sensitive endpoints shall additionally define:

Re-authentication

MFA requirement

Confirmation

Idempotency

END OF 36.74

### 36.75 API RATE LIMIT CONTRACT

Rate limits shall be defined by operation class rather than applying one identical limit to every endpoint.

Examples:

Authentication

Search

AI Generation

File Upload

Normal CRUD

Administrative Operations

Plugin Operations

AI-intensive endpoints shall use separate quotas because their cost and resource consumption are substantially different.

END OF 36.75

### 36.76 HIGH-CONCURRENCY REQUIREMENT

GSIR has a long-term requirement to support extremely high concurrent query volume, including the target of approximately:

10,000,000 concurrent queries/requests

This requirement shall not be interpreted as a single application server processing ten million operations synchronously.

The architecture must distribute workload across:

Load Balancers

API Gateway Instances

Stateless Application Instances

Caches

Queues

Workers

Database Replicas

Search Infrastructure

AI Workers

Provider Pools

The exact capacity must be established through load testing rather than assumed.

END OF 36.76

### 36.77 API BACKPRESSURE

When downstream systems are saturated:

Frontend

↓

API Gateway

↓

Capacity Check

↓

Queue / Rate Limit / Reject

The system must fail predictably rather than allowing uncontrolled resource exhaustion.

Long-running operations should be converted into asynchronous jobs.

END OF 36.77

### 36.78 REQUEST PRIORITY

Where required, requests shall be classified:

Critical

Interactive

Normal

Background

Bulk

Interactive AI requests must not be blocked indefinitely by large background processing jobs.

END OF 36.78

### 36.79 IDEMPOTENCY CONTRACT

The following operations shall support idempotency where retries can cause duplicate effects:

Create Chat

Send Message

Create Project

Create Note

Start Research Job

Create File Upload

Install Plugin

Create Connection

Payment Operation

Account Deletion Request

Data Export Request

The request shall include:

Idempotency-Key

where required by the endpoint.

END OF 36.79

### 36.80 IDEMPOTENCY RESPONSE

Repeated requests using the same valid idempotency key shall return the same logical operation result rather than creating duplicate resources.

The backend shall store sufficient idempotency state for the configured retention period.

END OF 36.80

### 36.81 REQUEST SIZE LIMITS

Every API endpoint shall have a maximum request size.

Large binary content shall use dedicated upload infrastructure.

AI prompts shall have explicit input limits.

The system must prevent oversized requests from consuming excessive resources.

END OF 36.81

### 36.82 API OBSERVABILITY CONTRACT

Every API request shall be traceable through:

requestId

traceId

service

endpoint

status

latency

Sensitive request bodies must not be logged by default.

AI prompts, uploaded documents, authentication credentials, and private research data require special logging controls.

END OF 36.82

### 36.91 API CONTRACT ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA

Part 36 shall be considered complete only when:

- A versioned API contract exists.

- Every major GSIR feature has an API contract.

- Response schemas are defined.

- Error schemas are defined.

- Authorization requirements are defined.

- Knowledge contracts are defined.

- Search contracts are defined.

- History contracts are defined.

- Notes contracts are defined.

- File contracts are defined.

- Connection contracts are defined.

- Plugin contracts are defined.

- Plugin permissions are represented.

- Plugins can appear in Connections/Links.

- Laboratory contracts are defined.

- Supplier contracts are defined.

- Notification contracts are defined.

- Account contracts are defined.

- Settings contracts are defined.

- Structured AI outputs are schema validated.

- Citation structures are defined.

- AI uncertainty/evidence fields are defined where required.

- Frontend types can be generated from contracts.

- Backend request validation is implemented.

- Backend response contracts are tested.

- Contract compatibility testing is implemented.

- Breaking changes are controlled.

- Idempotency is defined for unsafe retryable operations.

- Rate limiting is defined.

- Request size limits are defined.

- High-concurrency behavior is architecturally defined.

- Backpressure is defined.

- API observability is defined.

- Sensitive information is protected from API errors and logs.

- Database models remain separated from API models.

- AI provider models remain separated from the GSIR AI contract.

- Plugin providers remain isolated behind adapters.

- Frontend and backend use the same authoritative contract.

- Every major frontend feature has a traceable contract-to-backend connection.

# PART 37 — BACKEND PROJECT STRUCTURE, MODULE BOUNDARIES, EXACT FILE NAMES AND DEPENDENCY ARCHITECTURE

> **Translation note:** This Part was originally authored against a Node.js/TypeScript
> backend baseline. Per the Canonical Technology Decision Log at the top of this
> document, it has been translated to the canonical **Java 25 + Spring Boot**
> stack established in Volume II. All architectural principles, module
> boundaries, security rules, and acceptance criteria are preserved unchanged —
> only the concrete language, file extensions, directory layout, and
> framework-specific mechanisms have been translated. Package names extend the
> `com.gsir.*` convention already established in Volume II, §1.1. Where this
> Part introduces a module not yet listed in Volume II §1.1 (knowledge,
> research, search, history, notifications, connections, plugins, laboratory,
> suppliers, account, settings), add that package to §1.1's tree — it is not a
> new conflict, just an extension of the same structure.

## 37.1 PURPOSE

The GSIR backend shall be implemented as a modular, strongly typed, security-first application.

The purpose of this architecture is to ensure that:

Every feature → has a defined module → has defined files → has defined responsibilities → has defined dependencies → has defined API contracts → has defined database access → has defined tests.

The backend must remain understandable to developers while supporting the larger GSIR vision:

AI Assistant + Scientific Research Platform + Knowledge System + Projects + Laboratory Platform + Supplier Platform + Personalized AI + AI Scientist Architecture.

The backend must not become a single large application class or a collection of tightly coupled feature implementations.

END OF 37.1

## 37.2 BACKEND ARCHITECTURE PRINCIPLE

The backend shall follow this high-level structure:

HTTP / WebSocket / SSE → API Layer (`@RestController`) → Application Layer (`@Service`) → Domain Layer (entities, value objects, domain policies) → Infrastructure Layer (`@Repository`, adapters) → Database / Cache / Queue / Search / Object Storage → External Providers.

The dependency direction shall be:

API → Application → Domain → Infrastructure.

Infrastructure must not become the owner of business rules. In Spring terms: `@RestController` classes depend on `@Service` classes; `@Service` classes depend on domain classes and `@Repository` interfaces; domain classes must not import Spring or infrastructure packages.

END OF 37.2

## 37.3 BACKEND TECHNOLOGY BASELINE

The backend implementation shall use:

| Concern | Canonical Choice |
|---|---|
| Language | Java 25 |
| Framework | Spring Boot |
| Build tool | Maven |
| API | HTTP REST API (`@RestController`) |
| Realtime | SSE (`SseEmitter`) / WebSocket (`spring-websocket`) where required |
| API Contract | OpenAPI 3.1, generated via `springdoc-openapi` |
| Validation | Jakarta Bean Validation (`jakarta.validation`, `@Valid`) |
| Database | PostgreSQL |
| ORM / Persistence | Spring Data JPA + Hibernate |
| Migration | Flyway |
| Cache | Redis-compatible cache via Spring Cache abstraction (`spring-boot-starter-data-redis`) |
| Queue | Durable message/job queue (JVM-compatible; e.g. a Spring-integrated broker or a database-backed outbox/job table under `com.gsir.infrastructure.queue`) |
| Object Storage | S3-compatible object storage via AWS SDK v2 |
| Search | Dedicated search/index infrastructure where required (e.g. OpenSearch/Elasticsearch client) |
| Testing | JUnit 5 + Testcontainers: Unit + Integration + Contract + End-to-End + Load Testing |
| Architecture style | Modular Monolith |

The exact infrastructure provider may change without changing the domain architecture.

END OF 37.3

## 37.4 ROOT BACKEND DIRECTORY

The backend shall use the following root structure (standard Maven layout):

```
gsir-backend/
├── src/
│   ├── main/
│   │   ├── java/
│   │   └── resources/
│   └── test/
│       └── java/
├── scripts/
├── docs/
├── contracts/
├── pom.xml
├── checkstyle.xml
├── .env.example
├── Dockerfile
└── README.md
```

`package.json`/`tsconfig.json`/`eslint.config.js`/`prettier.config.js`/`vitest.config.ts` have no Java equivalent as separate files — their responsibilities map to: `pom.xml` (dependencies + build), `checkstyle.xml` or `spotless` Maven plugin config (linting/formatting), and JUnit 5 configuration inside `pom.xml`/`src/test/resources`.

END OF 37.4

## 37.5 COMPLETE SOURCE DIRECTORY

The primary source structure shall be (extends Volume II §1.1):

```
src/main/java/com/gsir/
├── GsirApplication.java        (entry point, was main.ts)
├── config/                     (was config/)
├── common/                     (was shared/ + api/errors/)
│   ├── web/                    (was api/middleware/)
│   ├── error/
│   ├── security/
│   ├── validation/
│   ├── idempotency/
│   └── clock/
├── <module>/                   (was modules/<name>/ — one package per feature module)
├── database/                   (was infrastructure/database/)
├── infrastructure/             (was infrastructure/cache|queue|storage|search|external/)
├── worker/                     (was workers/)
├── event/                      (was events/)
├── security/                   (was security/)
└── observability/              (was observability/ — mostly config classes; actual logging/metrics/tracing come from Spring Boot Actuator + Micrometer, not hand-written files)
```

Each package has a specific architectural responsibility, matching Volume II §1.1.

END OF 37.5

## 37.6 MAIN ENTRY FILE

Exact file:

`src/main/java/com/gsir/GsirApplication.java`

```java
package com.gsir;

import org.springframework.boot.SpringApplication;
import org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.SpringBootApplication;

@SpringBootApplication
public class GsirApplication {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SpringApplication.run(GsirApplication.class, args);
    }
}
```

Responsibilities: bootstraps the Spring application context, which in turn auto-registers configuration, controllers, and starts the embedded server. Spring Boot's component scanning and auto-configuration replace the manual "load config → init app → register routes → register middleware → start workers → start server" sequence that a hand-rolled Node.js `main.ts` requires.

`GsirApplication.java` must remain small. It must not contain: business logic, AI reasoning, database queries, feature-specific logic, prompt construction, or long configuration objects (those belong in `@Configuration` classes under `com.gsir.config`).

END OF 37.6

## 37.7 APPLICATION BOOTSTRAP

There is no direct Java equivalent to `app/createApp.ts` and its siblings — Spring Boot's auto-configuration performs this composition implicitly. Where explicit configuration is required, use dedicated `@Configuration` classes instead of one large bootstrap file:

- `com.gsir.config.WebMvcConfig` (implements `WebMvcConfigurer`) — replaces `registerMiddleware.ts` / `registerRoutes.ts` (interceptor registration; routes themselves come from `@RequestMapping` annotations on controllers, not a separate registration step)
- `com.gsir.common.error.GlobalExceptionHandler` (`@RestControllerAdvice`, already defined in Volume II Part 2) — replaces `registerErrorHandler.ts`
- `com.gsir.config.OpenApiConfig` — replaces `registerOpenApi.ts`, configures `springdoc-openapi`
- Spring Boot Actuator (`spring-boot-starter-actuator`), auto-configured — replaces `registerHealthChecks.ts`

END OF 37.7

## 37.8 CONFIGURATION PACKAGE

Exact package:

`com.gsir.config`

Files (as `@ConfigurationProperties`-bound classes, backed by `src/main/resources/application.yml` and environment variables):

- `EnvConfig.java`
- `AppConfig.java`
- `DatabaseConfig.java`
- `CacheConfig.java` (was `redisConfig.ts`)
- `QueueConfig.java`
- `StorageConfig.java`
- `SearchConfig.java`
- `AiConfig.java`
- `SecurityConfig.java`
- `ObservabilityConfig.java`

All environment variables must be validated during startup — use `@Validated` on `@ConfigurationProperties` classes with Jakarta Bean Validation annotations so Spring fails fast on invalid/missing configuration, exactly as the original rule requires.

END OF 37.8

## 37.9 API PACKAGE

Exact package:

`com.gsir.<module>.api` (per-module, following Volume II's per-feature package convention) plus shared API infrastructure in `com.gsir.common.web`:

```
com.gsir.common.web/       (cross-cutting: filters, request context)
com.gsir.common.error/     (exception → ApiError mapping, already in Volume II)
com.gsir.<module>.api/
├── <Module>Controller.java
├── dto/                   (request/response records — was schemas/)
└── mapper/                (entity ↔ DTO mapping — was serializers/)
```

There is no separate `routes/` package — Spring resolves routing from `@RequestMapping`/`@GetMapping`/`@PostMapping` annotations directly on the controller.

END OF 37.9

## 37.10 CROSS-CUTTING FILTERS (was API Middleware)

Exact package:

`com.gsir.common.web`

Files (Servlet `Filter` / Spring `HandlerInterceptor` implementations):

- `RequestIdFilter.java` — already defined in Volume II Part 2
- `AuthenticationFilter.java` (or Spring Security's authentication mechanism directly)
- `AuthorizationInterceptor.java`
- `RateLimitFilter.java`
- `SecurityHeadersFilter.java` (or configured via `HttpSecurity.headers()` in Spring Security)
- `RequestContextFilter.java`
- `LoggingFilter.java`

Request validation and error handling do not need dedicated filter files in Spring — validation is handled declaratively via `@Valid` on controller method parameters, and errors are handled centrally by `GlobalExceptionHandler` (`@RestControllerAdvice`).

Filters must perform cross-cutting concerns only. Business rules must remain outside filters.

END OF 37.10

## 37.11 REQUEST ID

Exact file:

`src/main/java/com/gsir/common/web/RequestIdFilter.java` — already implemented in Volume II, Part 2 (`RequestIdFilter extends OncePerRequestFilter`).

Every request shall receive or propagate a request identifier. The identifier must be available to: application logs, error logs, audit records, distributed tracing (via Micrometer Tracing / OpenTelemetry), AI execution logs, and external provider requests.

Sensitive user data must not be encoded into request IDs.

END OF 37.11

## 37.12 AUTHENTICATION

Exact package:

`com.gsir.security.authentication`, integrated with Spring Security's `SecurityFilterChain`.

Responsibilities: read authentication credentials → validate credentials → resolve authenticated principal (`Authentication`/`UserDetails`) → attach trusted identity to the request's `SecurityContext`.

It must not decide whether the user is allowed to access a particular resource — authorization handles that responsibility.

END OF 37.12

## 37.13 AUTHORIZATION

Exact package:

`com.gsir.security.authorization`, implemented via Spring Security method security (`@PreAuthorize`) and/or a dedicated `AuthorizationService`.

Authorization must evaluate: User + Organization + Role + Permission + Resource Ownership + Resource State.

The backend must never rely solely on frontend visibility for authorization.

END OF 37.13

## 37.14 RATE LIMITING

Exact package:

`com.gsir.security.ratelimit` (`RateLimitFilter.java`).

It shall support different rate-limit classes: Authentication, Search, AI, File Upload, Normal API, Administrative, Plugin, Research.

Rate limits shall be distributed (backed by the shared Redis-compatible cache), not maintained only in process memory — this matters more, not less, in a modular monolith that may run multiple instances behind a load balancer.

END OF 37.14

## 37.15 SECURITY HEADERS

Configured via Spring Security's `HttpSecurity.headers(...)` configuration in `com.gsir.security` rather than a standalone filter file, though a dedicated `SecurityHeadersFilter.java` is acceptable if finer control is needed.

Headers must be configured according to the actual frontend deployment architecture rather than copied blindly from another application.

END OF 37.15

## 37.16 REQUEST VALIDATION

Request processing:

Incoming Request → `@Valid` DTO binding (Jakarta Bean Validation) → Controller.

Validation is declarative in Spring: annotate DTO fields with `@NotNull`, `@Size`, `@Pattern`, etc., and annotate the controller method parameter with `@Valid`. Invalid requests are rejected automatically before reaching the method body and are converted to the standard `ApiError` response by `GlobalExceptionHandler`.

No controller should receive unvalidated public input.

END OF 37.16

## 37.17 CONTROLLERS

Controllers shall be located one per module, under `com.gsir.<module>.api`:

`AuthController.java`, `UsersController.java`, `ChatController.java` (covers conversations + messages), `AiController.java`, `ProjectsController.java`, `ResearchController.java`, `KnowledgeController.java`, `SearchController.java`, `HistoryController.java`, `NotesController.java`, `FilesController.java`, `ConnectionsController.java`, `PluginsController.java`, `LaboratoryController.java`, `SuppliersController.java`, `NotificationsController.java`, `AccountController.java`, `SettingsController.java`, `AdministrationController.java`, `HealthController.java` (largely superseded by Spring Boot Actuator's built-in health endpoint, customized via `HealthIndicator` beans).

END OF 37.17

## 37.18 CONTROLLER RESPONSIBILITY

A controller (`@RestController`) shall perform only:

Read validated request (`@Valid` DTO) → resolve request context (authenticated principal, tenant) → call application service (`@Service`) → map result to response DTO.

A controller must not contain: raw SQL or JPQL, AI prompts, model selection logic, complex business rules, file-processing algorithms, permission implementation, or provider-specific logic.

END OF 37.18

## 37.19 ROUTING

There is no separate routing package in Spring — routing is declared directly on each controller via `@RequestMapping` at the class level and `@GetMapping`/`@PostMapping`/`@PutMapping`/`@DeleteMapping` at the method level. This is simpler than the Node.js baseline's separate `routes/*.routes.ts` files plus a `routes/index.ts` assembler — Spring's component scan discovers all `@RestController` beans and assembles the route tree automatically at startup.

END OF 37.19

## 37.20 API DTO PACKAGE

Exact package (per module):

`com.gsir.<module>.api.dto`

Structure — one `dto` sub-package per module: `auth`, `users`, `chat`, `ai`, `projects`, `research`, `knowledge`, `search`, `history`, `notes`, `files`, `connections`, `plugins`, `laboratory`, `suppliers`, `notifications`, `account`, `settings`, plus `com.gsir.common.dto` for shared shapes.

Use Java `record` types for request/response DTOs — they are immutable, concise, and map cleanly to the JSON contracts established in Part 36.

These DTOs shall correspond to the API contract established in Part 36.

END OF 37.20

## 37.21 ENTITY-TO-DTO MAPPING (was Serialization)

Exact package:

`com.gsir.<module>.api.mapper`

Mappers (implemented with MapStruct, or hand-written if preferred): `UserMapper.java`, `ChatMapper.java`, `MessageMapper.java`, `AiRunMapper.java`, `ProjectMapper.java`, `ResearchMapper.java`, `KnowledgeMapper.java`, `FileMapper.java`, `NotificationMapper.java`, `AccountMapper.java`.

Mappers prevent internal JPA entities from being returned directly to clients (never expose `@Entity` classes through the API — always map to a DTO record).

END OF 37.21

## 37.22 API ERROR PACKAGE

Exact package:

`com.gsir.common.error` — already established in Volume II Part 2 (`ApiError.java`, `GsirException.java`, `GlobalExceptionHandler.java`).

Extend with specific exception subclasses of `GsirException`: `ValidationException.java`, `AuthenticationException.java`, `AuthorizationException.java`, `NotFoundException.java`, `ConflictException.java`, `RateLimitException.java`, `DependencyException.java`.

All public errors must map to the standardized `ApiError` contract via `GlobalExceptionHandler`.

END OF 37.22

## 37.23 MODULE ARCHITECTURE

Feature-specific business logic shall exist under:

`com.gsir.<module>` (one top-level package per feature, following Volume II §1.1)

Every module must be independently understandable. Each module should follow:

```
<module>/
├── domain/          (entities, value objects, domain policies)
├── application/     (@Service classes — commands and queries)
├── infrastructure/  (@Repository interfaces, external adapters)
└── api/             (@RestController, dto/, mapper/)
```

Not every module needs every sub-package immediately, but the architectural boundary must remain clear. In Java, "public module API" is enforced by keeping implementation classes **package-private** (no access modifier) and marking only the intended entry-point service(s) `public` — there is no `index.ts` equivalent; visibility is a language feature, not a convention.

END OF 37.23

## 37.24 AUTH MODULE

Exact package:

`com.gsir.auth` — already established in Volume II §1.1.

```
auth/
├── domain/
│   ├── entity/
│   ├── valueobject/
│   └── policy/
├── application/
│   └── AuthService.java  (commands + queries; split into CommandService/QueryService if it grows large)
├── infrastructure/
│   ├── repository/        (Spring Data JPA repositories)
│   └── security/          (JWT/OAuth provider integration)
└── api/
    ├── AuthController.java
    └── dto/
```

Authentication must remain isolated from general user profile logic.

END OF 37.24

## 37.25 USERS MODULE

Exact package:

`com.gsir.users` — already established.

Responsibilities: user identity, profile, research interests, preferences, personal context, user lifecycle.

Exact application services may include: `GetCurrentUserService.java`, `UpdateProfileService.java`, `UpdatePreferencesService.java`, `GetUserContextService.java` — or consolidated into a single `UserService.java` with clearly named methods, at the team's discretion, as long as each responsibility remains traceable.

END OF 37.25

## 37.26 CHAT MODULE

Exact package:

`com.gsir.chat` (covers what Volume II §1.1 lists separately as `conversations` + `messages` — treat `chat` as the umbrella package containing both, or keep them as sibling packages `com.gsir.conversations` and `com.gsir.messages`; pick one and apply it consistently, since Volume II already uses the split form).

```
chat/
├── domain/
│   ├── entity/
│   │   ├── Conversation.java
│   │   ├── Message.java
│   │   └── ChatTab.java
│   ├── valueobject/
│   └── policy/
├── application/
│   ├── command/
│   │   ├── CreateConversationCommand.java (+ handler, or a single ChatCommandService)
│   │   ├── SendMessageCommand.java
│   │   ├── EditMessageCommand.java
│   │   └── DeleteConversationCommand.java
│   └── query/
│       ├── GetConversationQuery.java
│       └── ListConversationsQuery.java
├── infrastructure/
│   └── repository/       (ConversationRepository, MessageRepository — Spring Data JPA)
└── api/
```

END OF 37.26

## 37.27 CHAT TAB MODEL

Chat tabs shall remain a UI concept but may reference persistent conversations.

The backend shall store on the `Conversation` entity: `conversationId` (UUIDv7), `title`, `projectId`, `mode`, `modelPreference`, `createdAt`, `updatedAt`.

Temporary browser-specific tab state shall remain frontend state (React component state, not persisted server-side).

END OF 37.27

## 37.28 MESSAGE MODULE BOUNDARY

Messages belong to the chat domain.

The message module (`com.gsir.chat` / `com.gsir.messages`) shall not directly invoke OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, the search engine, or the vector database.

Instead: `Message` → AI application service (`com.gsir.ai`) → `AiOrchestrator`.

This prevents chat persistence from becoming coupled to AI providers — enforced in Java by simply not injecting any `com.gsir.ai.provider.*` class into `com.gsir.chat.*` classes; only inject the AI module's public `AiApplicationService`.

END OF 37.28

## 37.29 AI MODULE

Exact package:

`com.gsir.ai` — already established in Volume II §1.1; extend its internal structure:

```
ai/
├── domain/
├── application/
├── infrastructure/
├── orchestration/
├── routing/
├── provider/
├── tool/
├── memory/
├── reasoning/
├── evaluation/
├── optimization/
├── streaming/           (SseEmitter-based streaming endpoints)
└── api/
```

This package is the central intelligence boundary of GSIR.

END OF 37.29

## 37.30 AI ORCHESTRATION

Exact package:

`com.gsir.ai.orchestration`

Required classes: `AiOrchestrator.java`, `AiRunManager.java`, `ContextBuilder.java`, `PromptBuilder.java`, `ToolPlanner.java`, `ResponseAssembler.java`, `ResponseValidator.java`, `CitationAssembler.java`, `UncertaintyProcessor.java`.

The orchestrator coordinates AI execution. It must not contain provider-specific API code.

END OF 37.30

## 37.31 AI ROUTING

Exact package:

`com.gsir.ai.routing`

Required classes: `ModelRouter.java`, `ModelRegistry.java`, `CapabilityMatcher.java`, `RoutingPolicy.java`, `FallbackPolicy.java`, `CostPolicy.java`, `LatencyPolicy.java`, `ProviderHealth.java`.

The model router shall select a model according to: Task + Required Capability + Context Size + Quality Requirement + Latency Requirement + Cost Constraint + Provider Availability + Safety Policy.

END OF 37.31

## 37.32 AI PROVIDERS

Exact package:

`com.gsir.ai.provider`

Required types: `AiProvider.java` (interface), `ProviderRegistry.java`, `ProviderFactory.java`, `OpenAiAdapter.java`, `AnthropicAdapter.java`, `GoogleAdapter.java`, `LocalModelAdapter.java`.

Additional providers may be added without modifying the AI orchestration layer — each new provider is a new class implementing `AiProvider`, registered with `ProviderRegistry`.

END OF 37.32

## 37.33 AI GATEWAY

Exact file:

`com.gsir.ai.infrastructure.AiGateway.java`

Responsibilities: receive normalized AI request → apply policy → call selected provider adapter → normalize provider response → return normalized result.

The AI gateway is the only normal application path to external AI providers.

END OF 37.33

## 37.34 REASONING MODULE

Exact package:

`com.gsir.ai.reasoning`

Required classes: `ReasoningEngine.java`, `ReasoningPolicy.java`, `TaskDecomposer.java`, `PlanValidator.java`, `EvidencePlanner.java`, `VerificationPlanner.java`, `ReasoningState.java`.

The reasoning architecture shall prioritize: understand task → determine required evidence → plan actions → retrieve information → use tools → validate results → construct answer → check uncertainty.

Internal chain-of-thought shall not be exposed as raw private reasoning.

END OF 37.34

research/

## 37.38 NOTES MODULE

Exact package:

## 37.51 RESULT TYPE

GSIR should use a standardized result/error pattern internally where appropriate. In Java 25, this is naturally expressed with a **sealed interface**:

```java
package com.gsir.common.result;

public sealed interface Result<T> permits Result.Success, Result.Failure {
    record Success<T>(T value) implements Result<T> {}
    record Failure<T>(GsirException error) implements Result<T> {}
}
```

Used with Java's `switch` pattern matching, this gives exhaustive, compiler-checked handling of both branches. Expected business failures should not require uncontrolled exception handling throughout the application — reserve thrown exceptions for truly exceptional/unexpected conditions, and use `Result<T>` for expected business-rule failures.

END OF 37.51

## 37.65 EVENT RULE

Events shall communicate meaningful state changes. Events must not be used as a substitute for ordinary method calls when synchronous execution is required.

Every event record shall define: `eventId`, `eventType`, `eventVersion`, `occurredAt`, `producer`, `payload`.

## 37.69 OBSERVABILITY

Exact package:

`com.gsir.observability` (mostly `@Configuration` classes — the actual instrumentation comes from Spring Boot Actuator + Micrometer, not hand-written logging/metrics engines):

- Logging: SLF4J + Logback (Spring Boot default), configured via `logback-spring.xml`
- Metrics: Micrometer (`spring-boot-starter-actuator` + a registry, e.g. Prometheus)
- Tracing: Micrometer Tracing (OpenTelemetry bridge)
- Health: Spring Boot Actuator `/actuator/health`, extended with custom `HealthIndicator` beans

Observability must support: request tracing, AI run tracing, queue tracing, database latency, cache performance, provider latency, error rates, token usage, cost monitoring.

END OF 37.69

## 37.70 HEALTH ENDPOINTS

Largely provided by Spring Boot Actuator (`/actuator/health`, `/actuator/health/liveness`, `/actuator/health/readiness` when `management.endpoint.health.probes.enabled=true`). Add custom `HealthIndicator` beans for dependency health (database, cache, queue, search, storage).

A liveness check must not fail merely because an external dependency is temporarily unavailable. Readiness may fail when the application cannot safely serve traffic.

END OF 37.70

## 37.71 DATABASE ACCESS RULE

No controller shall directly access the database.

Forbidden: Controller → SQL/JPQL directly.

Required: Controller → `@Service` → `@Repository` → Database.

Enforce with an architectural test (e.g. ArchUnit) asserting no class in an `.api` package depends on `jakarta.persistence.EntityManager`, `org.springframework.data.jpa.repository.JpaRepository`, or `javax.sql.DataSource` directly.

END OF 37.71

## 37.72 EXTERNAL PROVIDER ACCESS RULE

No controller or domain entity shall directly call an external provider.

Forbidden: Controller → OpenAI API directly.

Required: Controller → Application Service → AI Orchestrator → AI Gateway → Provider Adapter → Provider.

Enforce with the same ArchUnit-style rule as §37.71, scoped to `com.gsir.ai.provider.*` classes.

END OF 37.72

## 37.73 MODULE DEPENDENCY RULE

A module may depend on another module through an explicit public application service interface.

Example: `com.gsir.chat` → `com.gsir.ai`'s public `AiApplicationService` interface.

Not: `com.gsir.chat` → `com.gsir.ai.provider`'s internal repository or adapter classes directly.

This preserves modularity — enforced in Java by keeping internal classes package-private.

END OF 37.73

## 37.74 CIRCULAR DEPENDENCY PREVENTION

The architecture must prevent: Module A → Module B → Module A.

Enforce with ArchUnit's `SlicesRuleDefinition.slices().matching("com.gsir.(*)..").should().beFreeOfCycles()` (or equivalent) as a unit test that runs in CI. Circular imports shall fail the build. Shared abstractions should be extracted only when genuinely necessary.

END OF 37.74

## 37.75 DATABASE TRANSACTION RULE

Transactions shall be controlled by `@Transactional` at the application (`@Service`) layer, not scattered across repositories or controllers.

A transaction must not remain open while waiting for: AI provider, web search, large file processing, external API, human interaction, or a long-running queue operation. Keep `@Transactional` methods short and free of blocking external calls — perform the external call first, then persist the result in a short, separate transaction.

Database transactions must be short-lived.

END OF 37.75

## 37.76 AI AND DATABASE SEPARATION

The AI system must not directly manipulate database tables.

Required flow: AI → Validated Tool Call → Application Service → Authorization → Repository → Database.

This is critical for security and correctness — an AI-invoked tool call must go through the exact same `@Service` + `@PreAuthorize` path a human-initiated request would, never a shortcut directly to `@Repository` or `EntityManager`.

END OF 37.76

## 37.77 AI SELF-IMPROVEMENT BOUNDARY

The future self-improvement architecture must remain separated from production execution.

Exact packages:

`com.gsir.ai.evaluation` and `com.gsir.ai.optimization`.

The self-improvement system may: evaluate responses, identify failure patterns, compare model performance, evaluate prompts, evaluate routing, generate improvement proposals, run offline experiments.

It must not automatically rewrite production code or production policies without controlled validation and deployment procedures — i.e., no code path from `com.gsir.ai.optimization` may write to production configuration or deploy code without a human-gated release step, consistent with the Safety & Governance section of the GSIR Vision & Scoping Blueprint.

END OF 37.77

## 37.78 TEST DIRECTORY

Exact directory:

`src/test/java/com/gsir/` — mirrors the `src/main/java/com/gsir/` package structure, per standard Maven convention.

```
src/test/java/com/gsir/
    (mirrors main package structure, one test class per production class)
src/test/resources/
    application-test.yml
```

Organize by JUnit 5 `@Tag`, not by separate top-level directories: `@Tag("unit")`, `@Tag("integration")`, `@Tag("contract")`, `@Tag("e2e")`, `@Tag("security")`, `@Tag("performance")`, `@Tag("load")`, `@Tag("resilience")` — Maven Surefire/Failsafe can then select which tags to run per CI stage.

END OF 37.78

## 37.79 UNIT TESTS

Unit tests (`@Tag("unit")`, JUnit 5 + Mockito) shall verify: domain rules, application services, AI routing policies, permission policies, validation logic, cost policies, notification deduplication, research planning, search ranking.

Unit tests must not require real external providers or a real database — mock dependencies, or use pure in-memory objects for domain-level tests.

END OF 37.79

## 37.80 INTEGRATION TESTS

Integration tests (`@Tag("integration")`, using **Testcontainers** for real PostgreSQL/Redis/etc. in ephemeral Docker containers) shall verify: database, cache, queue, object storage, search, provider adapters.

Test infrastructure must use isolated environments — one Testcontainers instance per test class/suite, torn down after the run.

END OF 37.80

## 37.81 CONTRACT TESTS

Contract tests (`@Tag("contract")`) shall verify: frontend request compatibility, backend request validation, backend response schema, error schema, streaming event schema, OpenAPI consistency (e.g. via `springdoc-openapi`'s generated spec diffed against the committed contract from Part 36).

END OF 37.81

## 37.82 SECURITY TESTS

Security tests (`@Tag("security")`) shall cover: authentication bypass, authorization bypass, IDOR/resource ownership, session attacks, CSRF where applicable, input injection, file upload abuse, rate-limit bypass, privilege escalation, plugin permission bypass, secret exposure, sensitive logging.

END OF 37.82

## 37.83 LOAD TESTING

GSIR's extreme-scale target must be validated experimentally, using a JVM-compatible or language-agnostic load tool (e.g. Gatling, which integrates naturally with a JVM backend, or k6/JMeter).

The architecture shall include load-testing scenarios for: normal API traffic, search, chat creation, message creation, AI requests, streaming, file uploads, research jobs, notifications, database reads, database writes.

The target of approximately 10 million concurrent queries shall be treated as a capacity-engineering objective, not as an assumption that one deployment can automatically sustain that load.

END OF 37.83

## 37.84 FILE NAMING STANDARD

Backend filenames shall follow standard Java convention: **`PascalCase.java`**, where the filename exactly matches the public class/interface/record/enum it contains (this is a Java compiler requirement, not just a style preference).

Examples: `AiOrchestrator.java`, `ModelRouter.java`, `ChatRepository.java`, `RequestValidator.java` (if implemented as a class rather than via `@Valid`), `NotificationDeduplicator.java`.

Methods and fields use `camelCase`, per standard Java convention.

END OF 37.84

## 37.85 NO GENERIC FILE NAMES

Avoid classes such as `Utils.java`, `Helpers.java`, `Misc.java`, `Common.java` (as a catch-all — `common` as a *package* for genuinely shared abstractions is fine, per §37.49), `Manager.java`, `Service.java` (with no qualifying prefix) — unless their scope is genuinely clear.

Prefer: `DateTimeUtil.java`, `CitationAssembler.java`, `NotificationDeduplicator.java`, `ModelRouter.java`, `FileChecksumUtil.java`.

This keeps the architecture understandable.

END OF 37.85

## 37.86 MODULE PUBLIC SURFACE

There is no `index.ts`-style aggregator file in Java. Instead, a module's public surface is whatever classes are declared `public` inside it — everything else should be package-private (no modifier) so it cannot be imported from outside the module's package.

Example: `com.gsir.ai.AiApplicationService` is `public`; `com.gsir.ai.provider.OpenAiAdapter` is package-private (or `public` only within `com.gsir.ai.provider` if genuinely needed by sibling classes in that sub-package, but never imported directly by `com.gsir.chat`).

Other modules should depend on a module's public service interface rather than reaching into internal implementation classes.

END OF 37.86

## 37.87 PUBLIC AND PRIVATE MODULE APIs

Each module shall distinguish between Public Application Interfaces and Private Internal Implementation, using Java visibility modifiers rather than a convention-based `index.ts` export list.

Example:

AI public: `AiApplicationService.java`, `AiRunService.java`, `AiCapabilities.java` (all `public`)

AI private: provider adapters, prompt-construction internals, routing internals, provider-specific implementations (all package-private within `com.gsir.ai.provider` / `com.gsir.ai.orchestration`)

This allows internal implementation to evolve without breaking other modules — the Java compiler enforces this boundary at build time, which is stronger than a TypeScript `index.ts` convention that relies on developer discipline.

END OF 37.87

## 37.88 FRONTEND CONNECTION RULE

The frontend shall never call database infrastructure directly.

Required: Frontend → API Client → Backend API (`@RestController`) → Application Service (`@Service`) → Domain → Infrastructure (`@Repository`).

This rule is unaffected by the backend language change — the frontend remains React/Next.js and only ever talks to the backend over the REST/OpenAPI contract from Part 36.

END OF 37.88

## 37.89 FEATURE CONNECTION BLUEPRINT

Every feature must be documented using this pattern:

FEATURE → Frontend Component → Frontend Hook → Frontend API Service → API Endpoint → Controller (`@RestController`) → Application Service (`@Service`) → Domain Logic → Repository (`@Repository`) → Database / External Service → Event / Queue where required → Response → Frontend State → UI Update.

No feature is considered architecturally complete until this complete path is defined.

END OF 37.89

## 37.90 EXAMPLE — SAVE NOTE

The exact logical path shall be:

`NotesPage.tsx` → `useNotes.ts` → `notesApi.ts` → `POST /api/v1/notes` → `NotesController.java` → `CreateNoteService.java` (in `com.gsir.notes.application`) → Note domain validation → `NoteRepository` (Spring Data JPA) → PostgreSQL → `NoteSaved` event → Notification policy → `NoteMapper` (response mapping) → Frontend cache/state → Note card.

Auto-save must use a separate update path with debounce and deduplication (frontend debounce + an idempotent upsert on the backend).

END OF 37.90

## 37.91 EXAMPLE — AI CHAT

The exact logical path shall be:

`ChatComposer.tsx` → `useAiChat.ts` → `aiApi.ts` → `POST /api/v1/ai/runs` → `AiController.java` → `CreateAiRunService.java` → `AiOrchestrator` → `ContextBuilder` → `ReasoningEngine` → `ToolPlanner` → `ModelRouter` → `AiGateway` → `ProviderAdapter` → AI Provider → `ResponseValidator` → `CitationAssembler` → AiRun persistence (JPA) → Streaming Events (`SseEmitter`) → Frontend → Assistant Message.

END OF 37.91

## 37.92 EXAMPLE — PROJECT KNOWLEDGE

The exact path shall be:

Project UI → Project API → `ProjectService` → `KnowledgeService` (`com.gsir.knowledge`) → Retrieval Planner → Search / Vector / Database → Evidence Ranking → Citation Builder → AI Context Builder → AI Orchestrator.

If the user explicitly selects a project, project knowledge becomes an authorized context source. If no project is selected, project-private knowledge must not automatically enter the AI context.

END OF 37.92

## 37.93 EXAMPLE — FILE PROCESSING

Upload UI → Create Upload API → `FileService` (`com.gsir.files`) → Signed Upload → Object Storage → `FileUploaded` event → `FileScanWorker` → `FileExtractWorker` → `DocumentChunkWorker` → `EmbeddingWorker` → `KnowledgeIndexWorker` → Processing Complete → Project Knowledge Available.

END OF 37.93

## 37.94 EXAMPLE — PLUGIN CONNECTION

Connections UI → Plugin Connection API → `ConnectionController` → `ConnectionService` → Permission Policy → `SecretManager` → Plugin Adapter → External Provider → Validated Response → Audit Event → Frontend Connection Status.

END OF 37.94

## 37.95 EXAMPLE — RESEARCH JOB

Research UI → Research API → `ResearchController` → `CreateResearchJobService` → Research Job database record → Queue → `ResearchJobWorker` → Research Planner → Search / Knowledge / Tools → Evidence Verification → Research Synthesis → Research Result → Report Generation → Frontend.

END OF 37.95

## 37.96 DEVELOPMENT RULE — ONE SOURCE OF BUSINESS LOGIC

Business logic must have one authoritative implementation. Do not duplicate: permission rules, AI routing, cost calculation, research status transitions, notification deduplication, file ownership, project access — between frontend and backend.

Frontend may provide early UX validation, but backend (`@Service` layer) validation remains authoritative.

END OF 37.96

## 37.97 DEVELOPMENT RULE — FRONTEND IS UNTRUSTED

The backend shall assume that frontend data, browser state, local storage, client-generated IDs, client timestamps, and UI permissions may be manipulated.

Every sensitive decision must be independently verified server-side (in the `@Service`/`@PreAuthorize` layer, never trusting a value the client sent unchecked).

END OF 37.97

## 37.98 DEVELOPMENT RULE — DATABASE IS NOT THE API

Database schema changes (Flyway migrations) must not automatically change the public API. A migration may be implemented without changing the API contract. An API change must be deliberately mapped through the DTO/mapper layer to the domain and persistence layer.

END OF 37.98

## 37.99 DEVELOPMENT RULE — AI OUTPUT IS UNTRUSTED

AI output shall be treated as untrusted generated data. Before it can modify records, execute tools, change permissions, send external messages, delete data, or modify project state, it must pass the appropriate: Schema Validation (`@Valid` on the tool-call DTO), Authorization (`@PreAuthorize`), Policy Validation, Safety Validation, Confirmation Requirement.

END OF 37.99

## 37.100 DEVELOPMENT RULE — EXTERNAL DATA IS UNTRUSTED

Web pages, uploaded files, plugins, external APIs, research documents, and tool outputs must be treated as untrusted input. External content must never automatically become: system instruction, security policy, authorization rule, developer instruction, trusted application state.

This is essential for reducing prompt injection and indirect instruction attacks.

END OF 37.100

## 37.101 ARCHITECTURAL ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA

Part 37 shall be considered complete only when:

- The backend has a modular package structure under `com.gsir.*`.
- `com.gsir.GsirApplication` is the application entry point.
- Application composition (Spring auto-configuration + `@Configuration` classes) is separated from business logic.
- API routing (`@RequestMapping` on controllers) is separated from controller response-mapping logic.
- Controllers are separated from application services.
- Application services are separated from domain logic.
- Database access is isolated behind Spring Data JPA repositories.
- External providers are isolated behind adapters.
- AI providers are isolated behind the AI Gateway.
- Model routing is isolated from provider implementations.
- Reasoning is isolated from model providers.
- Research is isolated from chat.
- Knowledge is isolated from database infrastructure.
- Files have an independent processing pipeline.
- Plugins have an independent security boundary.
- Connections have independent lifecycle management.
- Laboratory functionality has its own module, and any physical-equipment code path is gated per the Safety & Governance boundary.
- Supplier functionality has its own module.
- Notifications have deduplication.
- Settings are typed (Bean Validation, not a loose map).
- Account operations are isolated.
- Security is a first-class backend subsystem (`com.gsir.security`).
- Audit logging is implemented as a dedicated subsystem.
- Secrets are isolated from normal application data.
- Workers are separated from HTTP request processing.
- Queues are separated from business modules.
- Events are explicitly typed (Java records implementing `DomainEvent`).
- API contracts from Part 36 are connected to the backend structure (DTOs match the contract).
- Frontend-to-backend feature paths are explicitly defined (§37.89–37.95).
- Database entities (`@Entity`) are not exposed directly through APIs — always mapped to DTOs.
- AI output is validated before sensitive actions.
- External data is treated as untrusted.
- Frontend permissions are never trusted as authorization.
- Circular module dependencies are prohibited and checked by an ArchUnit test in CI.
- Unit, integration, contract, security, E2E, load and resilience test tags all exist and run in CI.
- High-concurrency requirements are treated as distributed-systems engineering requirements.
- Every major backend class has one clear responsibility.
- Every major feature has an identifiable module owner.
- The architecture permits future scaling without rewriting the entire application.
- The architecture remains understandable and maintainable for developers.

END OF PART 37

PART 37 COMPLETED.


## PART 38 — COMPLETE API SECURITY, AUTHORIZATION, DATA PROTECTION AND ZERO-TRUST ARCHITECTURE

### 38.1 PURPOSE

GSIR shall be designed as a security-first AI research platform.

Security shall not be implemented as a final layer after development. Authentication, authorization, tenant isolation, data protection, AI security, plugin security, file security, API security, auditability, abuse prevention, and privacy shall be built into every architectural layer.

GSIR shall follow a zero-trust principle:

Every request

↓

Authenticate

↓

Identify actor

↓

Validate request

↓

Authorize action

↓

Authorize resource

↓

Authorize fields

↓

Apply policy

↓

Execute

↓

Audit

The system shall never assume that a request is trustworthy merely because it originated from the frontend, an authenticated user, an internal service, an AI model, or a connected third-party service.

This is especially important because GSIR exposes APIs, user data, research data, uploaded files, AI tools, external connections, plugins, laboratory information, and potentially sensitive scientific information. OWASP identifies broken object authorization, broken authentication, property-level authorization, unrestricted resource consumption, SSRF, security misconfiguration, improper API inventory, and unsafe third-party API consumption among major API security risks. 

END OF 38.1

### 38.2 SECURITY ARCHITECTURE PRINCIPLE

   ↓

   ↓

Domain Security

   ↓

Data Access Policy

   ↓

Database / Search / Object Storage

AI-specific security:

User Input

   ↓

Input Security

   ↓

Prompt Classification

   ↓

Context Authorization

   ↓

Tool Authorization

   ↓

AI Gateway

   ↓

Model

   ↓

Output Validation

   ↓

Citation / Evidence Validation

   ↓

Policy Validation

   ↓

User

END OF 38.2

### 38.5 AUTHENTICATION PRINCIPLE

Authentication answers:

Who are you?

Authorization answers:

What are you allowed to do?

Resource authorization answers:

Which specific resource are you allowed to access?

Field authorization answers:

Which properties of that resource are you allowed to see or modify?

All four levels shall be implemented independently.

END OF 38.5

### 38.6 SESSION ARCHITECTURE

GSIR shall use server-controlled session security.

A session shall conceptually contain:

Session

├── sessionId

├── userId

├── deviceId

├── createdAt

├── lastActivityAt

├── expiresAt

├── revokedAt

├── authenticationMethod

└── securityVersion

Sessions shall be revocable.

Logout from all devices shall invalidate all active sessions for the user.

END OF 38.6

### 38.7 TOKEN SECURITY

Authentication credentials shall never be exposed unnecessarily to frontend JavaScript.

Where browser sessions are used, secure cookie-based authentication should be preferred where compatible with the application architecture.

Security properties shall include:

Secure

HttpOnly

SameSite

Short-lived access state

Server-side revocation

Tokens shall never be stored in:

localStorage

URL parameters

query strings

logs

analytics events

error messages

unless a specific architecture requires an exception that has been formally reviewed.

END OF 38.7

### 38.8 PASSWORD SECURITY

Passwords shall never be stored in plaintext.

The backend shall use a modern password hashing algorithm designed for password storage.

The password service shall be:

backend/src/security/authentication/password.service.ts

The service shall provide:

hashPassword()

verifyPassword()

validatePasswordPolicy()

Password hashes must never be returned through API responses.

END OF 38.8

### 38.9 MULTI-FACTOR AUTHENTICATION

GSIR shall support MFA.

MFA architecture:

Password

   ↓

Primary Authentication

   ↓

MFA Challenge

   ↓

Verification

   ↓

Authenticated Session

MFA shall be especially important for:

Account recovery

Password changes

Security setting changes

Connected account changes

API key management

Sensitive data export

Account deletion

Administrative access

END OF 38.9

### 38.10 EMAIL VERIFICATION

Email verification shall use:

backend/src/security/authentication/email-verification.service.ts

The verification token shall:

Expire

Be single-use

Be securely generated

Be invalidated after use

Not expose account secrets

The system shall prevent unlimited verification attempts.

END OF 38.10

### 38.11 OTP SECURITY

OTP functionality shall use:

backend/src/security/authentication/otp.service.ts

OTP protections shall include:

Short expiration

Attempt limit

Rate limit

Single-use enforcement

Replay protection

Abuse detection

OTP values must never appear in logs.

END OF 38.11

### 38.12 ACCOUNT RECOVERY

Password recovery shall follow:

Recovery Request

↓

Rate Limit

↓

Identity Verification

↓

Short-Lived Recovery Challenge

↓

Password Reset

↓

Revoke Existing Sensitive Sessions

↓

Security Notification

The API shall not reveal whether an arbitrary email address belongs to an account when doing so could enable account enumeration.

END OF 38.12

### 38.13 OBJECT-LEVEL AUTHORIZATION

Every resource access must verify ownership or explicit permission.

Example:

GET /api/v1/projects/{projectId}

The backend must not perform:

SELECT project WHERE id = projectId

and return it solely because the ID exists.

It must enforce:

projectId

+

authenticated user

+

organization / tenant

+

resource permissions

OWASP identifies Broken Object Level Authorization as a primary API risk and recommends object-level access control checks whenever APIs use user-supplied identifiers to access data. 

END OF 38.13

### 38.14 RESOURCE ACCESS SERVICE

All important resource authorization shall be centralized through:

backend/src/security/authorization/resource-access.service.ts

Example conceptual methods:

canReadResource()

canUpdateResource()

canDeleteResource()

canShareResource()

canExecuteResourceAction()

Feature services may call this service rather than implementing inconsistent authorization logic.

END OF 38.14

### 38.15 TENANT ISOLATION

If GSIR supports organizations, laboratories, teams, enterprise accounts, or shared projects, tenant isolation shall be mandatory.

Every tenant-owned resource shall be associated with the appropriate tenant boundary.

Conceptually:

Organization

   ↓

User

   ↓

Project

   ↓

Conversation

   ↓

Message

A user from Organization A must never access Organization B's resources merely by changing an identifier.

END OF 38.15

### 38.16 FIELD-LEVEL AUTHORIZATION

Authorization shall also apply to individual fields.

For example, a user may be allowed to view a supplier record but not:

internalNotes

privateContactData

administrativeRiskScore

securityMetadata

billingMetadata

Field access shall be handled through:

backend/src/security/authorization/field-access.service.ts

END OF 38.16

### 38.17 FUNCTION-LEVEL AUTHORIZATION

Administrative operations must never be protected only by hiding buttons in the frontend.

For example:

Delete User

Suspend User

Change Subscription

View Audit Logs

Manage Plugins

Manage Providers

Manage AI Models

must require explicit backend permissions.

OWASP identifies Broken Function Level Authorization as a distinct API security risk. 

END OF 38.17

### 38.18 ROLE SYSTEM

GSIR shall use role-based access control as one layer.

Possible roles:

user

researcher

professional

laboratory_manager

organization_admin

security_admin

system_admin

Roles shall map to permissions.

Roles must not be used as the only authorization mechanism when resource ownership or contextual rules are required.

=

+

+

+

### 38.21 AI AUTHORIZATION

AI must not bypass normal authorization.

If the user asks:

"Show me my project documents."

the AI retrieval system must retrieve only documents the user is authorized to access.

The AI model must never decide authorization itself.

Correct architecture:

User

↓

AI

↓

Tool Request

↓

Authorization Service

↓

Authorized Resource Query

↓

Data

↓

AI Context

Incorrect architecture:

User

↓

AI

↓

Database

END OF 38.21

### 38.22 AI MEMORY SECURITY

AI memory shall be treated as protected user data.

Memory access must enforce:

Project scope

Organization scope

Memory type

Retention policy

Consent

Privacy settings

A user's private memory must never become available to another user's AI session.

END OF 38.22

### 38.23 AI CONTEXT ISOLATION

AI context shall have explicit boundaries.

Possible scopes:

Global System Context

User Context

Organization Context

Project Context

Conversation Context

Message Context

Temporary Run Context

END OF 38.23

### 38.24 PROMPT INJECTION DEFENSE

GSIR must assume that retrieved documents, web pages, uploaded files, emails, plugins, and external API responses may contain malicious instructions.

External content shall be treated as data, not trusted instructions.

Architecture:

External Content

↓

Untrusted Data Boundary

↓

Content Classification

↓

Prompt Injection Detection

↓

Context Isolation

↓

Tool Authorization

↓

AI

The AI must never gain permission merely because a document instructs it to perform an action.

END OF 38.24

### 38.25 TOOL AUTHORIZATION

Every AI tool shall have a permission definition.

Example:

Tool: web.search

Permission: research.web.search

Tool: project.read

Permission: project.read

Permission: file.delete

Tool: account.export

Permission: account.export

END OF 38.25

### 38.26 HIGH-RISK AI ACTIONS

The following operations should require explicit user confirmation unless a trusted workflow specifically authorizes automation:

Delete data

Send external message

Modify account security

Create financial transaction

Publish content

Change permissions

Install plugin

Execute destructive tool

Modify laboratory records

The AI shall not silently execute high-impact operations.

Because GSIR supports web search, retrieved URLs must be treated as untrusted.

The system must protect internal network resources from user-controlled URLs.

Client

↓

TLS

↓

Backend

↓

Encrypted Storage

END OF 38.31

### 38.32 ENCRYPTION SERVICE

backend/src/security/encryption/encryption.service.ts

### 38.37 PLUGIN SECURITY

Permissions

### 38.38 PLUGIN SANDBOXING

↓

↓

Sandbox

↓

↓

### 38.39 THIRD-PARTY API SECURITY

External API responses shall be treated as untrusted input.

The system shall validate:

Schema

Size

Content type

Encoding

Expected fields

Authentication state

Response integrity

GSIR must not assume that third-party APIs are trustworthy merely because they are configured as official integrations. OWASP specifically identifies unsafe consumption of APIs as a security risk. 

END OF 38.39

### 38.40 DATABASE SECURITY

Application users must not have unrestricted database access.

The application database layer shall enforce:

Least privilege

Parameterized queries

Connection limits

Timeouts

Tenant isolation

Migration controls

Audit controls

END OF 38.40

### 38.41 MASS-ASSIGNMENT PROTECTION

Request objects shall never be directly merged into database entities.

Unsafe:

entity = {

  ...requestBody

}

Safe architecture:

Request DTO

↓

Allowed Fields

↓

Validated Domain Command

↓

Domain Logic

↓

Persistence

This protects privileged fields from unauthorized modification.

END OF 38.41

### 38.42 INPUT VALIDATION

All external input must be validated.

Input sources include:

HTTP body

Query parameters

Path parameters

Headers

Uploaded files

Webhooks

OAuth callbacks

AI tool outputs

Third-party API responses

Plugin outputs

Web content

### 38.43 OUTPUT ENCODING

This applies especially to:

HTML

Code

URLs

File names

Research documents

AI-generated content

END OF 38.43

### 38.44 XSS PROTECTION

GSIR shall protect against:

HTML injection

### 38.45 CSRF PROTECTION

### 38.47 SECURITY HEADERS

backend/src/security/middleware/security-headers.middleware.ts

### 38.48 RATE LIMITING

Rate limiting shall operate at multiple levels:

IP

User

API key

Session

Endpoint

Operation

Different limits shall exist for:

Login

Distributed rate limits

Asynchronous auditing

Batch processing

Risk-based inspection

Security must not become a single centralized bottleneck.

END OF 38.66

### 38.67 ZERO-TRUST INTERNAL SERVICES

Internal services shall not automatically trust one another.

Service-to-service communication shall establish:

Service Identity

Authentication

Authorization

Request Context

Trace Identity

A compromised service must not automatically obtain unrestricted access to every other service.

END OF 38.67

### 38.68 SERVICE ACCOUNT PERMISSIONS

Each backend service shall receive only the permissions it requires.

Example:

AI Worker

→ AI provider access

→ task queue

→ required conversation read/write

File Worker

→ object storage

→ file metadata

→ processing queue

Notification Worker

→ notification database

→ messaging infrastructure

Services shall not share a universal database superuser credential.

END OF 38.68

### 38.70 AUTHORIZATION TEST MATRIX

Revoked session → denied

Missing permission → denied

Wrong resource ID → denied

This testing must be automated.

### 38.75 SECURITY ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA

Part 38 shall be considered complete only when:

- Zero-trust architecture is defined.

- Authentication is separated from authorization.

- Resource authorization is implemented.

- Field-level authorization is implemented.

- Function-level authorization is implemented.

- Tenant isolation is implemented.

- Session management is implemented.

- Password security is implemented.

- MFA architecture is defined.

- OTP security is defined.

- Email verification is defined.

- Account recovery is secured.

- API keys are protected.

- OAuth connections are protected.

- AI memory is isolated.

- AI context is authorization-aware.

- Prompt injection is treated as a security threat.

- AI tools have explicit permissions.

- High-risk AI actions require appropriate confirmation.

- Web retrieval is protected against SSRF.

- File uploads are validated and isolated.

- Database access follows least privilege.

- Mass assignment is prevented.

- Input validation is centralized.

- Output rendering is protected.

- XSS protections are implemented.

- CSRF protections are implemented where required.

- CORS is explicitly configured.

- Security headers are implemented.

- Rate limiting is implemented.

- AI cost abuse is controlled.

- Security audit logs are implemented.

- Anomaly detection is implemented.

- Bot protection is implemented.

- Security configuration is validated.

- Debug endpoints are isolated.

- API inventory is maintained.

- Third-party API responses are treated as untrusted.

- Plugin permissions are enforced.

- Plugin execution is isolated where required.

- Sensitive data is minimized.

- AI provider data sharing is policy-controlled.

- Internal services use least privilege.

- Service-to-service trust is explicitly established.

- Security tests are automated.

- Authorization matrices are tested.

- AI security tests are automated.

- Data leakage tests are automated.

- Tenant isolation tests are automated.

- Security is included in the production release gate.

- Security architecture does not create an unnecessary centralized performance bottleneck.

- All security-sensitive operations have traceable audit events.

- No frontend-only security control is treated as authoritative.

- No AI-generated instruction can override authorization policy.

- No user-controlled identifier can bypass resource authorization.

## PART 39 — COMPLETE API CONTRACT, REQUEST/RESPONSE, ERROR HANDLING AND SERVICE COMMUNICATION ARCHITECTURE

### 39.1 PURPOSE

GSIR shall use a strict, versioned, typed, predictable API architecture.

Every frontend feature, backend service, database operation, AI operation, background worker, external provider, and internal service communication must follow defined contracts.

The API architecture must ensure:

Frontend

↓

API Contract

↓

Validation

↓

Authentication

↓

Authorization

↓

Application Service

↓

Domain Logic

↓

Repository

↓

Database / External Service

The response must travel back through controlled layers:

Database / External Service

↓

Repository

↓

Domain Result

↓

Application Service

↓

Response Mapper

↓

API Contract

↓

Frontend

No frontend component shall directly depend on database structures.

No controller shall contain business logic.

No AI model shall directly access the database.

No external provider response shall be returned directly to the frontend.

END OF 39.1

### 39.2 API ARCHITECTURE PRINCIPLES

GSIR APIs shall follow these principles:

- Strong typing.

- Explicit request schemas.

- Explicit response schemas.

- Versioned APIs.

- Consistent error structures.

- Consistent pagination.

- Consistent filtering.

- Consistent sorting.

- Consistent validation.

- Consistent authentication.

- Consistent authorization.

- Consistent request IDs.

- Consistent tracing.

- Consistent audit behavior.

- Backward compatibility where required.

- Idempotency for appropriate operations.

- Streaming support for AI responses.

- Asynchronous processing for expensive operations.

- No unnecessary data exposure.

- No database schema leakage.

END OF 39.2

### 39.6 CONTROLLER RESPONSIBILITY

A controller shall not:

Call an AI provider directly

Implement business rules

Implement authorization rules manually

Process large files

Perform long-running research

Contain complex reasoning

### 39.10 GPT-STYLE TYPED DATA ARCHITECTURE

├── id

### 39.13 AI RESPONSE STRUCTURE

The AI response architecture shall separate visible answer content from supporting metadata.

### 39.22 PAGINATION

201 → Created

202 → Accepted for asynchronous processing

204 → Successful request without response body

403 → Forbidden

409 → Conflict
