Database Conversation

        ↓

Conversation Domain Model

        ↓

ConversationResponse

This prevents database implementation changes from breaking the frontend.

END OF 39.47

### 39.48 API MAPPING LAYER

Response mapping shall be centralized.

Example:

backend/src/api/v1/mappers/conversation.mapper.ts

The mapper shall:

Select public fields

Transform internal types

Remove sensitive fields

Format timestamps

Normalize nested objects

Build API response

END OF 39.48

### 39.49 DATABASE QUERY BOUNDARY

Controllers and API contracts shall never execute database queries.

Correct:

Controller

↓

Service

↓

Repository

↓

Database

Incorrect:

Controller

↓

Database

END OF 39.49

### 39.50 AI PROVIDER BOUNDARY

AI API endpoints shall never directly call OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, local models, or any other provider.

Correct:

AI Controller

↓

AI Application Service

↓

AI Orchestrator

↓

Model Router

↓

Provider Adapter

↓

Provider

This ensures provider replacement does not require rewriting the application.

END OF 39.50

### 39.51 EXTERNAL PROVIDER RESPONSE NORMALIZATION

Provider-specific responses shall be converted into GSIR's internal AI contract.

Provider A Response

Provider B Response

Provider C Response

Local Model Response

        ↓

Provider Adapter

        ↓

NormalizedAIResponse

The frontend shall never depend on provider-specific response formats.

END OF 39.51

### 39.52 API TIMEOUT ARCHITECTURE

Every network operation shall have a defined timeout.

Timeouts shall exist for:

Frontend → API

API → Service

Service → Database

Service → Queue

AI Gateway → Provider

Provider → External Tool

Web Search → Website

File Processing

Infinite waits are prohibited.

END OF 39.52

### 39.53 REQUEST CANCELLATION

Long-running operations shall support cancellation where technically possible.

For AI:

User presses Stop

↓

Cancellation Request

↓

AI Run Manager

↓

Provider Adapter

↓

Provider cancellation

↓

Persist cancelled state

↓

Frontend updated

Cancellation must not leave the database in an inconsistent state.

END OF 39.53

### 39.54 CONCURRENCY CONTROL

Concurrent modifications must be protected.

Examples:

Two browser tabs editing the same note

Two workers updating the same research job

Repeated save requests

Multiple AI workers processing the same task

The system shall use appropriate:

Optimistic locking

Version numbers

Idempotency keys

Distributed locks where necessary

Database constraints

END OF 39.54

### 39.55 API CACHING

Caching shall be applied only where safe.

Suitable candidates:

Public configuration

Model metadata

Static settings

Permission metadata

Frequently accessed non-sensitive reference data

Private user data shall use user-aware cache keys and appropriate invalidation.

AI responses shall not be globally cached merely because two requests have similar text.

END OF 39.55

### 39.56 API PERFORMANCE

The API layer shall be designed for high concurrency.

It shall use:

Stateless application instances

Connection pooling

Async I/O

Caching

Queues

Horizontal scaling

Efficient serialization

Pagination

Batch operations

Streaming

Backpressure

The one-crore-query objective shall not be interpreted as requiring one process to execute ten million requests simultaneously.

Instead, the architecture shall distribute the workload horizontally.

END OF 39.56

### 39.57 ONE-CRORE-QUERY SCALING MODEL

Target:

10,000,000 concurrent/request-scale workloads

The architecture shall use:

Users

↓

CDN / Edge

↓

Load Balancers

↓

API Gateway Cluster

↓

Stateless API Cluster

↓

Queues

↓

Worker Cluster

↓

Distributed Database

↓

Search Cluster

↓

Object Storage

AI workloads shall be separated from ordinary CRUD traffic.

CRUD Traffic

        ↓

API Cluster

AI Traffic

        ↓

AI Gateway

        ↓

AI Worker Cluster

END OF 39.57

### 39.58 BACKPRESSURE

When downstream systems cannot process additional work, the API must not continue accepting unlimited work.

The system shall use:

Queue limits

Concurrency limits

Provider quotas

User quotas

Organization quotas

Priority queues

Load shedding

Retry policies

This prevents cascading failures.

END OF 39.58

### 39.59 PRIORITY QUEUES

GSIR shall support workload priorities.

Example:

Critical

High

Normal

Low

Background

Possible mapping:

Interactive Chat → High

Research Job → Normal

File Indexing → Normal

Analytics → Normal

Self-Improvement Experiment → Background

Large Reindex → Background

END OF 39.59

### 39.60 API OBSERVABILITY

Every API request shall be measurable.

Metrics:

Request count

Success rate

Error rate

Latency

P50

P95

P99

Timeouts

Rate-limit events

Payload size

Database latency

External provider latency

AI latency

Metrics shall be associated with:

endpoint

method

status

service

region

request class

Sensitive user data must not be used as metric labels.

END OF 39.60

### 39.61 API HEALTH ENDPOINTS

The backend shall expose appropriate health checks.

Conceptually:

/health/live

/health/ready

Liveness answers:

Is the process alive?

Readiness answers:

Can this instance safely receive traffic?

Deep dependency checks should not make basic liveness checks unnecessarily expensive.

END OF 39.61

### 39.62 API SECURITY INTEGRATION

Every API endpoint must connect to the security architecture defined in Part 38.

↓

↓

Authorization Middleware

↓

Rate Limit Middleware

↓

Validation

↓

Controller

No endpoint may bypass these controls without an explicit documented exception.

END OF 39.62

Every endpoint shall have:

        ↕

OpenAPI contract

        ↕

Backend response

Breaking API changes must fail CI before deployment.

END OF 39.64

Repository

### 39.73 PART 39 ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA

Part 39 shall be considered complete only when:

- API versioning is defined.

- API routes are modular.

- Controllers are thin.

- Request contracts are typed.

- Response contracts are typed.

- API errors are standardized.

- HTTP status mapping is standardized.

- Pagination is standardized.

- Filtering is validated.

- Sorting is validated.

- Search contracts are defined.

- Chat contracts are defined.

- AI responses are structured.

- AI streaming events are structured.

- Stream sequence numbers are defined.

- Request IDs are propagated.

- Trace IDs are supported.

- Async jobs are defined.

- Job state transitions are defined.

- Idempotency is supported where required.

- Retry behavior is explicitly defined.

- Cancellation is supported where required.

- Concurrency control is defined.

- Frontend API access is centralized.

- Database structures are separated from API structures.

- Response mapping is centralized.

- AI provider responses are normalized.

- Provider-specific formats do not leak into the frontend.

- API timeouts are defined.

- Backpressure is implemented.

- Priority queues are supported.

- API observability is implemented.

- Health checks are implemented.

- Security middleware is mandatory.

- API contract testing is implemented.

- Integration testing is implemented.

- AI-specific integration testing is implemented.

- Failure recovery is implemented.

- All major frontend features have corresponding APIs.

- Every endpoint has a documented owner.

- Duplicate business logic is prohibited.

- OpenAPI documentation is maintained.

- Breaking API changes are detected before deployment.

- API performance supports horizontal scaling.

- The architecture supports the one-crore-query scalability objective through distributed infrastructure rather than a single-process design.

- Every API operation has a defined security, validation, error, and observability path.

END OF PART 39

PART 39 COMPLETED.

# PART 40 — COMPLETE DATABASE ARCHITECTURE, DATA MODEL, RELATIONSHIPS, STORAGE STRATEGY AND DATABASE IMPLEMENTATION BLUEPRINT

## 40.1 PURPOSE

The GSIR database shall be the authoritative persistence layer for application state, user data, project data, conversations, messages, notes, files, research metadata, laboratory information, supplier information, AI configuration, usage information, security records, notifications, jobs, and system governance data.

The database architecture must support:

Correctness

Scalability

High concurrency

Strong data isolation

Low operating cost

Fast reads

Fast writes

Reliable transactions

Auditing

Data recovery

Future extensibility

AI workloads

Research workloads

Large-scale search

The database must not become a bottleneck for the one-crore-query scalability objective.

The architecture shall therefore separate transactional data, search/index data, object/file storage, cache data, and high-volume event/job data according to workload.

END OF 40.1

## 40.2 DATABASE ARCHITECTURE PRINCIPLE

GSIR shall follow the principle:

One authoritative transactional source

+

Specialized storage for specialized workloads

The primary transactional database shall contain authoritative application records.

Other systems may contain derived or optimized representations.

Example:

PostgreSQL

    ↓

Authoritative application state

Search Index

    ↓

Search-optimized representation

Vector Index

    ↓

Semantic retrieval representation

Redis

    ↓

Temporary/cache/session/rate-limit state

Object Storage

    ↓

Files and binary objects

Event/Queue System

    ↓

Asynchronous processing state

No derived storage shall silently become the authoritative source of truth.

END OF 40.2

## 40.3 DATABASE TECHNOLOGY STRATEGY

The initial GSIR architecture shall prefer PostgreSQL as the primary relational database.

Reason:

Strong relational model

ACID transactions

Rich indexing

JSON support

Constraints

Mature ecosystem

Excellent SQL capabilities

Reliable tooling

Horizontal scaling options

Strong TypeScript ecosystem

The system should avoid introducing multiple database engines prematurely.

Additional storage systems shall be introduced only when the workload requires them.

END OF 40.3

## 40.4 DATABASE LAYER STRUCTURE

The backend database layer shall use:

backend/

└── src/

    └── database/

        ├── database.module.ts

        ├── client.ts

        ├── config.ts

        ├── migrations/

        ├── seeds/

        ├── repositories/

        ├── models/

        ├── queries/

        ├── transactions/

        ├── mappers/

        └── index.ts

The database layer must remain independent from HTTP controllers.

END OF 40.4

## 40.5 EXACT DATABASE FILE RESPONSIBILITIES

### database.module.ts

Responsible for initializing the database subsystem.

### client.ts

Responsible for database connection/client management.

### config.ts

Responsible for database configuration.

### migrations/

Contains version-controlled schema changes.

### seeds/

Contains controlled development/test/reference data.

### repositories/

Contains persistence operations.

### models/

Contains database-facing models/types.

### queries/

Contains complex reusable database queries.

### transactions/

Contains transaction utilities and transaction boundaries.

### mappers/

Converts database records into domain representations.

END OF 40.5

## 40.6 DATABASE DOMAIN ORGANIZATION

Database code shall be organized around GSIR domains.

Recommended structure:

backend/src/database/repositories/

├── user.repository.ts

├── profile.repository.ts

├── account.repository.ts

├── session.repository.ts

├── project.repository.ts

├── conversation.repository.ts

├── message.repository.ts

├── note.repository.ts

├── file.repository.ts

├── source.repository.ts

├── research.repository.ts

├── search.repository.ts

├── notification.repository.ts

├── settings.repository.ts

├── laboratory.repository.ts

├── supplier.repository.ts

├── connection.repository.ts

├── ai-run.repository.ts

├── model.repository.ts

├── usage.repository.ts

├── job.repository.ts

├── audit.repository.ts

└── index.ts

END OF 40.6

## 40.7 CORE DATABASE DOMAINS

The database shall contain the following major domains:

## 40.8 TENANCY AND DATA OWNERSHIP

GSIR shall be designed so that user-owned data is explicitly associated with its owner.

The architecture shall support future organization/workspace tenancy.

├── Policies

└── Billing

## 40.56 DATABASE TRANSACTIONS

Transactions shall be used when multiple related changes must succeed or fail together.

Example:

Create Project

↓

Create Project Membership

↓

Create Project Settings

If any mandatory operation fails:

ROLLBACK

The system must not leave partially initialized projects.

## 40.57 TRANSACTION BOUNDARY

Transaction boundaries shall be owned by application services rather than controllers.

Correct:

Controller

↓

ProjectService

↓

BEGIN TRANSACTION

├── Create Project

├── Create Membership

└── Create Settings

COMMIT

## 40.58 DATABASE CONSTRAINTS

Critical business rules shall be enforced at the database level wherever possible.

Examples:

NOT NULL

UNIQUE

FOREIGN KEY

CHECK

PRIMARY KEY

Application validation remains necessary, but database constraints provide a final integrity boundary.

END OF 40.58

## 40.59 FOREIGN KEY STRATEGY

Foreign keys shall be used for relationships where referential integrity is required.

Examples:

messages.conversation_id

→ conversations.id

conversations.project_id

→ projects.id

projects.owner_id

→ users.id

Deletion behavior must be explicitly defined.

No uncontrolled cascading deletion shall be introduced.

END OF 40.59

## 40.60 SOFT DELETE

Soft deletion shall be used where recovery, auditing, or legal retention requires it.

Typical fields:

deleted_at

deleted_by

Soft-deleted records must not accidentally appear in normal application queries.

Repositories shall provide explicit filtering.

END OF 40.60

## 40.61 HARD DELETE

Hard deletion shall be reserved for cases where permanent removal is required.

Account deletion must follow the data-retention and deletion workflow.

Related data shall be handled systematically rather than through uncontrolled cascading operations.

END OF 40.61

## 40.62 DATABASE INDEXING

Indexes shall be created based on actual query patterns.

Important indexes include:

users.email

conversations.user_id

conversations.project_id

conversations.updated_at

messages.conversation_id

messages.created_at

notes.user_id

notes.project_id

files.owner_id

files.project_id

research_jobs.project_id

notifications.user_id

audit_logs.user_id

ai_runs.user_id

ai_runs.created_at

Indexes must be reviewed using real query plans.

END OF 40.62

## 40.63 COMPOSITE INDEXES

Where queries frequently combine fields, composite indexes shall be considered.

Example:

conversations(user_id, updated_at)

This supports:

Get user's conversations ordered by recent activity

Indexes must reflect real access patterns rather than being added indiscriminately.

END OF 40.63

## 40.64 DATABASE PARTITIONING

High-volume tables may eventually require partitioning.

Candidates include:

messages

ai_usage_records

audit_logs

search_history

events

Partitioning shall be introduced only after workload analysis demonstrates the need.

Time-based partitioning may be appropriate for high-volume historical records.

END OF 40.64

## 40.65 READ SCALING

Read-heavy workloads may use read replicas.

Architecture:

Application

├── Write Operations

│      ↓

│   Primary DB

│

└── Read Operations

       ↓

    Read Replica

The application must understand replication lag.

Strongly consistent reads shall go to the primary database where necessary.

END OF 40.65

## 40.66 WRITE SCALING

Write scaling shall not be attempted through arbitrary database duplication.

The architecture shall first optimize:

Indexes

Queries

Transactions

Batching

Connection pooling

Partitioning

Queue-based writes

Only then should more advanced sharding strategies be introduced.

END OF 40.66

## 40.67 SHARDING PREPARATION

GSIR shall be designed so that future sharding is possible.

Potential shard keys:

organization_id

user_id

region

The initial implementation may remain on a single logical PostgreSQL cluster while keeping domain boundaries clean.

END OF 40.67

## 40.68 DATABASE CONNECTION POOLING

The backend must use connection pooling.

Every application instance shall have controlled connection limits.

The system must not create one database connection per incoming HTTP request.

Connection usage shall be monitored.

END OF 40.68

## 40.69 DATABASE QUERY RULE

Repositories shall never construct unsafe dynamic SQL from user input.

All user-controlled values must use parameterized queries or a safe ORM/query builder mechanism.

END OF 40.69

## 40.70 N+1 QUERY PREVENTION

Repository implementations must avoid N+1 query patterns.

Example:

Incorrect:

Load 100 conversations

↓

Run one query for each conversation

Correct:

Load conversations

↓

Batch-load required related records

Performance tests shall detect common N+1 patterns.

END OF 40.70

## 40.71 DATABASE CACHE

Short-lived cache

Rate limits

Temporary session state

Frequently accessed reference data

Redis shall not replace PostgreSQL as the authoritative database.

END OF 40.71

## 40.72 CACHE INVALIDATION

Whenever cached data changes:

Database Update

↓

Cache Invalidation / Update

↓

Future Read

User-specific data must never leak through shared cache keys.

## 40.83 DATABASE COST OPTIMIZATION

To maintain maximum output at low cost:

Use efficient indexes

Avoid unnecessary writes

Batch writes

Use asynchronous processing

Archive cold data

Use object storage for large files

Use read replicas when justified

Use caching for safe hot data

Partition high-volume tables when necessary

Avoid storing duplicate representations unnecessarily

## 40.84 ONE-CRORE-QUERY DATABASE STRATEGY

The one-crore-query objective requires workload separation.

Architecture:

10,000,000-scale traffic

        │

        ▼

Load Balancer

        │

        ▼

Stateless API Cluster

        │

   ┌────┼──────────────┐

   │    │              │

   ▼    ▼              ▼

Cache  PostgreSQL    Search

   │    │              │

   │    ├── Primary   │

   │    └── Replicas  │

   │                   │

   └────────┬──────────┘

            ▼

       Object Storage

Not every request shall reach PostgreSQL.

The architecture shall aggressively eliminate unnecessary database traffic through:

Caching

Search indexes

Local application state

Batching

Pagination

Event-driven updates

END OF 40.84

PART 41 — COMPLETE BACKEND DOMAIN ARCHITECTURE, APPLICATION SERVICES, USE-CASE LAYER, DOMAIN LOGIC AND MODULE CONNECTION BLUEPRINT

41.1 PURPOSE

The GSIR backend shall be organized as a modular domain-driven application in which every major feature has a clearly defined responsibility, input, output, business logic, persistence boundary, API boundary, testing strategy, and connection to other modules.

The backend must not become a collection of controllers containing business logic or a collection of database queries directly exposed to the frontend.

The required architecture is:

Frontend ↓ API Route ↓ Controller ↓ Request DTO Validation ↓ Application Service / Use Case ↓ Domain Logic ↓ Repository Interface ↓ Repository Implementation ↓ Database / External Infrastructure ↓ Application Result ↓ Response DTO ↓ Frontend

The architecture must preserve strict separation between:

- Transport logic

- Application/use-case logic

- Domain/business logic

- Persistence logic

- External provider logic

- AI orchestration logic

- Background processing

- Security

- Observability

END OF 41.1

41.2 CORE BACKEND PRINCIPLE

Every backend feature shall answer the following questions before implementation:

- What problem does this module solve?

- What data does it own?

- What input does it accept?

- What validation does it perform?

- What business rules does it enforce?

- Which repository does it use?

- Which external services does it call?

- What output does it produce?

- What errors can occur?

- What events are generated?

- What permissions are required?

- How is the feature tested?

- How is the feature monitored?

- How does the feature scale?

No feature shall be implemented only because a frontend button exists.

Every frontend capability must map to a complete backend use case.

END OF 41.2

41.3 EXACT BACKEND ROOT STRUCTURE

The GSIR backend shall use the following modular structure:

backend/ └── src/ ├── app/ ├── config/ ├── common/ ├── modules/ ├── domain/ ├── database/ ├── infrastructure/ ├── ai/ ├── jobs/ ├── events/ ├── security/ ├── observability/ ├── health/ ├── api/ └── main.ts

This structure shall remain stable as the application grows.

END OF 41.3

41.4 APPLICATION ROOT

The application root shall contain:

backend/src/app/

Files:

backend/src/app/app.module.ts backend/src/app/app.bootstrap.ts backend/src/app/app.lifecycle.ts backend/src/app/app.constants.ts

Responsibilities:

app.module.ts → Registers major application modules.

app.bootstrap.ts → Initializes the application.

app.lifecycle.ts → Handles startup and shutdown lifecycle.

app.constants.ts → Contains application-level constants that are not secrets.

END OF 41.4

41.5 CONFIGURATION MODULE

Directory:

backend/src/config/

Files:

backend/src/config/config.module.ts backend/src/config/env.schema.ts backend/src/config/app.config.ts backend/src/config/database.config.ts backend/src/config/ai.config.ts backend/src/config/storage.config.ts backend/src/config/cache.config.ts backend/src/config/queue.config.ts backend/src/config/security.config.ts backend/src/config/observability.config.ts backend/src/config/index.ts

The configuration layer shall load and validate configuration before the application becomes ready.

Invalid configuration must prevent unsafe startup.

END OF 41.5

41.6 COMMON MODULE

Directory:

backend/src/common/

Structure:

backend/src/common/ ├── constants/ ├── errors/ ├── types/ ├── enums/ ├── utils/ ├── validators/ ├── pagination/ ├── serialization/ ├── id/ ├── time/ └── index.ts

This directory contains genuinely shared utilities.

Business-specific logic must not be placed here merely to avoid creating a domain module.

END OF 41.6

41.7 MODULE ARCHITECTURE

Each major GSIR feature shall become a backend module.

Required modules include:

backend/src/modules/ ├── auth/ ├── users/ ├── profiles/ ├── projects/ ├── conversations/ ├── messages/ ├── notes/ ├── files/ ├── sources/ ├── research/ ├── search/ ├── memory/ ├── notifications/ ├── settings/ ├── connections/ ├── laboratory/ ├── suppliers/ ├── ai/ ├── usage/ ├── billing/ ├── accessibility/ ├── exports/ ├── audit/ └── admin/

Additional modules may be added only when a distinct responsibility exists.

END OF 41.7

41.8 STANDARD MODULE STRUCTURE

Every module should follow a predictable structure.

Example:

backend/src/modules/projects/

├── projects.module.ts ├── controllers/ │ └── projects.controller.ts ├── dto/ │ ├── create-project.request.ts │ ├── update-project.request.ts │ ├── project.response.ts │ └── project-list.response.ts ├── application/ │ ├── commands/ │ ├── queries/ │ ├── services/ │ └── use-cases/ ├── domain/ │ ├── entities/ │ ├── value-objects/ │ ├── rules/ │ └── interfaces/ ├── repositories/ │ └── projects.repository.ts ├── mappers/ │ └── project.mapper.ts ├── policies/ │ └── project.policy.ts ├── events/ │ └── project.events.ts ├── tests/ └── index.ts

END OF 41.8

41.9 CONTROLLER RESPONSIBILITY

Controllers shall remain thin.

A controller may:

- Receive HTTP input.

- Read authenticated identity.

- Validate request DTOs.

- Call an application use case.

- Translate the result into an HTTP response.

- Return appropriate status/error information.

A controller must not:

- Execute database queries directly.

- Contain complex business rules.

- Call an AI provider directly.

- Perform long-running research.

- Implement authorization logic inline.

- Construct complex domain objects manually.

- Manage database transactions directly unless the architecture explicitly delegates transaction execution through an application service.

END OF 41.9

41.10 APPLICATION SERVICE RESPONSIBILITY

Application services coordinate complete use cases.

Example:

Create Project:

Controller ↓ CreateProjectUseCase ↓ Authorization ↓ Validation ↓ Project Domain ↓ Project Repository ↓ Project Event ↓ Response

Application services are responsible for orchestration, not for replacing the domain model with an enormous service class.

END OF 41.10

41.11 USE-CASE FILE NAMING

Each meaningful business operation shall have an explicit use-case file.

Examples:

backend/src/modules/projects/application/use-cases/create-project.use-case.ts

backend/src/modules/projects/application/use-cases/update-project.use-case.ts

backend/src/modules/projects/application/use-cases/archive-project.use-case.ts

backend/src/modules/projects/application/use-cases/get-project.use-case.ts

backend/src/modules/projects/application/use-cases/list-projects.use-case.ts

backend/src/modules/projects/application/use-cases/delete-project.use-case.ts

This naming makes the system understandable to developers.

END OF 41.11

41.12 COMMAND AND QUERY SEPARATION

GSIR shall distinguish state-changing operations from read operations.

Commands:

Create Update Delete Archive Restore Save Send Start Cancel Verify Approve

Queries:

Get List Search Retrieve Find History Statistics

Commands may modify state.

Queries must not unexpectedly modify persistent state.

END OF 41.12

41.13 COMMAND STRUCTURE

Example:

backend/src/modules/projects/application/commands/create-project.command.ts

The command represents application intent.

Conceptual structure:

CreateProjectCommand ├── actorId ├── name ├── description ├── visibility └── optional project metadata

The command must not contain HTTP-specific objects.

END OF 41.13

41.14 QUERY STRUCTURE

Example:

backend/src/modules/projects/application/queries/get-project.query.ts

A query contains the minimum information required to retrieve data.

Example:

GetProjectQuery ├── actorId └── projectId

The query layer may use optimized read projections when the complete domain entity is unnecessary.

END OF 41.14

41.15 DOMAIN ENTITY

Domain entities represent important business objects.

Examples:

User Project Conversation Message Note ResearchJob ResearchFinding Laboratory Supplier AI Run

Entities shall contain domain behavior where that behavior belongs to the entity.

END OF 41.15

41.16 VALUE OBJECTS

Value objects shall be used for important validated concepts.

Examples:

EmailAddress ProjectName ConversationTitle FileHash ModelIdentifier ResearchConfidence Timezone Currency TokenCount UserPreference

Value objects prevent invalid data from spreading through the application.

END OF 41.16

41.17 DOMAIN RULES

Domain rules shall be placed in explicit rule/policy files when they become complex.

Example:

backend/src/modules/projects/domain/rules/project-access.rule.ts

Possible rule:

A user may modify a project only when:

User is owner OR User is an authorized project member OR User has an explicitly granted administrative permission.

END OF 41.17

41.18 AUTHORIZATION ARCHITECTURE

Authentication answers:

“Who is this user?”

Authorization answers:

“Is this user allowed to perform this action?”

These must remain separate.

Required authorization flow:

Request ↓ Authentication ↓ Actor Identity ↓ Resource Lookup ↓ Authorization Policy ↓ Use Case ↓ Execution

END OF 41.18

41.19 POLICY FILES

Authorization policies shall use explicit files.

Examples:

backend/src/modules/projects/policies/project.policy.ts

backend/src/modules/conversations/policies/conversation.policy.ts

backend/src/modules/files/policies/file.policy.ts

backend/src/modules/research/policies/research.policy.ts

backend/src/modules/laboratory/policies/laboratory.policy.ts

Policies must prevent ID-based unauthorized access.

END OF 41.19

41.20 REPOSITORY INTERFACE

Repositories provide the persistence boundary.

Example:

backend/src/modules/projects/repositories/projects.repository.ts

The repository interface shall expose domain-oriented operations.

Examples:

create() findById() findForUser() update() archive() delete()

Repositories shall not receive HTTP request DTOs.

Repositories shall not return HTTP response DTOs.

END OF 41.20

41.21 REPOSITORY IMPLEMENTATION

The persistence implementation shall live in the infrastructure/database layer.

Example:

backend/src/database/repositories/project.repository.ts

Connection:

ProjectsUseCase ↓ ProjectsRepository Interface ↓ ProjectRepository Implementation ↓ Database Client ↓ PostgreSQL

END OF 41.21

41.22 WHY THE REPOSITORY BOUNDARY EXISTS

The repository boundary allows the application layer to remain independent from the database implementation.

This provides:

- Easier testing.

- Database implementation flexibility.

- Better separation of responsibilities.

- Safer refactoring.

- Controlled data access.

- Better observability.

- Easier future scaling.

No module shall bypass its repository and directly query PostgreSQL.

END OF 41.22

41.23 DTO ARCHITECTURE

GSIR shall use separate types for different boundaries.

Required conceptual type layers:

API Request DTO ↓ Application Command/Input ↓ Domain Entity / Value Object ↓ Persistence Model ↓ Application Result ↓ API Response DTO

A database entity must never automatically become the public API response.

END OF 41.23

41.24 REQUEST DTO

Example:

backend/src/modules/projects/dto/create-project.request.ts

Purpose:

Validate incoming API data.

The request DTO shall contain only fields the client is allowed to submit.

The client must never be able to submit protected fields such as:

owner_id created_at updated_at internal_status security_flags billing_state

END OF 41.24

41.25 RESPONSE DTO

Example:

backend/src/modules/projects/dto/project.response.ts

The response DTO defines exactly what the frontend receives.

Internal database fields must remain hidden.

Sensitive fields must never be returned merely because they exist on an entity.

END OF 41.25

41.26 GSIR RESPONSE ARCHITECTURE

All normal API responses shall follow a consistent structure.

Conceptual success response:

{ "success": true, "data": {}, "meta": {} }

Conceptual error response:

{ "success": false, "error": { "code": "", "message": "", "details": {} }, "requestId": "" }

The exact serialization implementation shall be centralized.

END OF 41.26

41.27 RESPONSE DATA RULE

The API response shall contain only data required by the frontend.

The backend must avoid:

- Returning complete database records unnecessarily.

- Returning internal provider information.

- Returning secrets.

- Returning internal stack traces.

- Returning unnecessary system metadata.

- Returning another user's information.

END OF 41.27

41.28 ERROR ARCHITECTURE

GSIR shall use structured error classes.

Directory:

backend/src/common/errors/

Files:

backend/src/common/errors/app.error.ts backend/src/common/errors/auth.error.ts backend/src/common/errors/authorization.error.ts backend/src/common/errors/validation.error.ts backend/src/common/errors/not-found.error.ts backend/src/common/errors/conflict.error.ts backend/src/common/errors/rate-limit.error.ts backend/src/common/errors/provider.error.ts backend/src/common/errors/database.error.ts backend/src/common/errors/timeout.error.ts backend/src/common/errors/index.ts

END OF 41.28

41.29 ERROR CODES

Errors shall use stable machine-readable codes.

Examples:

AUTH_REQUIRED AUTH_INVALID ACCESS_DENIED RESOURCE_NOT_FOUND VALIDATION_FAILED RESOURCE_CONFLICT RATE_LIMITED AI_PROVIDER_UNAVAILABLE AI_TIMEOUT AI_CONTENT_INVALID DATABASE_UNAVAILABLE INTERNAL_ERROR

Frontend behavior must depend on error codes rather than fragile error-message text.

END OF 41.29

41.30 TRANSACTION ARCHITECTURE

Transactions shall be controlled at the application use-case level.

Example:

CreateProjectUseCase ↓ Transaction ├── Create Project ├── Create Membership ├── Create Settings └── Create Audit Event ↓ Commit

Failure:

Rollback

END OF 41.30

41.31 MODULE DEPENDENCY RULE

Dependencies shall flow inward toward stable business logic.

Correct:

Controller ↓ Application ↓ Domain

Infrastructure ↓ implements interfaces

Incorrect:

Domain ↓ Controller

Domain ↓ HTTP

Domain ↓ PostgreSQL

Domain ↓ AI Provider SDK

END OF 41.31

41.32 AI MODULE ISOLATION

The general application modules shall not directly call OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, local models, or other model providers.

Correct:

Conversation Module ↓ AI Application Interface ↓ AI Orchestrator ↓ Model Router ↓ Provider Adapter ↓ External Model

This prevents provider-specific code from spreading across the backend.

END OF 41.32

41.33 AI MODULE STRUCTURE

backend/src/ai/

├── ai.module.ts ├── contracts/ ├── orchestration/ ├── routing/ ├── providers/ ├── reasoning/ ├── context/ ├── memory/ ├── retrieval/ ├── tools/ ├── streaming/ ├── safety/ ├── evaluation/ ├── optimization/ └── index.ts

Detailed AI architecture shall be defined in the dedicated AI architecture parts of this master document.

END OF 41.33

41.34 CONVERSATION MODULE CONNECTION

Conversation flow:

backend/src/modules/conversations/

ConversationController ↓ ConversationService / Use Case ↓ ConversationPolicy ↓ ConversationRepository ↓ PostgreSQL

For AI execution:

Conversation ↓ Message ↓ AI Run ↓ AI Orchestrator

END OF 41.34

41.35 MESSAGE MODULE CONNECTION

Message flow:

MessageController ↓ SendMessageUseCase ↓ ConversationPolicy ↓ ConversationRepository ↓ MessageRepository ↓ AI Orchestrator ↓ Streaming Layer ↓ Message Persistence ↓ Response Stream

END OF 41.35

41.36 CHAT RESPONSE RELIABILITY

The AI response process shall not assume that generation always succeeds.

State progression:

queued ↓ processing ↓ streaming ↓ completed

Failure states:

failed cancelled timeout

The frontend must receive a deterministic final state.

END OF 41.36

41.37 STREAMING ARCHITECTURE

Streaming shall be separated from model generation.

Architecture:

AI Orchestrator ↓ Provider Stream ↓ Stream Adapter ↓ AI Stream Service ↓ API Streaming Transport ↓ Frontend

The streaming layer must not directly expose provider-specific response formats.

END OF 41.37

41.38 RESEARCH MODULE

Research shall be implemented as a workflow rather than a single AI request.

Research flow:

ResearchController ↓ CreateResearchJobUseCase ↓ Research Job Repository ↓ Queue ↓ Research Worker ↓ Search ↓ Source Collection ↓ Document Processing ↓ Retrieval ↓ Reasoning ↓ Claim Extraction ↓ Verification ↓ Research Findings ↓ Final Report

END OF 41.38

41.39 RESEARCH JOB ISOLATION

Long-running research must never block the normal HTTP request.

The API shall:

- Create the job.

- Persist job state.

- Queue the job.

- Return a job identifier.

- Process asynchronously.

- Update progress.

- Store results.

- Notify the frontend.

This prevents long-running research from consuming API worker capacity.

END OF 41.39

41.40 NOTES MODULE

Notes shall support:

Create Read Update Delete Archive Restore Autosave Versioning Search Project association

Architecture:

NotesController ↓ Note Use Case ↓ Note Policy ↓ Note Repository ↓ PostgreSQL

Autosave:

Frontend debounce ↓ Autosave API ↓ UpdateNoteUseCase ↓ Note Repository ↓ Database

END OF 41.40

41.41 NOTIFICATION MODULE

Notifications shall be divided into:

Transient notifications Persistent notifications System notifications Security notifications Research notifications AI notifications

Autosave notifications shall normally be transient.

Critical security events may be persistent.

END OF 41.41

41.42 NOTIFICATION DEDUPLICATION

The backend must support deduplication.

Example:

Note autosave ↓ Generate event ↓ Notification Service ↓ Deduplication key ↓ Existing notification? ├── Yes → update/refresh └── No → create

This prevents notification spam.

END OF 41.42

41.43 FILE MODULE

File architecture:

FileController ↓ UploadFileUseCase ↓ Authorization ↓ File Metadata Repository ↓ Object Storage ↓ Processing Job ↓ Document Processing ↓ Chunk Storage ↓ Search/Vector Index

END OF 41.43

41.44 PROJECT CONTEXT

Project context shall be assembled through a dedicated context service.

Example:

backend/src/ai/context/project-context.service.ts

Context flow:

Project ├── Project instructions ├── Conversations ├── Notes ├── Files ├── Sources ├── Research findings └── User permissions ↓ Project Context ↓ AI Orchestrator

END OF 41.44

41.45 USER CONTEXT

User context shall include only information explicitly permitted for AI use.

Flow:

User ↓ Profile ↓ Preferences ↓ Research Interests ↓ Allowed Memory ↓ User Context ↓ AI Context Builder

END OF 41.45

41.46 CONTEXT PRIORITY

Context shall be ranked rather than blindly concatenated.

Priority:

- Current user request

- Explicit project instructions

- Relevant conversation context

- Verified project knowledge

- Verified user memory

- Retrieved sources

- Lower-confidence historical context

Irrelevant context must be excluded.

END OF 41.46

41.47 MEMORY MODULE

Memory operations shall be isolated.

Required files:

backend/src/modules/memory/memory.module.ts

backend/src/modules/memory/controllers/memory.controller.ts

backend/src/modules/memory/application/use-cases/create-memory.use-case.ts

backend/src/modules/memory/application/use-cases/update-memory.use-case.ts

backend/src/modules/memory/application/use-cases/delete-memory.use-case.ts

backend/src/modules/memory/application/use-cases/retrieve-memory.use-case.ts

backend/src/modules/memory/repositories/memory.repository.ts

backend/src/modules/memory/policies/memory.policy.ts

END OF 41.47

41.48 MEMORY SAFETY

Memory must not automatically store every conversation statement.

A memory candidate must pass:

Candidate Detection ↓ Relevance Check ↓ User Scope Check ↓ Confidence Check ↓ Persistence Policy ↓ Memory Storage

Sensitive information must follow stricter handling rules.

END OF 41.48

41.49 SEARCH MODULE

Search shall be independent from ordinary CRUD operations.

Structure:

backend/src/modules/search/

├── search.module.ts ├── controllers/ ├── application/ ├── providers/ ├── ranking/ ├── filters/ ├── indexes/ ├── repositories/ └── tests/

END OF 41.49

41.50 HYBRID SEARCH

GSIR search shall eventually support:

Keyword search + Semantic search + Metadata filtering + Permission filtering + Project filtering + Recency + Source quality + Research relevance

The search module shall return ranked candidates rather than directly generating AI answers.

END OF 41.50

41.51 LABORATORY MODULE

Laboratory architecture:

LaboratoryController ↓ Laboratory Use Cases ↓ Laboratory Policy ↓ Laboratory Repository ↓ PostgreSQL

Separate capabilities:

Laboratory Profile Equipment Ratings Permissions Safety Technical Support Cost Staff Chemicals Instruments

END OF 41.51

41.52 SUPPLIER MODULE

Supplier architecture:

SupplierController ↓ Supplier Use Cases ↓ Supplier Policy ↓ Supplier Repository ↓ PostgreSQL

Supplier search shall remain independent from AI generation.

AI may consume supplier information only through authorized APIs/services.

END OF 41.52

41.53 SETTINGS MODULE

Settings shall be divided into domain-specific use cases.

Examples:

UpdateGeneralSettingsUseCase UpdateAISettingsUseCase UpdatePrivacySettingsUseCase UpdateChatSettingsUseCase UpdateAccessibilitySettingsUseCase UpdateVoiceSettingsUseCase

This prevents a single massive settings service.

END OF 41.53

41.54 ACCOUNT MODULE

Account operations shall include:

Change Password Verify Email Verify Mobile Connected Accounts Subscription Account Status Delete Account

Security-sensitive operations shall require stronger authentication where appropriate.

END OF 41.54

41.55 EXPORT MODULE

Data export shall be asynchronous.

Flow:

User requests export ↓ Authorization ↓ Create export job ↓ Queue ↓ Collect authorized data ↓ Generate export ↓ Object Storage ↓ Secure download reference ↓ Expiration

END OF 41.55

41.56 AUDIT MODULE

Audit events shall be generated from important application operations.

Example:

DeleteAccountUseCase ↓ Delete workflow ↓ AuditService ↓ AuditRepository ↓ audit_logs

END OF 41.56

41.57 EVENT ARCHITECTURE

Important asynchronous events shall use explicit event types.

Examples:

UserCreated ProjectCreated ProjectUpdated ConversationCreated MessageCreated AIResponseCompleted FileUploaded FileProcessed ResearchJobCompleted NoteSaved SecurityEventDetected

END OF 41.57

41.58 EVENT FILES

Event contracts shall be organized under:

backend/src/events/

Files:

backend/src/events/event-bus.ts backend/src/events/event.types.ts backend/src/events/event-publisher.ts backend/src/events/event-consumer.ts backend/src/events/index.ts

Domain-specific event definitions remain inside their modules when appropriate.

END OF 41.58

41.59 BACKGROUND JOB ARCHITECTURE

Jobs shall be used for operations that are:

- Long-running.

- Expensive.

- Retryable.

- Non-interactive.

- Asynchronous.

- Resource-intensive.

Examples:

Document processing Embedding generation Research Exports Analytics Email Notification processing Evaluation Model testing

END OF 41.59

41.60 JOB FILE STRUCTURE

backend/src/jobs/

├── job.module.ts ├── queues/ ├── workers/ ├── processors/ ├── handlers/ ├── retry/ └── index.ts

Each worker must have a clearly defined input and output contract.

END OF 41.60

41.61 RETRY ARCHITECTURE

Retries shall not be unlimited.

Every retryable job shall define:

max attempts backoff retryable errors non-retryable errors dead-letter behavior

Example:

Transient provider timeout → Retry

Invalid user input → Do not retry

Permanent authentication failure → Do not retry

END OF 41.61

41.62 IDEMPOTENCY

Important write operations shall support idempotency where duplicate execution could cause damage.

Examples:

Create payment Start research job Submit export Send external notification Process uploaded file

Repeated identical requests must not unintentionally create duplicate resources.

END OF 41.62

41.63 REQUEST ID

Every incoming request shall receive a request identifier.

Flow:

Request ↓ Request ID ↓ Controller ↓ Service ↓ Repository ↓ Logs ↓ Response

The request ID allows one operation to be traced across the complete backend.

END OF 41.63

41.64 CORRELATION ID

Long-running workflows shall use correlation identifiers.

Example:

Research Request ↓ Correlation ID ├── Search ├── Source Retrieval ├── Document Processing ├── AI Run ├── Verification └── Final Report

This is essential for debugging complex AI workflows.

END OF 41.64

41.65 LOGGING RULE

Application logs shall contain:

timestamp level service module operation requestId correlationId user-safe identifiers duration status error code

Logs must not contain passwords, access tokens, API keys, or sensitive secrets.

END OF 41.65

41.66 PERFORMANCE ARCHITECTURE

Backend performance shall be designed around:

Stateless API workers Connection pooling Caching Batch operations Asynchronous jobs Streaming Pagination Cursor-based retrieval Search indexes Read replicas when required Database query optimization

END OF 41.66

41.67 ONE-CRORE-QUERY APPLICATION STRATEGY

The one-crore-query requirement shall not mean that every request reaches every backend component.

Correct architecture:

10,000,000-scale request load ↓ Load Balancer ↓ Stateless API Instances ↓ Request Classification ├── Cache hit ├── Read API ├── Write API ├── Search ├── AI └── Async Job ↓ Specialized execution path

Only the required systems shall be contacted for each request.

END OF 41.67

41.68 AI REQUEST COST CONTROL

AI requests shall pass through:

Request ↓ Classification ↓ Cache Check ↓ Context Selection ↓ Model Selection ↓ Token Budget ↓ AI Execution

The system must avoid sending the entire project, entire history, and entire knowledge base to the model for every request.

END OF 41.68

41.69 HALLUCINATION CONTROL

Before final AI output:

Generation ↓ Evidence Check ↓ Citation Check ↓ Contradiction Check ↓ Confidence Assessment ↓ Response Formatter ↓ User

For high-risk research workflows, unsupported claims must be explicitly identified rather than presented as verified facts.

END OF 41.69

41.70 AI RESPONSE TYPES

The backend shall distinguish response types.

Examples:

DirectAnswer ResearchAnswer SearchAnswer ProjectAnswer FileAnswer ToolResult ClarificationRequest ErrorResponse PartialResponse

This allows the frontend to render the correct interface.

END OF 41.70

41.71 FRONTEND-BACKEND CONTRACT

Every frontend feature must have:

Frontend component ↓ API contract ↓ Request DTO ↓ Use case ↓ Domain logic ↓ Repository ↓ Database ↓ Response DTO ↓ Frontend state update

END OF 41.71

41.72 FEATURE COMPLETENESS RULE

A feature is not considered complete when the UI exists.

A feature is complete only when:

UI + API + Validation + Authorization + Business Logic + Persistence + Error Handling + Loading State + Empty State + Retry Behavior + Observability + Testing + Security + Performance + Recovery

are implemented and tested.

END OF 41.72

41.73 TESTING STRUCTURE

Every module shall contain:

Unit Tests Integration Tests Repository Tests API Tests Authorization Tests Error Tests

Important workflows shall additionally contain:

End-to-End Tests Concurrency Tests Performance Tests Failure Tests

END OF 41.73

41.74 EXACT TEST FILE NAMING

Example:

backend/src/modules/projects/tests/create-project.use-case.spec.ts

backend/src/modules/projects/tests/projects.repository.spec.ts

backend/src/modules/projects/tests/projects.controller.spec.ts

backend/src/modules/projects/tests/project.authorization.spec.ts

backend/src/modules/projects/tests/projects.e2e.spec.ts

END OF 41.74

41.75 MOCKING RULE

Unit tests shall not require real external AI providers, real payment providers, or real third-party services.

External dependencies shall be represented through interfaces and test doubles.

Integration tests shall separately validate real infrastructure behavior.

END OF 41.75

41.76 CONTRACT TESTING

API contracts shall be tested so that frontend and backend do not silently diverge.

Tests shall verify:

Request schema Response schema Error schema Required fields Optional fields Enum values Pagination Streaming behavior where applicable

END OF 41.76

41.77 MODULE OWNERSHIP RULE

Each module must own its business logic.

For example:

Projects module owns project rules.

Conversations module owns conversation rules.

Messages module owns message rules.

Research module owns research workflow rules.

Laboratory module owns laboratory rules.

Supplier module owns supplier rules.

No unrelated module may directly modify another module's database tables.

END OF 41.77

41.78 CROSS-MODULE COMMUNICATION

Preferred:

Module A ↓ Application Interface / Event ↓ Module B

Avoid:

Module A ↓ Module B Repository ↓ Module B Database Tables

END OF 41.78

41.79 DATABASE OWNERSHIP ENFORCEMENT

Even when PostgreSQL is initially shared, logical ownership shall be enforced.

Example:

Projects module → owns projects

Conversations module → owns conversations

Messages module → owns messages

Research module → owns research_jobs and research_findings

Other modules must access those records through approved application interfaces.

END OF 41.79

41.80 FUTURE SERVICE EXTRACTION

The modular monolith shall be designed so high-load modules can later become independent services.

Potential future services:

AI Gateway Research Service Search Service File Processing Service Notification Service Identity Service Billing Service Laboratory Service

The initial implementation should not create unnecessary distributed-system complexity.

END OF 41.80

41.81 MODULAR MONOLITH STRATEGY

Initial GSIR deployment should favor:

One backend application + Strong internal module boundaries + Shared PostgreSQL infrastructure + Dedicated workers + Specialized search infrastructure where needed + Object storage + Cache

Later:

High-load module ↓ Extract into service ↓ API/event boundary ↓ Independent scaling

END OF 41.81

41.82 BACKEND DIRECTORY CONNECTION MAP

Complete high-level connection:

backend/src/main.ts ↓ app/app.module.ts ↓ modules/ ├── auth ├── users ├── profiles ├── projects ├── conversations ├── messages ├── notes ├── files ├── sources ├── research ├── search ├── memory ├── notifications ├── settings ├── connections ├── laboratory ├── suppliers ├── ai ├── usage ├── billing ├── accessibility ├── exports ├── audit └── admin ↓ application use cases ↓ domain rules ↓ repository interfaces ↓ database repositories ↓ PostgreSQL / Redis / Search / Object Storage ↓ events ↓ workers ↓ derived systems

END OF 41.82

41.83 CRITICAL ARCHITECTURAL RULES

Rule 1: Frontend never accesses the database directly.

Rule 2: Controllers never contain major business logic.

Rule 3: Repositories never contain HTTP logic.

Rule 4: Domain entities never depend on HTTP or database frameworks.

Rule 5: AI providers never appear directly inside feature controllers.

Rule 6: External services must be accessed through adapters/interfaces.

Rule 7: User authorization must occur before protected resource access.

Rule 8: Database ownership must remain explicit.

Rule 9: Long-running workflows must be asynchronous.

Rule 10: Every critical operation must be observable.

Rule 11: Every important operation must be testable.

Rule 12: Every production data mutation must have a clear persistence path.

Rule 13: Every API contract must have a defined request and response type.

Rule 14: No hidden business logic may exist inside utility functions.

Rule 15: No feature is complete until its complete vertical path works.

END OF 41.83

41.90 COMPLETE ARCHITECTURAL QUALITY GATE

Before any module is marked complete, developers must verify:

- Exact file structure exists.

- Module responsibility is documented.

- API contract exists.

- Request DTO exists.

- Response DTO exists.

- Use case exists.

- Authorization policy exists.

- Domain rules exist where required.

- Repository interface exists.

- Repository implementation exists.

- Database migration exists.

- Error handling exists.

- Logging exists.

- Metrics exist.

- Events are defined where required.

- Background processing exists where required.

- Retry behavior exists where required.

- Idempotency exists where required.

- Unit tests exist.

- Integration tests exist.

- API tests exist.

- Authorization tests exist.

- Failure tests exist.

- Performance tests exist where required.

- Frontend integration works.

- Database integration works.

- Security checks pass.

- No unauthorized data is exposed.

- No direct database access exists outside approved persistence boundaries.

- Production configuration is validated.

END OF 41.90

41.91 PART 41 FINAL ARCHITECTURAL RESULT

The GSIR backend shall therefore operate as a modular, testable, scalable application architecture:

Frontend ↓ API ↓ Controllers ↓ DTO Validation ↓ Authentication ↓ Authorization ↓ Application Use Cases ↓ Domain Logic ↓ Repository Interfaces ↓ Infrastructure Implementations ↓ PostgreSQL / Redis / Search / Object Storage ↓ Events ↓ Workers ↓ AI / Research / Processing Systems

The architecture provides a clear separation between what the user requests, what the application decides, what the domain permits, what the database stores, what external systems execute, and what the frontend receives.

This structure is the foundation required for GSIR to grow from the current AI research assistant into the larger Scientific Research Operating System vision without allowing the backend to become an unmaintainable collection of tightly coupled code.

END OF PART 41

The database must remain strongly structured while allowing GSIR to evolve without destructive redesign.

END OF 42.1

42.2 DATABASE ARCHITECTURE PRINCIPLE

The primary transactional database shall be PostgreSQL.

The architecture shall use:

PostgreSQL + Redis + Object Storage + Search Infrastructure + Vector Search Infrastructure + Queue Infrastructure

Each system has a specific responsibility.

PostgreSQL: Transactional source of truth.

Redis: Cache, short-lived state, rate limiting, distributed coordination and selected high-speed data.

Object Storage: Large files and binary artifacts.

Search Infrastructure: Large-scale text and retrieval workloads.

Vector Infrastructure: Semantic retrieval when required.

Queue: Asynchronous processing.

END OF 42.2

42.3 DATABASE RESPONSIBILITY BOUNDARY

PostgreSQL must store authoritative structured application state.

PostgreSQL shall not be used as an uncontrolled storage location for:

- Large binary files.

- Temporary AI streams.

- Massive transient cache data.

- Unbounded logs.

- Provider-specific raw payloads without retention policy.

- High-frequency ephemeral events that belong in a queue or cache.

Large objects shall be stored outside PostgreSQL and referenced through metadata records.

END OF 42.3

42.4 DATABASE ROOT STRUCTURE

The backend database directory shall use:

backend/src/database/

Structure:

backend/src/database/ ├── database.module.ts ├── database.client.ts ├── database.config.ts ├── migrations/ ├── schemas/ ├── repositories/ ├── transactions/ ├── query/ ├── seed/ ├── fixtures/ ├── health/ └── index.ts

END OF 42.4

42.5 DATABASE SCHEMA ORGANIZATION

Database schema definitions shall be grouped by domain.

Recommended structure:

backend/src/database/schemas/ ├── auth/ ├── users/ ├── projects/ ├── conversations/ ├── messages/ ├── files/ ├── sources/ ├── research/ ├── memory/ ├── ai/ ├── search/ ├── laboratory/ ├── suppliers/ ├── notifications/ ├── settings/ ├── connections/ ├── usage/ ├── billing/ ├── exports/ ├── audit/ └── admin/

END OF 42.5

42.6 DATABASE OWNERSHIP MODEL

Every major domain module shall own its tables.

Ownership:

Auth → authentication/session/security tables.

Users → user identity and account tables.

Profiles → profile and preference data.

Projects → projects and project membership.

Conversations → conversations and conversation configuration.

Messages → messages and message metadata.

Files → file metadata and processing state.

Sources → source metadata and source records.

Research → research jobs, findings, claims and evidence.

Memory → user/project memory.

AI → AI runs, model routing records and tool execution.

Laboratory → laboratory information.

Suppliers → supplier information.

Notifications → notification state.

Usage → token and resource usage.

Billing → subscription/payment records.

Audit → audit records.

END OF 42.6

42.7 PRIMARY DATABASE ENTITIES

The initial logical entity model shall include:

User Account Session UserProfile UserPreference Project ProjectMember Conversation Message MessageAttachment File FileVersion FileProcessingJob Source SourceDocument ResearchJob ResearchTask ResearchFinding ResearchClaim Evidence Citation Note NoteVersion Memory AIRun AIMessage AIUsage ToolExecution ModelExecution SearchQuery SearchResult Laboratory LaboratoryContact LaboratoryCapability Supplier SupplierProduct Notification Connection Setting ExportJob AuditLog UsageRecord Subscription

users

42.19 MESSAGE CONTENT STORAGE

Short structured message content may be stored directly.

Large generated artifacts shall be stored in object storage and referenced by:

content_reference content_type content_size content_hash

42.20 MESSAGE ORDERING

The system shall use:

or an equivalent server-controlled ordering mechanism.

The frontend must never determine authoritative message ordering.

42.56 RELATIONSHIP PRINCIPLE

Foreign keys shall be used for authoritative relational integrity.

Examples:

projects.owner_id → users.id

project_members.project_id → projects.id

project_members.user_id → users.id

conversations.project_id → projects.id

messages.conversation_id → conversations.id

research_jobs.project_id → projects.id

research_findings.research_job_id → research_jobs.id

evidence.claim_id → research_claims.id

evidence.source_id → sources.id

END OF 42.56

42.57 CASCADE RULE

Cascade deletion must not be used blindly.

Before configuring ON DELETE CASCADE, determine whether the related data:

- Can safely disappear.

- Must be retained.

- Must be anonymized.

- Must be archived.

- Must be moved to another state.

Scientific research records and audit records may require retention even after a user or project is deleted.

END OF 42.57

42.58 SOFT DELETE

Soft deletion shall be used where historical preservation is important.

Typical field:

deleted_at

Possible states:

active archived deleted

Soft deletion must not replace proper data-retention policies.

END OF 42.58

42.59 DATABASE CONSTRAINTS

Important invariants shall be enforced at the database level where practical.

Examples:

NOT NULL UNIQUE CHECK FOREIGN KEY PRIMARY KEY

Application validation remains necessary, but critical integrity must not depend solely on frontend behavior.

END OF 42.59

42.60 UNIQUE CONSTRAINTS

Examples:

users.email project_members(project_id, user_id) messages(conversation_id, client_message_id) file_versions(file_id, version_number) note_versions(note_id, version_number)

Additional unique constraints shall be defined as domain requirements are finalized.

END OF 42.60

42.61 INDEXING PRINCIPLE

Indexes shall be created according to real query patterns.

Do not create indexes on every column.

Every index has:

Storage cost Write cost Maintenance cost

Indexes must therefore be justified by query behavior.

END OF 42.61

42.62 PRIMARY INDEXES

Every primary key automatically provides the fundamental lookup path.

Foreign-key columns frequently used for joins and filtering shall receive appropriate indexes.

END OF 42.62

42.63 REQUIRED INITIAL INDEXES

Examples:

users(email)

project_members(project_id, user_id)

project_members(user_id)

conversations(project_id, updated_at)

messages(conversation_id, sequence_number)

files(project_id, created_at)

sources(project_id, created_at)

research_jobs(project_id, created_at)

research_tasks(research_job_id, status)

research_findings(research_job_id)

research_claims(research_job_id)

evidence(claim_id)

evidence(source_id)

notes(project_id, updated_at)

memories(user_id, status)

ai_runs(user_id, created_at)

ai_runs(project_id, created_at)

notifications(user_id, status, created_at)

audit_logs(actor_id, created_at)

END OF 42.63

42.64 COMPOSITE INDEX RULE

Composite indexes must follow actual filtering and ordering patterns.

Example:

messages(conversation_id, sequence_number)

is preferable for:

WHERE conversation_id = ? ORDER BY sequence_number

when that is the dominant access pattern.

END OF 42.64

42.65 PARTIAL INDEXES

Partial indexes may be used for frequently accessed subsets.

Example:

active notifications pending research jobs unprocessed files

This reduces index size when the inactive population is much larger than the active population.

END OF 42.65

42.66 FULL-TEXT SEARCH

PostgreSQL full-text capabilities may be used for moderate transactional search requirements.

Large-scale scientific search shall use the dedicated search architecture defined elsewhere in the master plan.

END OF 42.66

42.67 VECTOR DATA

Vector embeddings shall not automatically be stored in ordinary transactional tables if the scale or workload makes this inefficient.

The architecture shall support:

PostgreSQL vector capabilities or dedicated vector infrastructure

The selected implementation must be evaluated according to:

Dataset size Latency Filtering requirements Cost Recall Operational complexity

END OF 42.67

42.68 DATABASE TRANSACTION PRINCIPLE

Transactions must protect business invariants.

Example:

Create Project:

BEGIN → create project → create owner membership → create project settings → create audit event COMMIT

If any required operation fails:

ROLLBACK

END OF 42.68

42.69 TRANSACTION BOUNDARY

A transaction should normally correspond to one business operation.

Do not hold database transactions open while waiting for:

AI generation External HTTP requests Large file processing Long research workflows User input

External operations must occur outside long-lived database transactions.

END OF 42.69

42.70 OUTBOX PATTERN

For important events that must not be lost:

Database Transaction ↓ Business Data + Outbox Event ↓ Commit ↓ Outbox Worker ↓ Event Bus / Queue ↓ Consumer

This prevents the failure scenario where database state commits but the corresponding event is lost.

END OF 42.70

42.71 OUTBOX TABLE

Table:

outbox_events

Fields:

id event_type aggregate_type aggregate_id payload_reference status attempt_count available_at processed_at created_at

The outbox worker shall process pending events safely and idempotently.

END OF 42.71

42.72 IDEMPOTENT EVENT PROCESSING

Every event consumer must tolerate duplicate delivery.

A consumer may maintain an event-processing record.

Table:

processed_events

Fields:

event_id consumer_name processed_at

Unique constraint:

event_id + consumer_name

END OF 42.72

42.73 DATABASE MIGRATION ARCHITECTURE

All schema changes must use versioned migrations.

Migration directory:

backend/src/database/migrations/

Naming convention:

001_initial_schema.sql 002_add_user_profiles.sql 003_add_projects.sql 004_add_conversations.sql 005_add_messages.sql

The exact migration numbers shall follow the actual repository history and must never be reused.

END OF 42.73

42.74 MIGRATION RULE

A migration must be:

- Deterministic.

- Version controlled.

- Repeatable in a fresh environment.

- Tested.

- Reversible where practical.

- Safe for production deployment.

Manual production database modifications are prohibited except under controlled emergency procedures.

END OF 42.74

42.75 EXPENSIVE MIGRATION RULE

Large production migrations must avoid long table locks.

Examples:

Adding a large index Adding a non-null field Rebuilding large tables Changing large data types

These operations must use staged migration strategies.

END OF 42.75

42.76 SEED DATA

Seed data shall be separated from production business data.

Directory:

backend/src/database/seed/

Files:

backend/src/database/seed/system.seed.ts backend/src/database/seed/roles.seed.ts backend/src/database/seed/plans.seed.ts backend/src/database/seed/development.seed.ts

END OF 42.76

42.77 DATABASE FIXTURES

Test fixtures shall exist separately.

Directory:

backend/src/database/fixtures/

Fixtures must generate deterministic test data.

Production credentials or real user data must never be included in fixtures.

END OF 42.77

42.78 CONNECTION POOLING

Database access must use controlled connection pooling.

The application must not create a new database connection for every request.

Pool size shall be configured according to:

API worker count Database capacity Expected concurrency Query duration Background workers Read/write workload

END OF 42.78

42.79 ONE-CRORE-QUERY DATABASE STRATEGY

The one-crore-query requirement must be handled through workload distribution.

Architecture:

Massive Request Volume ↓ Load Balancer ↓ Stateless API ↓ Cache ↓ Read Optimization ↓ Connection Pool ↓ Database + Read Replicas where required + Search Infrastructure + Async Queues

The primary PostgreSQL instance must not be treated as the destination for every request.

END OF 42.79

42.80 CACHE STRATEGY

Redis shall cache data that is:

Frequently read Expensive to compute Safe to cache Reasonably stable

Examples:

User permission snapshots Project metadata System configuration AI routing configuration Rate-limit counters Short-lived search results

END OF 42.80

42.81 CACHE INVALIDATION

Every cached resource must have a defined invalidation strategy.

Options:

TTL Explicit invalidation Versioned keys Event-driven invalidation

No critical authorization decision shall rely indefinitely on stale cache data.

END OF 42.81

42.82 CACHE KEY ARCHITECTURE

Cache keys shall be namespaced.

Examples:

gsir:user:{userId} gsir:project:{projectId} gsir:permissions:{userId}:{projectId} gsir:ai-route:{routeKey} gsir:search:{hash}

END OF 42.82

42.83 DATABASE READ OPTIMIZATION

Read-heavy operations shall use:

Projection queries Selective columns Pagination Cursor pagination Prepared queries Indexes Caching Read replicas where required

Do not load complete entities when only a few fields are required.

END OF 42.83

42.84 CURSOR PAGINATION

Large datasets shall use cursor-based pagination.

Avoid:

OFFSET 1000000

for extremely large datasets.

Prefer:

WHERE id > cursor

or another stable indexed cursor.

This is particularly important for:

messages research findings audit records notifications AI runs usage records

END OF 42.84

42.85 WRITE OPTIMIZATION

Write-heavy workloads shall use:

Batch inserts Bulk updates where safe Asynchronous processing Queue workers Connection pooling Efficient transactions

Avoid unnecessary database writes from frontend events.

END OF 42.85

42.86 AUTOSAVE DATABASE STRATEGY

Autosave shall not write every keystroke.

Frontend:

Typing ↓ Debounce ↓ Autosave request

Backend:

Validate ↓ Version check ↓ Persist only when necessary

This prevents unnecessary database load.

END OF 42.86

42.87 AI DATABASE LOAD CONTROL

AI generation must not produce excessive transactional writes.

The system shall avoid storing every internal reasoning token as a separate database row.

Persist:

Required user-visible content Important execution metadata Tool calls when required Evidence Citations Usage Audit information

Internal transient execution state should use appropriate temporary infrastructure.

END OF 42.87

42.88 RESEARCH DATABASE LOAD CONTROL

Research workers shall batch writes where possible.

Instead of:

Finding 1 → database write Finding 2 → database write Finding 3 → database write

Prefer controlled batches:

Finding batch ↓ Validation ↓ Bulk persistence ↓ Commit

END OF 42.88

42.89 DATA RETENTION

Every major data category must have a retention policy.

Categories:

User data Conversation data AI runs Research jobs Files Audit logs Usage data Notifications Temporary processing data

Retention policies shall consider:

Legal requirements User expectations Storage cost Product requirements Scientific reproducibility

END OF 42.89

42.90 DATA DELETION

Deletion workflows must identify:

Primary record Child records External files Search indexes Vector indexes Cache entries Events Backups Audit requirements

Deleting a PostgreSQL row alone does not necessarily delete all representations of that data.

END OF 42.90

42.91 DATA CONSISTENCY MODEL

GSIR shall distinguish:

Strong transactional consistency from eventual consistency.

Strong consistency is required for:

Permissions Ownership Critical account state Billing state Important transactional operations

Eventual consistency is acceptable for:

Search indexes Analytics Notifications Embeddings Derived AI metadata

END OF 42.91

42.92 DATABASE SECURITY

Database access must use:

Least privilege Separate credentials Encrypted connections Secret management Network restrictions Connection limits Audit logging Migration controls

The application must never expose database credentials to the frontend.

END OF 42.92

42.93 DATABASE BACKUP

Production PostgreSQL must have:

Automated backups Point-in-time recovery where supported Backup verification Restore testing Retention policy Disaster recovery procedures

A backup that has never been restored successfully must not be considered fully reliable.

END OF 42.93

42.94 DATABASE HEALTH CHECK

Required backend file:

backend/src/database/health/database.health.ts

The health system shall verify:

Database connectivity Connection pool health Query responsiveness Migration state Critical dependency availability

END OF 42.94

42.95 DATABASE OBSERVABILITY

Metrics shall include:

Connection pool utilization Query latency Slow query count Transaction duration Deadlocks Lock waits Error rate Replication lag Cache hit rate Database CPU Database memory Storage growth

END OF 42.95

42.96 SLOW QUERY CONTROL

Slow queries must be identified through observability.

The development process shall use query plans for important queries.

No frequently executed query should remain unoptimized merely because it works functionally.

END OF 42.96

42.97 DATABASE TESTING

Database testing shall include:

Schema tests Migration tests Constraint tests Repository tests Transaction tests Concurrency tests Performance tests Backup/restore tests Failure tests

END OF 42.97

42.98 DATABASE-BACKEND CONNECTION

The final backend connection shall be:

Controller ↓ Request DTO ↓ Use Case ↓ Domain ↓ Repository Interface ↓ Repository Implementation ↓ Database Client ↓ PostgreSQL

For asynchronous operations:

Use Case ↓ Transaction ↓ Business Record + Outbox Event ↓ Commit ↓ Queue ↓ Worker ↓ Database / External Infrastructure

END OF 42.98

42.99 DATABASE-FRONTEND CONNECTION

The frontend must never depend on database schema names.

Correct:

Frontend ↓ API Contract ↓ Response DTO ↓ Application Model ↓ UI

Incorrect:

Frontend ↓ PostgreSQL Table Structure

END OF 42.99

42.100 DATABASE ARCHITECTURAL QUALITY GATE

The database architecture shall be considered complete for a feature only when:

- Tables are defined.

- Ownership is defined.

- Primary keys are defined.

- Foreign keys are defined.

- Unique constraints are defined.

- Required indexes are defined.

- Delete behavior is defined.

- Retention behavior is defined.

- Migration exists.

- Repository exists.

- Transaction boundary exists where required.

- Cache strategy exists where required.

- Queue strategy exists where required.

- Observability exists.

- Security is verified.

- Backup implications are understood.

- Performance has been tested.

- Concurrency has been tested.

- Failure recovery has been tested.

- Frontend integration has been tested.

END OF 42.100

42.101 FINAL DATABASE ARCHITECTURE

The GSIR database architecture shall therefore operate as:

Frontend ↓ Backend API ↓ Application Use Cases ↓ Domain Logic ↓ Repository Interfaces ↓ Database Repositories ↓ PostgreSQL + Redis + Object Storage + Search Infrastructure + Vector Infrastructure + Queue Infrastructure

PostgreSQL remains the transactional source of truth.

Redis handles high-speed transient workloads.

Object storage handles large files.

Search infrastructure handles large-scale retrieval.

Vector infrastructure handles semantic retrieval.

Queues handle asynchronous workloads.

This separation is required to achieve high throughput, low cost, predictable performance, maintainability and future scalability toward the complete GSIR Scientific Research Operating System.

PART 43 — COMPLETE AI GATEWAY, MODEL ROUTER, PROVIDER ADAPTER, TOKEN/COST OPTIMIZATION, STREAMING, FALLBACK AND AI RESPONSE ARCHITECTURE

43.1 PURPOSE

The GSIR AI Gateway shall be the controlled entry point between GSIR application workflows and all AI model infrastructure.

The AI Gateway must prevent individual application modules from directly depending on model-provider SDKs.

Required architecture:

GSIR Feature ↓ AI Application Interface ↓ AI Gateway ↓ Request Validation ↓ Policy Enforcement ↓ Context/Prompt Preparation ↓ Model Router ↓ Cost/Token Optimizer ↓ Provider Adapter ↓ AI Provider ↓ Model ↓ Normalized AI Response ↓ Validation ↓ Streaming / Persistence ↓ GSIR Feature

The gateway shall provide a single abstraction for all AI-capable features while allowing multiple models and providers to be added without rewriting the application layer.

END OF 43.1

43.2 AI GATEWAY DESIGN PRINCIPLE

The AI Gateway shall provide centralized control over:

- Model access.

- Provider access.

- Model selection.

- Routing.

- Fallback.

- Token budgets.

- Cost limits.

- Rate limits.

- Streaming.

- Timeouts.

- Retries.

- Provider normalization.

- Usage tracking.

- AI execution tracing.

- Safety policies.

- Prompt versioning.

- Response validation.

- AI quality evaluation.

- Caching.

- AI observability.

The gateway must remain stateless wherever possible so it can scale horizontally.

END OF 43.2

Strategy 3: Latency-first.

Strategy 4: Quality-first.

Strategy 5: Balanced.

Strategy 6: Fallback-first reliability.

Strategy 7: Task-specific routing.

43.18 TASK-SPECIFIC ROUTING

Examples:

Simple classification → low-cost model.

Short summarization → economy/standard model.

Complex scientific reasoning → advanced reasoning model.

Large document extraction → long-context model.

Embedding → embedding model.

Reranking → reranking model.

Research synthesis → advanced reasoning model.

This prevents expensive models from being used unnecessarily.

43.25 CIRCUIT BREAKER

Each provider may have a circuit breaker.

OPEN ↓ Provider temporarily blocked

HALF_OPEN ↓ Limited health-testing requests

END OF 43.25

43.26 RETRY POLICY

Retries shall be limited and error-aware.

Retryable:

Transient network failure Temporary provider outage Rate-limit response where retry-after is available Temporary upstream timeout

Non-retryable:

Invalid request Authentication failure Unsupported capability Invalid model Permanent policy rejection

END OF 43.26

43.27 EXPONENTIAL BACKOFF

Retries should use controlled backoff.

Conceptual:

Attempt 1 → short delay

Attempt 2 → longer delay

Attempt 3 → longer delay

Maximum retry duration must be bounded.

Random jitter should be added where concurrent requests could otherwise synchronize.

END OF 43.27

43.28 FALLBACK ARCHITECTURE

Fallback must be explicit.

Primary Model ↓ Primary Provider ↓ Failure ↓ Fallback Policy ↓ Alternative Model/Provider ↓ Response

Fallback must not silently reduce quality beyond the allowed request policy.

END OF 43.28

43.29 FALLBACK LEVELS

Possible fallback hierarchy:

Level 0: Same model, same provider retry.

Level 1: Same model, alternative provider.

Level 2: Equivalent-capability model.

Level 3: Lower-cost/lower-capability model.

Level 4: Graceful failure.

The request policy determines which levels are permitted.

END OF 43.29

43.30 QUALITY-PRESERVING FALLBACK

For scientific research requests, fallback must preserve minimum quality requirements.

Example:

Advanced reasoning required ↓ Provider A unavailable ↓ Provider B equivalent reasoning capability ↓ Use Provider B

If no equivalent model exists:

Do not silently downgrade to a weak model.

Return a controlled degraded-state response or queue the request for later processing.

END OF 43.30

43.33 TOKEN ESTIMATION

The system shall estimate input tokens before execution.

If the request exceeds the model context limit:

- Remove irrelevant context.

- Compress context.

- Summarize older messages.

- Retrieve only relevant documents.

- Reduce tool payloads.

- Use a larger-context model if permitted.

The request must not simply fail because excessive context was assembled unnecessarily.

Pipeline:

- Model routing.

- Context reduction.

- Prompt caching.

- Response caching where safe.

- Batch processing.

- Smaller models for simple tasks.

- Structured outputs.

- Retrieval instead of full-context injection.

- Reusing embeddings.

- Avoiding duplicate AI calls.

- Early termination.

- Parallelization where beneficial.

- User authorization occurs before context construction.

- Tool permissions are explicit.

43.100 FINAL AI GATEWAY ARCHITECTURE

The complete GSIR AI architecture is:

GSIR Feature ↓ AI Application Contract ↓ AI Gateway ↓ Authentication / Authorization ↓ Request Validation ↓ Safety Policy ↓ Budget Check ↓ Context Builder ↓ Prompt Registry ↓ Cache ↓ Model Router ↓ Token/Cost Optimizer ↓ Provider Registry ↓ Provider Adapter ↓ AI Model ↓ Retry / Fallback / Circuit Breaker ↓ Response Normalization ↓ Response Validation ↓ Streaming ↓ Usage + Cost Recording ↓ AI Run Persistence ↓ Evaluation / Telemetry ↓ Frontend / Research Workflow / Agent Workflow

The AI Gateway becomes the central control plane for GSIR intelligence.

It provides provider independence, model flexibility, controlled cost, predictable failure handling, streaming, observability, security and future extensibility toward multi-model scientific reasoning.

This architecture allows GSIR to add or replace AI providers without rewriting the project, conversation, research, document, laboratory or other application modules.

PART 45 — COMPLETE RESEARCH ORCHESTRATION, WORKFLOW ENGINE, TASK QUEUE, JOB SCHEDULING AND LONG-RUNNING SCIENTIFIC EXECUTION ARCHITECTURE

45.1 PURPOSE

The GSIR Research Orchestration Layer shall coordinate complex, long-running scientific workflows that require multiple agents, models, tools, research sources, datasets, experiments, verification stages and asynchronous execution.

The architecture shall support:

1. Research project execution.

2. Multi-step workflows.

3. Sequential execution.

4. Parallel execution.

5. Dependency-based execution.

6. Multi-agent coordination.

7. Task queues.

8. Job scheduling.

9. Long-running jobs.

10. Checkpointing.

11. Resume and recovery.

12. Retry handling.

13. Cancellation.

14. Priority management.

15. Resource management.

16. Budget management.

17. Workflow verification.

18. Human approval gates.

19. Research reproducibility.

20. Complete execution traceability.

END OF 45.1

45.2 ORCHESTRATION PRINCIPLE

The orchestration layer shall separate:

WHAT SHOULD BE DONE

from

HOW EACH STEP IS EXECUTED.

↓

Task Graph

↓

↓

↓

Agents / AI Gateway / Tools

↓

↓

↓

↓

↓

↓

C

B ──→ D

The graph determines which tasks may execute concurrently.

Temporary resource shortage

Non-retryable:

Permission failure

Unsupported operation

Flow:

Task

↓

Retry

↓

Retry

↓

Retry limit reached

↓

Dead-Letter Queue

↓

Failure Analysis

END OF 45.25

45.26 TASK TIMEOUT

↓

Persist timeout state

↓

Release resources

↓

↓

↓

Persist state

↓

Mark timeout

↓

Generate recovery information

45.43 CHECKPOINT PURPOSE

Checkpoints shall protect long-running workflows from losing completed work.

Checkpoint data may contain:

Task states

Completed outputs

Evidence references

Agent states

Iteration number

Budget state

Recovery metadata

END OF 45.43

45.44 CHECKPOINT FREQUENCY

Checkpoints shall occur:

After important workflow stages

After expensive tasks

Before risky transitions

After successful task completion

Before long-running external operations

At configured time intervals where necessary

END OF 45.44

45.45 CHECKPOINT STORAGE

Durable workflow state shall be stored in PostgreSQL.

Large artifacts shall use object storage.

The system shall not place large research artifacts directly inside Redis.

45.46 WORKFLOW RECOVERY

Workflow Failure

↓

Load Latest Checkpoint

↓

↓

Identify Safe Tasks

↓

Rebuild Dependency State

↓

Resume Remaining Tasks

45.47 EXACTLY-ONCE VS AT-LEAST-ONCE

The orchestration system shall assume that distributed task execution can result in duplicate delivery.

Therefore tasks must be designed to be idempotent where possible.

Every task shall have a unique task execution identifier.

Side effects shall use idempotency keys where appropriate.

END OF 45.47

45.48 IDEMPOTENT TASK EXECUTION

Example:

Task ID:

task_123

First execution:

creates result.

Duplicate execution:

detects existing result and avoids duplicating the side effect.

45.62 SCHEDULED JOB PROTECTION

↓

Previous run still active

↓

Concurrency policy

↓

Skip / queue / replace according to configuration

45.64 BACKGROUND RESEARCH

45.65 INTERACTIVE VS ASYNCHRONOUS

User request

→ immediate AI response.

Asynchronous:

User request

→ create job

→ background execution

→ notification/result retrieval.

The system shall select the mode based on expected execution duration and workflow policy.

×
