61.31 EXPERIMENT PARAMETERS

Execution parameters shall be stored with the execution record or an immutable parameter snapshot.

This prevents later changes to the experiment definition from altering historical execution interpretation.

END OF 61.31

61.32 EXPERIMENT RESULTS

Results shall reference the execution that produced them.

Execution

↓

Measurements

↓

Derived Results

↓

Analysis

Results shall preserve their provenance.

END OF 61.32

61.33 TASK DATA

The task table shall support asynchronous operations.

Possible fields:

Task ID

Task Type

Owner

Related Resource

Status

Priority

Attempts

Progress

Created At

Started At

Completed At

Error

Large task payloads may be stored externally with database references.

END OF 61.33

61.34 TASK PRIORITY

Tasks may have priority levels.

Example:

CRITICAL

HIGH

NORMAL

LOW

Priority shall not permit users to bypass authorization or resource quotas.

END OF 61.34

61.35 NOTIFICATION DATA

Notifications shall contain:

Notification ID

User ID

Type

Title

Message

Related Resource

Read Status

Created At

Read At

Notification data shall remain separate from the operation that generated it.

END OF 61.35

61.36 AUDIT DATA

Audit records shall be append-oriented.

Possible fields:

Audit ID

Actor ID

Organization ID

Action

Resource Type

Resource ID

Timestamp

Request ID

Result

Metadata

Audit records shall not normally be updated to rewrite historical events.

END OF 61.36

61.37 TIMESTAMP STANDARD

All persistent timestamps shall use a consistent timezone strategy.

The recommended internal representation shall be UTC.

User-facing timezone conversion shall occur at the application boundary.

END OF 61.37

61.38 IDENTIFIER STRATEGY

GSIR shall use stable unique identifiers.

Identifiers shall:

Remain Unique

Be Non-Colliding

Avoid Predictable Enumeration Where Necessary

Be Consistent Across Services

Internal database identifiers and public resource identifiers may be different when security or architectural requirements justify it.

END OF 61.38

61.39 PRIMARY KEYS

Every major entity shall have a primary key.

Example:

user_id

project_id

file_id

conversation_id

message_id

research_run_id

source_id

experiment_id

task_id

Primary keys shall never depend on mutable user-facing names.

END OF 61.39

61.40 FOREIGN KEYS

Relationships requiring database-level integrity shall use foreign keys where appropriate.

Examples:

message.conversation_id

file.project_id

research_run.project_id

evidence.source_id

experiment.project_id

Foreign-key usage shall be balanced against high-volume or independently managed data requirements.

END OF 61.40

61.41 UNIQUE CONSTRAINTS

Important uniqueness requirements shall be enforced by the database.

Examples:

Unique Membership

Unique External Identifier

Unique Idempotency Key

Unique Resource Version

Application checks alone shall not be relied upon where concurrent requests can create duplicates.

END OF 61.41

61.42 CHECK CONSTRAINTS

Database constraints may enforce simple invariants such as:

Non-Negative Values

Valid Status Combinations

Required Relationships

Complex domain rules shall remain in the domain/service layer.

END OF 61.42

61.43 NULLABILITY

Fields shall be nullable only when absence has a defined meaning.

The schema shall avoid excessive nullable columns that make the data model ambiguous.

END OF 61.43

61.44 NORMALIZATION

Transactional data shall be normalized sufficiently to preserve consistency and reduce unnecessary duplication.

Denormalization may be introduced only when justified by:

Performance

Read Patterns

Analytics

Search

Caching

and shall have a defined synchronization strategy.

END OF 61.44

61.45 DATABASE INDEXING

Indexes shall be created based on actual query patterns.

Important candidates may include:

Project ID

User ID

Organization ID

Created At

Updated At

Status

Foreign Keys

External Identifiers

Search Fields

Indexes shall not be added indiscriminately because they increase storage and write costs.

END OF 61.45

61.46 COMPOSITE INDEXES

Composite indexes shall match frequent query patterns.

Example:

(project_id, created_at)

may support queries that retrieve project resources ordered by creation time.

Index design shall be validated against actual query plans.

END OF 61.46

61.47 UNIQUE INDEXES

Unique indexes shall be used when uniqueness is both a business and database requirement.

Examples:

organization_slug

external_provider_id

idempotency_key

END OF 61.47

61.48 QUERY PERFORMANCE

Repositories shall avoid:

N+1 Queries

Unbounded Queries

Full Table Scans Where Avoidable

Repeated Identical Queries

Unnecessary Joins

Large Unfiltered Results

Query performance shall be measured rather than assumed.

END OF 61.48

61.49 PAGINATION

Large datasets shall always use controlled pagination.

The backend shall never return unlimited rows simply because the database can technically produce them.

END OF 61.49

61.50 CURSOR PAGINATION

Cursor pagination shall be used where stable traversal of large or rapidly changing datasets is required.

Cursors shall be opaque to clients where appropriate.

END OF 61.50

61.51 TRANSACTIONS

Transactions shall be used when multiple changes must succeed or fail together.

Example:

Create Project

+

Create Membership

+

Create Initial Configuration

shall be committed atomically when the domain requires atomicity.

END OF 61.51

61.52 TRANSACTION SIZE

Transactions shall remain short.

The following shall not normally occur inside long database transactions:

AI Calls

Web Searches

Large File Processing

Experiment Execution

Long Network Requests

END OF 61.52

61.53 CONCURRENCY CONTROL

GSIR shall protect against concurrent updates.

Mechanisms may include:

Optimistic Locking

Version Numbers

Database Constraints

Row Locks Where Required

Idempotency

The appropriate mechanism shall depend on the resource.

END OF 61.53

61.54 SOFT DELETION

Soft deletion may be used where historical traceability is required.

Example:

deleted_at

shall indicate logical deletion.

Soft-deleted resources shall not automatically appear in ordinary queries.

END OF 61.54

61.55 ARCHIVING

Large historical datasets may be archived.

Archiving shall preserve:

Identity

Relationships

Provenance

Auditability

Recovery Path

Archived data shall remain distinguishable from permanently deleted data.

END OF 61.55

61.56 DATA RETENTION

GSIR shall define retention policies for:

Messages

Files

Research Runs

Logs

Audit Events

Temporary Data

AI Execution Records

Task Records

Retention shall follow product requirements, legal requirements and configured organizational policies.

END OF 61.56

61.57 DATA DELETION

Deletion operations shall distinguish:

User Deletion

Resource Deletion

Soft Deletion

Permanent Deletion

Retention Expiration

Dependent data shall be handled according to explicit deletion policies.

END OF 61.57

61.58 CASCADE BEHAVIOR

Cascading deletion shall be used only when the resulting behavior is clearly intended.

For critical scientific or audit records, explicit deletion workflows shall be preferred over uncontrolled cascading deletion.

END OF 61.58

61.59 DATABASE MIGRATIONS

All schema changes shall use version-controlled migrations.

A migration shall define:

Upgrade

Rollback Where Practical

Compatibility Requirements

Data Transformation

Validation

Manual production schema modifications shall be avoided.

END OF 61.59

61.60 MIGRATION SAFETY

Large migrations shall be designed to minimize downtime.

For significant changes:

Expand

↓

Migrate

↓

Validate

↓

Switch

↓

Contract

shall be preferred over abrupt destructive schema changes.

END OF 61.60

61.61 BACKUP ARCHITECTURE

The database shall be backed up according to defined recovery objectives.

Backups shall support:

Point-in-Time Recovery Where Available

Periodic Full Recovery

Disaster Recovery

Operational Recovery

END OF 61.61

61.62 BACKUP SECURITY

Backups shall be protected with:

Access Control

Encryption

Retention Policies

Auditability

Isolation From Primary Environment

A backup shall not become an easier path to sensitive data than the production database.

END OF 61.62

61.63 RESTORE TESTING

Backups shall periodically be restored in a controlled environment.

A backup that has never been successfully restored shall not be treated as proven disaster recovery.

END OF 61.63

61.64 DATABASE HIGH AVAILABILITY

Production deployments shall use an availability strategy appropriate to the required reliability.

Possible mechanisms include:

Replication

Managed Database Failover

Read Replicas

Automated Recovery

The architecture shall avoid unnecessary high-availability cost where the workload does not require it.

END OF 61.64

61.65 READ REPLICAS

Read replicas may be used for workloads such as:

Analytics

Heavy Search

Reporting

Non-Critical Read Operations

Critical immediately-after-write reads shall use an authoritative source when replica lag could produce incorrect behavior.

END OF 61.65

61.66 DATABASE CONNECTION MANAGEMENT

Application services shall use controlled database connection pools.

The system shall prevent:

Connection Leaks

Unlimited Connections

Long Idle Transactions

Pool Exhaustion

END OF 61.66

61.67 DATABASE SECURITY

Database access shall use:

Authentication

Least Privilege

Network Isolation

Encryption

Credential Rotation

Audit Logging

Application services shall receive only the permissions they require.

END OF 61.67

61.68 SECRET MANAGEMENT

Database credentials shall not be hard-coded into source code.

They shall be supplied through secure configuration or secret-management infrastructure.

END OF 61.68

61.69 DATA ENCRYPTION

Sensitive data shall be protected appropriately both:

At Rest

In Transit

Encryption requirements shall be determined according to data sensitivity and deployment environment.

END OF 61.69

61.70 DATA CLASSIFICATION

GSIR data shall be classified according to sensitivity.

Example:

Public

Internal

Private

Sensitive

Highly Sensitive

Storage, logging, caching and access policies shall respect the classification.

END OF 61.70

61.71 DATABASE ACCESS LAYER

All normal application database access shall pass through repositories or clearly defined data-access modules.

The following shall be avoided:

Route

↓

Raw SQL

The preferred structure is:

Route

↓

Service

↓

Repository

↓

Database

END OF 61.71

61.72 REPOSITORY RESPONSIBILITY

Repositories shall handle:

Persistence

Queries

Mapping

Pagination

Transactions Where Appropriate

Database-Specific Operations

Repositories shall not contain UI behavior or AI orchestration.

END OF 61.72

61.73 DATA TRANSFER OBJECTS

Database entities shall not automatically become API response objects.

The architecture shall use explicit mappings:

Database Entity

↓

Domain Model

↓

DTO / Response Schema

↓

API

This protects the database schema from becoming the public API contract.

END OF 61.73

61.74 SEARCH STORAGE

Full-text search shall use an appropriate search mechanism when relational queries become insufficient.

The search index shall be treated as a derived representation.

The primary database shall remain authoritative for transactional records.

END OF 61.74

61.75 VECTOR STORAGE

Embeddings shall be stored in an appropriate vector-capable storage layer.

Vector records shall retain references to:

Source Object

Document

Chunk

Project

Embedding Model

Embedding Version

This permits reproducibility when embedding models change.

END OF 61.75

61.76 EMBEDDING VERSIONING

Every stored embedding shall identify the embedding model or version used to generate it.

When the embedding model changes:

Old Embeddings

≠

New Embeddings

without an explicit migration or re-indexing process.

END OF 61.76

61.77 CHUNK DATA

Document chunks shall maintain:

Chunk ID

Document ID

Version ID

Sequence

Text Reference

Page / Location

Metadata

Embedding Reference

Chunk ordering shall remain deterministic.

END OF 61.77

61.78 CACHE DATA

Cache data shall never be treated as the authoritative source for critical information.

If cache data disappears:

Application

↓

Rebuild / Refetch

↓

Authoritative Store

shall restore the required state.

END OF 61.78

61.79 DATA CONSISTENCY

GSIR shall distinguish between:

Strong Consistency

Eventual Consistency

Derived Data

Cached Data

Each subsystem shall explicitly define which consistency model it requires.

END OF 61.79

61.80 EVENTUAL CONSISTENCY

Eventual consistency may be acceptable for:

Search Indexes

Analytics

Notifications

Derived Knowledge Views

Usage Dashboards

Caches

It shall not silently be used for operations requiring immediate transactional correctness.

END OF 61.80

61.81 DATA PROVENANCE

Scientific data shall preserve provenance across transformations.

Original Source

↓

Imported Data

↓

Processed Data

↓

Derived Data

↓

Analysis

↓

Result

Every important transformation shall remain traceable.

END OF 61.81

61.82 IMMUTABLE SCIENTIFIC RECORDS

Where scientific reproducibility requires it, historical records shall be immutable.

Corrections shall create new versions or explicit correction records rather than silently rewriting historical results.

END OF 61.82

61.83 DATA VERSIONING

Versioned resources shall contain:

Version Number

Created At

Created By

Parent Version

Change Metadata

The system shall be able to determine which version was used to produce a historical result.

END OF 61.83

61.84 REPRODUCIBILITY

Research and experiment records shall preserve the relevant state required to reproduce or interpret an execution.

This may include:

Input Version

Parameter Snapshot

Model Version

Prompt Version

Tool Version

Source Set

Code Version

Environment Metadata

END OF 61.84

61.85 DATABASE OBSERVABILITY

Database monitoring shall include:

Query Latency

Connection Usage

CPU

Memory

Storage

Replication Lag

Lock Contention

Error Rate

Slow Queries

END OF 61.85

61.86 DATABASE PERFORMANCE TESTING

Performance testing shall use realistic workloads.

Testing shall include:

Concurrent Users

Large Projects

Large Documents

Large Message Histories

Large Research Runs

High Task Volume

END OF 61.86

61.87 DATABASE FAILURE TESTING

The system shall test controlled failures such as:

Database Unavailable

Connection Exhaustion

Replica Lag

Storage Limit

Transaction Conflict

Migration Failure

Expected recovery behavior shall be documented.

END OF 61.87

61.88 DATABASE SCALING

Scaling shall occur according to workload.

Potential strategies include:

Query Optimization

Index Optimization

Connection Pool Tuning

Read Replicas

Partitioning

Archiving

Caching

Database Scaling

The simplest effective strategy shall be preferred before introducing complex distributed database architecture.

END OF 61.88

61.89 PARTITIONING

Large tables may eventually require partitioning based on:

Time

Tenant

Project

Resource Type

Partitioning shall be introduced only after workload analysis demonstrates a need.

END OF 61.89

61.90 MULTI-TENANT DATA ISOLATION

If GSIR supports multiple organizations, every tenant-owned record shall have an explicit tenant relationship where appropriate.

Queries shall enforce tenant scope at the repository/service boundary.

END OF 61.90

61.91 CROSS-TENANT PROTECTION

The system shall prevent:

Tenant A

↓

Unauthorized Query

↓

Tenant B Data

through:

Authorization

Query Scoping

Database Constraints Where Appropriate

Testing

Auditability

END OF 61.91

61.92 DATABASE TEST DATA

Development and test environments shall use isolated datasets.

Production data shall not be copied into development environments without an approved privacy and security process.

END OF 61.92

61.93 SEED DATA

Required seed data shall be version controlled and deterministic.

Seed operations shall not accidentally overwrite production records.

END OF 61.93

61.94 DATABASE TESTING LEVELS

Database testing shall include:

Repository Unit Tests

Integration Tests

Migration Tests

Constraint Tests

Query Tests

Performance Tests

Recovery Tests

END OF 61.94

61.95 DATABASE ARCHITECTURE COMPLETION CRITERIA

The database architecture shall be considered complete when:

- Core transactional data has defined ownership.

- Database boundaries are documented.

- Repositories isolate persistence.

- API schemas are separated from database entities.

- Primary keys are standardized.

- Foreign-key relationships are defined.

- Constraints protect important invariants.

- Indexes support real query patterns.

- Pagination is enforced for large datasets.

- Transactions have defined boundaries.

- Concurrency control exists.

- File binaries are separated from metadata.

- Search storage is separated from transactional storage.

- Vector storage preserves provenance and model versions.

- Research data preserves evidence relationships.

- Experiment data preserves execution history.

- Scientific records can be versioned where required.

- Audit records preserve historical actions.

- Retention policies exist.

- Deletion policies exist.

- Backup and restore procedures exist.

- Database security is implemented.

- Tenant isolation is implemented where required.

- Migration procedures are version controlled.

- Database monitoring exists.

- Failure recovery is tested.

- Scaling strategies are defined.

END OF 61.95

61.96 FINAL DATABASE ARCHITECTURE PRINCIPLE

The GSIR database shall be treated as an authoritative foundation for transactional state, while specialized storage systems shall serve specialized workloads.

The final architecture shall follow:

                    GSIR APPLICATION

                           │

                           ▼

                    SERVICE LAYER

                           │

                           ▼

                    REPOSITORY LAYER

                           │

             ┌─────────────┼─────────────┐

             ▼             ▼             ▼

        RELATIONAL      OBJECT        SPECIALIZED

        DATABASE        STORAGE       STORAGE

             │             │          ┌──────┴──────┐

             │             │          ▼             ▼

             │             │       SEARCH         VECTOR

             │             │

             └─────────────┴───────────────┐

                                           ▼

                                  AUTHORITATIVE DATA

                                      + PROVENANCE

                                      + VERSIONING

                                      + AUDIT

The database architecture shall preserve correctness first, while allowing GSIR to scale through specialized storage, caching, indexing, asynchronous processing and workload-specific optimization.

END OF 61.96

END OF PART 61

PART 61 COMPLETED.

GSIR — GLOBAL SCIENTIFIC INTELLIGENT RESEARCH

PART 62 — SEARCH, RETRIEVAL, RAG AND KNOWLEDGE ACCESS ARCHITECTURE

62.1 PURPOSE

The GSIR retrieval architecture shall provide the foundation for finding, ranking, filtering, grounding and delivering relevant information to the AI reasoning system.

The retrieval system shall support:

Documents

Scientific Publications

Web Sources

Datasets

Research Results

Knowledge Graphs

Project Files

Structured Records

Previous Research

The architecture shall separate retrieval from reasoning so that the AI system can obtain evidence without directly depending on a single storage technology.

END OF 62.1

62.2 RETRIEVAL ARCHITECTURE

The primary retrieval flow shall be:

User / Agent Query

↓

Query Understanding

↓

Query Planning

↓

Retrieval Strategy Selection

↓

Parallel Retrieval

├── Keyword Search

├── Semantic Search

├── Metadata Search

├── Knowledge Graph Search

└── Structured Data Search

↓

Result Fusion

↓

Reranking

↓

Evidence Filtering

↓

Context Construction

↓

Reasoning Engine

GSIR shall support layered retrieval rather than relying exclusively on vector similarity.

END OF 62.2

62.3 RETRIEVAL PRINCIPLE

Retrieval shall optimize for:

Relevance

Accuracy

Evidence Quality

Coverage

Freshness

Diversity

Provenance

Latency

Cost

A highly similar document shall not automatically be considered the best evidence.

END OF 62.3

62.4 SEARCH INDEX

The search subsystem shall maintain an index optimized for textual retrieval.

It shall support:

Exact Terms

Keyword Matching

Phrase Matching

Field Search

Filtering

Ranking

Faceting Where Required

The search index shall be treated as derived data and shall be rebuildable from authoritative sources.

END OF 62.4

62.5 VECTOR INDEX

The vector subsystem shall support semantic retrieval.

Each vector record shall preserve references to:

Source

Document

Document Version

Chunk

Project

Embedding Model

Embedding Version

This allows embeddings to be regenerated when models change.

END OF 62.5

62.6 HYBRID RETRIEVAL

GSIR shall support hybrid retrieval:

Keyword Retrieval

        +

Semantic Retrieval

        +

Metadata Filtering

The resulting candidates shall be combined before final ranking.

This approach shall allow exact scientific terminology and semantic similarity to complement each other.

END OF 62.6

62.7 QUERY UNDERSTANDING

Before retrieval, the system shall determine:

User Intent

Research Topic

Entities

Constraints

Time Range

Required Source Type

Required Evidence Quality

Project Scope

The query representation may contain multiple retrieval subqueries.

END OF 62.7

62.8 QUERY DECOMPOSITION

Complex research questions may be decomposed.

Example:

Question

↓

Subquestion A

Subquestion B

Subquestion C

Subquestion D

↓

Independent Retrieval

↓

Combined Evidence

Decomposition shall be used when it improves coverage rather than automatically splitting every query.

END OF 62.8

62.9 QUERY EXPANSION

The retrieval engine may generate:

Synonyms

Scientific Terminology

Abbreviations

Alternative Names

Related Concepts

Controlled Vocabulary Terms

Query expansion shall preserve the original intent and shall not introduce unsupported assumptions.

END OF 62.9

62.10 ENTITY-AWARE RETRIEVAL

Recognized entities shall be used to improve retrieval.

Example:

Entity:

"CRISPR-Cas9"

Possible Retrieval Terms:

CRISPR-Cas9

CRISPR Cas 9

Cas9

Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats

Entity normalization shall be domain-aware.

END OF 62.10

62.11 METADATA FILTERING

Retrieval shall support filters such as:

Project

Source Type

Author

Publication Date

Document Type

Language

Scientific Domain

Evidence Status

Access Scope

Filtering shall occur before or during ranking where possible to reduce irrelevant candidates.

END OF 62.11

62.12 PROJECT-SCOPED RETRIEVAL

Project-scoped queries shall automatically enforce project access boundaries.

Query

↓

Authenticated User

↓

Project Scope

↓

Authorized Sources

↓

Retrieval

A retrieval result shall never expose a resource merely because its text is semantically similar.

END OF 62.12

62.13 TENANT-SCOPED RETRIEVAL

For multi-tenant deployments:

Tenant

↓

Authorization Scope

↓

Search Filter

↓

Vector Filter

↓

Retrieved Results

shall prevent cross-tenant retrieval.

END OF 62.13

62.14 DOCUMENT CHUNKING

Documents shall be divided into retrieval units.

A chunk shall preserve:

Document ID

Version ID

Chunk ID

Sequence

Section

Page

Location

Text

Metadata

Chunking shall preserve enough surrounding context for meaningful interpretation.

END OF 62.14

62.15 SEMANTIC CHUNKING

Where useful, chunks shall follow semantic boundaries such as:

Paragraph

Section

Subsection

Table

Figure Description

Method Step

Experiment Result

The system shall avoid splitting critical scientific statements arbitrarily.

END OF 62.15

62.16 CHUNK SIZE

Chunk size shall be configurable.

The appropriate size shall depend on:

Document Type

Language

Embedding Model

Retrieval Task

Context Window

Information Density

A single fixed chunk size shall not be assumed to be optimal for all scientific content.

END OF 62.16

62.17 OVERLAPPING CHUNKS

Limited overlap may be used where context crosses chunk boundaries.

Overlap shall be controlled to avoid excessive duplicate retrieval.

END OF 62.17

62.18 TABLE RETRIEVAL

Scientific tables shall receive specialized processing where required.

The system shall preserve:

Table Identity

Headers

Rows

Units

Captions

Source Location

Table data shall not be treated as ordinary prose when doing so would destroy its meaning.

END OF 62.18

62.19 FIGURE RETRIEVAL

Figures and diagrams shall preserve:

Figure Number

Caption

Document

Page

Associated Text

Where multimodal processing is supported, extracted visual information shall remain linked to the original figure.

END OF 62.19

62.20 CODE RETRIEVAL

Scientific code and notebooks shall be indexed with structure-aware metadata.

Retrieval may operate on:

Functions

Classes

Modules

Notebook Cells

Comments

Documentation

Configuration

Code chunks shall preserve file and repository provenance.

END OF 62.20

62.21 DATASET RETRIEVAL

Datasets shall be represented through metadata and, where appropriate, indexed descriptions.

Retrieval may consider:

Dataset Name

Variables

Domain

Time Range

Units

Source

License

Version

Raw datasets shall not automatically be embedded in full.

END OF 62.21

62.22 KNOWLEDGE GRAPH RETRIEVAL

The knowledge graph shall support structured retrieval.

Example:

Entity

↓

Relationships

↓

Connected Entities

↓

Supporting Evidence

Graph retrieval shall complement document retrieval.

END OF 62.22

62.23 GRAPH + DOCUMENT RETRIEVAL

GSIR shall be able to combine:

Graph Facts

+

Document Evidence

Example:

Knowledge Graph

→ identifies relevant compounds

Document Search

→ retrieves supporting publications

Evidence Layer

→ validates provenance

This provides both structured relationships and textual evidence.

END OF 62.23

62.24 STRUCTURED DATA RETRIEVAL

Structured databases shall be queried through controlled interfaces.

The AI system shall not receive unrestricted database access merely to answer a question.

END OF 62.24

62.25 TEXT-TO-SQL RETRIEVAL

Where appropriate, GSIR may translate natural-language questions into SQL through a controlled pipeline:

Natural Language

↓

Intent Analysis

↓

Schema Retrieval

↓

SQL Generation

↓

SQL Validation

↓

Permission Validation

↓

Execution

↓

Result Verification

Generated SQL shall never bypass authorization.

END OF 62.25

62.26 RETRIEVAL CANDIDATE GENERATION

Each retrieval source shall produce a candidate set.

Example:

Keyword Search → 50

Vector Search → 50

Graph Search → 20

Metadata Search → 30

Candidates shall then be normalized and merged.

END OF 62.26

62.27 RESULT NORMALIZATION

Every retrieval result shall be converted into a common internal representation.

Example:

RetrievalResult

├── Resource ID

├── Source Type

├── Text

├── Score

├── Metadata

├── Provenance

└── Access Scope

This prevents downstream components from depending on a specific search engine.

END OF 62.27

62.28 RESULT DEDUPLICATION

Duplicate or near-duplicate results shall be removed or consolidated.

Deduplication may use:

Document ID

Chunk ID

Canonical URL

Checksum

Semantic Similarity

The original provenance shall remain available after consolidation.

END OF 62.28

62.29 RESULT FUSION

Results from multiple retrieval strategies shall be combined using a configurable fusion method.

The fusion mechanism shall consider:

Search Score

Semantic Score

Source Quality

Freshness

Evidence Status

Query Match

No single score shall automatically dominate without evaluation.

END OF 62.29

62.30 RERANKING

Top candidates shall optionally be reranked using a stronger ranking model.

Initial Retrieval

↓

Top N Candidates

↓

Reranker

↓

Top K Results

Reranking shall be applied only where its additional latency and cost are justified.

END OF 62.30

62.31 SOURCE QUALITY

Source quality shall influence ranking.

Possible source classes:

Peer-Reviewed Publication

Official Dataset

Government Source

Institutional Repository

Technical Documentation

Preprint

Web Page

User-Uploaded Material

Unverified Source

Source quality shall not replace evidence evaluation.

END OF 62.31

62.32 SOURCE FRESHNESS

Time-sensitive research shall consider publication or update time.

Freshness shall be weighted according to query intent.

Historical research may intentionally prefer older sources.

END OF 62.32

62.33 EVIDENCE QUALITY

Evidence quality shall consider:

Source Reliability

Directness

Specificity

Verification Status

Provenance

Consistency

Retrieval ranking shall not treat popularity as equivalent to scientific validity.

END OF 62.33

62.34 DIVERSITY

The final result set should avoid returning ten nearly identical documents when multiple independent sources are available.

Diversity may consider:

Source

Author

Publication

Institution

Document

Method

Perspective

This is particularly important for research synthesis.

END OF 62.34

62.35 CONTRADICTORY EVIDENCE

The retrieval system shall not automatically discard contradictory evidence.

Where relevant:

Supporting Evidence

+

Contradicting Evidence

shall both be retrievable.

The reasoning layer shall determine how contradictions are evaluated.

END OF 62.35

62.36 EVIDENCE GROUPING

Retrieved evidence may be grouped by:

Claim

Source

Research Question

Method

Experiment

Publication

This allows the reasoning system to compare evidence systematically.

END OF 62.36

62.37 CONTEXT CONSTRUCTION

The context builder shall convert retrieved evidence into a structured reasoning context.

Question

↓

Relevant Evidence

↓

Source Metadata

↓

Provenance

↓

Constraints

↓

Reasoning Context

Only relevant material shall be included where context limits exist.

END OF 62.37

62.38 CONTEXT BUDGET

The context builder shall respect:

Model Context Limit

Token Budget

Latency Budget

Cost Budget

Evidence Priority

The system shall not simply insert every retrieved document into the model prompt.

Claim Extraction

↓

↓

↓

↓

↓

↓

↓

↓

Structured Search

Cached Results

Reranking

Context Construction

62.60 PROMPT-INJECTION PROTECTION

Developer / Application Policy

User Request

Retrieved Content

Tool Results

Caching

Parallel Search

Top-K Limits

Metadata Filtering

Query Reuse

Efficient Indexes

Selective Reranking

62.63 RETRIEVAL LATENCY

Search Time

Vector Search Time

Reranking Time

Context Construction Time

    query,

    scope,

    filters,

    strategy,

    top_k

)

↓

- Citation provenance is preserved.

- Multi-step retrieval is supported.

- Retrieval caching is controlled.

- Index versioning exists.

- Reindexing is supported.

- Embedding migration is supported.

- Retrieval evaluation exists.

- RAG evaluation exists.

- Retrieval observability exists.

- Retrieval failure handling exists.

- Prompt-injection protection exists.

- Retrieval security is enforced.

- External source provenance is preserved.

- Knowledge ingestion is observable.

- Retrieval cost is controlled.

- Retrieval performance can be measured.

                              ▼

                              │

                              ▼

                              │

                              ▼

                    GROUNDED GSIR RESPONSE

PART 63 — AI ORCHESTRATION, MODEL ROUTING, REASONING ENGINE AND AGENT EXECUTION ARCHITECTURE

63.1 PURPOSE

The GSIR AI orchestration architecture shall coordinate models, tools, retrieval, memory, reasoning, validation and execution without allowing any individual AI model to become the entire intelligence layer.

The architecture shall provide:

Task Understanding

Planning

Model Selection

Tool Selection

Retrieval

Reasoning

Verification

Execution

Reflection

Final Response

The AI architecture shall remain modular so that models, providers and reasoning strategies can be replaced without redesigning the complete application.

END OF 63.1

63.2 AI ARCHITECTURE

The high-level execution architecture shall be:

User Request

↓

Request Understanding

↓

Task Classification

↓

AI Orchestrator

↓

Planner

↓

Context / Memory / Retrieval

↓

Reasoning Engine

↓

Tool Execution Where Required

↓

Verification

↓

Reflection

↓

Response Generation

For complex research tasks, the system shall support iterative execution rather than relying exclusively on a single model call.

END OF 63.2

63.3 AI ORCHESTRATOR

The AI orchestrator shall be the central coordinator of AI operations.

It shall determine:

Which Model

Which Prompt / Policy

Which Tools

Which Retrieval Strategy

Which Memory

Which Reasoning Mode

Which Validation

Which Output Format

The orchestrator shall coordinate these components rather than implementing every capability itself.

END OF 63.3

GSIR shall expose a normalized internal model interface.

Conceptually:

Model Request

├── Messages

├── Context

├── Tools

├── Output Schema

├── Constraints

└── Execution Policy

END OF 63.4

AI Orchestrator

↓

Model Router

├── Provider A

├── Provider B

├── Provider C

└── Local Model

Providers may be changed without rewriting research, knowledge or project services.

Availability

→ General Purpose

→ Local / Private Execution

Example:

Advanced Reasoning

↓

General Reasoning

↓

Fast Model

The final system shall record when degraded execution occurred.

END OF 63.52

63.53 MODEL ENSEMBLES

For high-value tasks, multiple model outputs may be compared.

Model A

Model B

Model C

↓

Comparison

↓

Verification

↓

Selected Result

Ensembling shall be used selectively because it increases cost and latency.

END OF 63.53

63.54 SELF-CHECK

The system may ask a model or secondary evaluator to inspect an intermediate result.

Checks may include:

Logical Consistency

Evidence Support

Missing Information

Instruction Compliance

Output Schema

Contradictions

Self-checking shall not be treated as guaranteed correctness.

END OF 63.54

63.55 INDEPENDENT VERIFICATION

Critical results should use an independent verification path where feasible.

Generation

↓

Independent Evaluation

↓

Comparison

↓

Final Decision

This reduces the risk of a single model error passing through the entire pipeline.

END OF 63.55

63.56 CRITIC / EVALUATOR

The evaluator shall assess outputs against explicit criteria.

Accuracy

Completeness

Grounding

Reasoning

Citation Quality

Safety

Format

Evaluator results shall remain separate from the original generation.

END OF 63.56

63.57 REFLECTION

For complex tasks, the system may perform controlled reflection.

Result

↓

What Is Missing?

↓

What Is Unsupported?

↓

What Conflicts?

↓

What Should Be Rechecked?

Reflection shall generate actionable corrections rather than unrestricted recursive reasoning.

END OF 63.57

63.58 CORRECTION LOOP

The correction loop shall be bounded.

Generate

↓

Evaluate

↓

Correct

↓

Evaluate

↓

Accept / Stop

A maximum number of correction cycles shall be enforced.

END OF 63.58

63.59 STOP CONDITIONS

AI execution shall stop when:

Objective Satisfied

Evidence Sufficient

Required Confidence Achieved

Budget Exhausted

Unrecoverable Failure

User Cancellation

Safety Restriction

The system shall not continue indefinitely in pursuit of marginal improvements.

END OF 63.59

63.60 HUMAN-IN-THE-LOOP

Human approval shall be supported for high-impact operations.

Examples:

Publishing Research

Executing Expensive Experiments

Changing Critical Knowledge

External Communication

Destructive Operations

Approving Important Findings

The required approval level shall depend on risk.

END OF 63.60

63.61 AI ACTION AUTHORIZATION

The AI system shall never inherit unlimited authority from the user's session.

Actions shall be checked against:

User Permissions

Project Permissions

Tool Permissions

Resource Limits

Operation Risk

END OF 63.61

63.62 WRITE OPERATIONS

AI-generated write operations shall be treated more cautiously than read operations.

Examples:

Create Knowledge

Modify Project

Execute Experiment

Delete Resource

Publish Result

Send External Message

may require explicit authorization or approval.

END OF 63.62

63.63 DESTRUCTIVE OPERATIONS

Destructive actions shall require stronger safeguards.

Delete

Overwrite

Permanent Modification

External Publication

shall use explicit confirmation or policy-based authorization as appropriate.

END OF 63.63

63.64 AI OUTPUT SCHEMAS

Important AI operations shall use structured output schemas.

Example:

ResearchPlan

{

    objective,

    steps,

    dependencies,

    evidence_requirements,

    budget

}

Structured outputs shall reduce ambiguity between models and backend services.

END OF 63.64

63.65 OUTPUT VALIDATION

Generated structured outputs shall be validated before use.

Model Output

↓

Schema Validation

↓

Semantic Validation

↓

Permission Validation

↓

Execution

Invalid outputs shall not directly control backend operations.

END OF 63.65

63.66 AI EXECUTION RECORD

Each significant AI execution shall record:

Execution ID

Task ID

Model

Provider

Model Version

Prompt / Policy Version

Input References

Tool Calls

Retrieval References

Token Usage

Latency

Cost

Status

Validation Result

This supports debugging, evaluation and reproducibility.

END OF 63.66

63.67 PROMPT VERSIONING

Production prompts and orchestration templates shall be version controlled.

A historical AI execution shall be associated with the prompt or policy version used at execution time.

END OF 63.67

63.68 MODEL VERSIONING

The system shall record the model identifier and relevant version information for important executions.

This shall allow later comparison when model behavior changes.

END OF 63.68

63.69 AI OBSERVABILITY

AI observability shall include:

Model Latency

Token Usage

Cost

Failure Rate

Tool Calls

Retrieval Calls

Retry Count

Fallback Count

END OF 63.69

63.70 AI TRACE

A trace may contain:

Request

↓

Plan

↓

Retrieval

↓

Tool Call

↓

Observation

↓

Reasoning Decision

↓

Verification

↓

Final Output

END OF 63.70

63.71 AI SECURITY

The AI layer shall protect against:

Prompt Injection

Data Exfiltration

Unauthorized Tool Use

Privilege Escalation

Malicious Documents

Untrusted Tool Results

Model Manipulation

Sensitive Data Leakage

Security shall be enforced outside the model as well as through model instructions.

END OF 63.71

63.72 PROMPT INJECTION BOUNDARY

External content shall never be treated as trusted instructions.

External Content

↓

Untrusted Data

↓

Retrieval / Analysis

The orchestrator shall retain control of tool permissions and execution policies regardless of what retrieved content requests.

END OF 63.72

63.73 DATA LEAKAGE PROTECTION

Before model execution, the system shall determine whether sensitive information is permitted in the selected model environment.

If not:

Sensitive Data

↓

Redaction / Transformation

↓

Approved Model

or execution shall remain within a permitted environment.

END OF 63.73

63.74 PRIVACY-AWARE MODEL ROUTING

Model routing may depend on data sensitivity.

Public Data

→ External Model Allowed

Private Project Data

→ Approved Provider

Highly Sensitive Data

→ Private / Local Model

The exact policy shall be configurable by deployment.

END OF 63.74

63.75 COST-AWARE ORCHESTRATION

The orchestrator shall optimize total execution cost.

It shall prefer:

Caching

Retrieval Reuse

Smaller Models

Batching

Parallel Independent Work

Early Stopping

Selective Verification

while maintaining required quality.

END OF 63.75

63.76 LATENCY-AWARE ORCHESTRATION

The system shall identify latency-sensitive tasks.

Interactive tasks shall prefer:

Fast Models

Limited Retrieval

Minimal Tool Calls

Streaming

Long-running research may use deeper execution pipelines asynchronously.

END OF 63.76

63.77 ASYNCHRONOUS AI EXECUTION

Complex AI operations shall run as background tasks.

API Request

↓

Create AI Execution

↓

Queue

↓

Worker

↓

AI Orchestrator

↓

Progress / Events

↓

Completion

The user shall be able to observe execution status.

END OF 63.77

63.78 AI STREAMING

Interactive responses may be streamed where appropriate.

Streaming shall not bypass final validation for operations requiring structured or verified results.

END OF 63.78

63.79 CONCURRENT AI TASKS

Independent AI tasks may execute concurrently.

Concurrency shall be limited by:

Model Capacity

Provider Limits

User Quota

Project Quota

System Capacity

Cost Budget

END OF 63.79

63.80 AI QUEUE PRIORITY

AI tasks may have priorities.

High-priority tasks shall still respect global resource limits and authorization policies.

END OF 63.80

63.81 RETRY POLICY

AI operations shall retry only when failures are likely transient.

Retryable examples:

Temporary Provider Error

Network Timeout

Rate Limit

Temporary Service Unavailability

Non-retryable examples:

Invalid Request

Permission Denied

Invalid Schema

Policy Rejection

END OF 63.81

63.82 IDEMPOTENT AI OPERATIONS

Operations that may be retried shall have idempotency protection.

This is particularly important for actions that create resources or modify state.

END OF 63.82

63.83 AI CACHE

Safe deterministic operations may be cached.

Cache keys shall account for:

Model Version

Prompt Version

Relevant Input

Tool Results

Retrieval Version

Policy Version

Stale cached outputs shall not silently replace current required information.

END OF 63.83

63.84 AI QUALITY GATES

Important outputs shall pass quality gates before being released.

Possible gates:

Schema Valid

Evidence Present

Citations Valid

No Required Field Missing

Permission Valid

Safety Valid

Confidence Threshold

END OF 63.84

63.85 RESEARCH AGENT

The GSIR research agent shall combine:

Planner

Retriever

Memory

Reasoning Engine

Tool Layer

Evidence Validator

Critic

Synthesizer

The agent shall operate through explicit state and bounded execution.

END OF 63.85

63.86 RESEARCH AGENT LOOP

The research loop shall be:

Understand

↓

Plan

↓

Search

↓

Read

↓

Analyze

↓

Evaluate Evidence

↓

Identify Gaps

↓

Search Again if Required

↓

Synthesize

↓

Verify

↓

Finalize

This design supports iterative research rather than single-shot generation.

END OF 63.86

63.87 RESEARCH STOPPING LOGIC

The research agent shall stop searching when:

Evidence Coverage Is Sufficient

Major Claims Are Supported

Additional Search Has Low Expected Value

Budget Is Near Limit

Required Confidence Is Reached

This prevents endless searching.

END OF 63.87

63.88 RESEARCH GAP DETECTION

The agent shall identify:

Missing Evidence

Unsupported Claims

Unresolved Contradictions

Missing Sources

Insufficient Data

These gaps shall drive subsequent retrieval or clearly appear in the final research result.

END OF 63.88

63.89 DISCOVERY MODE

GSIR may support exploratory discovery where the goal is to find unexpected relationships.

The discovery workflow may use:

Known Concepts

↓

Graph Expansion

↓

Related Literature

↓

Unexpected Connections

↓

Hypothesis Generation

↓

Evidence Validation

Discovery results shall remain clearly distinguished from established findings.

END OF 63.89

63.90 REASONING AND RETRIEVAL FEEDBACK

The reasoning engine shall be able to inform retrieval when evidence is insufficient.

Reasoning

↓

Evidence Gap

↓

Query Reformulation

↓

Retrieval

↓

New Evidence

↓

Reasoning

This creates an adaptive retrieval-reasoning loop.

END OF 63.90

63.91 RETRIEVAL AND PLANNING FEEDBACK

Plan

↓

Retrieve

↓

New Information

↓

Plan Revision

↓

Continue

END OF 63.91

63.92 CONTEXT AND MEMORY FEEDBACK

↓

Validation

↓

↓

Approval / Policy

↓

Project Memory

This allows GSIR to improve continuity without treating every model output as permanent knowledge.

END OF 63.92

63.93 AI SELF-IMPROVEMENT BOUNDARY

GSIR may improve its orchestration through evaluation and feedback.

However:

Observed Failure

↓

Evaluation

↓

Improvement Candidate

↓

Controlled Testing

↓

Approval

↓

Production

shall be used instead of allowing the production AI to arbitrarily rewrite itself.

END OF 63.93

63.94 ORCHESTRATION POLICY VERSIONING

END OF 63.94

63.95 AI EXPERIMENTATION

New models and orchestration strategies shall be tested through controlled experiments.

Possible comparison:

Strategy A

vs

Strategy B

↓

Quality

Cost

Latency

Reliability

↓

Decision

END OF 63.95

63.96 CANARY DEPLOYMENT

New AI configurations may be introduced gradually.

New Configuration

↓

Small Traffic Percentage

↓

Observe

↓

Evaluate

↓

Increase

↓

Full Deployment

END OF 63.96

63.97 AI ARCHITECTURE TESTING

Testing shall include:

Unit Tests

Integration Tests

Tool Tests

Retrieval Tests

Model Contract Tests

Agent Workflow Tests

Security Tests

Evaluation Benchmarks

Failure Tests

Load Tests

END OF 63.97

63.98 AGENT EVALUATION

Agent evaluation shall measure the complete trajectory, not only the final text.

Metrics may include:

Task Success

Evidence Quality

Tool Selection

Tool Efficiency

Retrieval Quality

Reasoning Accuracy

Citation Accuracy

Cost

Latency

Failure Recovery

This is important because an agent may produce a correct final answer through an unnecessarily expensive or unreliable path.

END OF 63.98

63.99 AI ARCHITECTURE COMPLETION CRITERIA

The AI architecture shall be considered complete when:

- A centralized AI orchestrator exists.

- Models are accessed through normalized interfaces.

- Provider adapters isolate external APIs.

- Model routing is capability-aware.

- Task complexity influences routing.

- Planning is structured.

- Plans support dependencies.

- Plans can adapt during execution.

- Reasoning operates over structured context.

- Evidence and inference are distinguished.

- Claims can be represented and verified.

- Contradictions are preserved.

- Uncertainty is represented.

- Hypothesis generation is separated from factual knowledge.

- Tools are registered and permission controlled.

- Tool inputs are schema validated.

- Tool execution is isolated where necessary.

- Tool results are normalized and verified.

- Short-term and long-term memory are separated.

- Memory writes are controlled.

- Context assembly is governed.

- AI execution has explicit state.

- Checkpoints exist for long-running operations.

- Execution budgets are enforced.

- Model fallback exists.

- Retry behavior is defined.

- AI outputs are schema validated.

- Prompt and model versions are recorded.

- AI execution is observable.

- AI security controls exist.

- Privacy-aware routing exists.

- Research agents support iterative retrieval.

- Research stopping conditions exist.

- Evidence gaps can trigger additional retrieval.

- AI self-improvement is controlled.

- AI experimentation is supported.

- Agent trajectories can be evaluated.

- Cost and latency are measurable.

- High-risk actions can require human approval.

- The complete AI execution can be audited and reproduced where required.

END OF 63.99

63.100 FINAL AI ORCHESTRATION PRINCIPLE

GSIR shall not depend on a single large language model as its complete intelligence architecture.

The system shall instead combine specialized capabilities:

                               ▼

                       AI ORCHESTRATOR

          ┌────────────────────┼────────────────────┐

                         ▼           ▼

                    RETRIEVAL      TOOLS

                         │           │

                         └─────┬─────┘

                               ▼

                        REASONING ENGINE

                               │

                               ▼

                         CLAIM ANALYSIS

                               │

                               ▼

                         VERIFICATION

                               │

                               ▼

                           REFLECTION

                               │

                               ▼

                         FINAL SYNTHESIS

                               │

                               ▼

                         QUALITY GATE

                               │

                               ▼

                         GSIR RESPONSE

The architecture shall make GSIR capable of combining retrieval, memory, reasoning, tools, verification and controlled learning into a unified scientific intelligence system.

The system shall optimize not merely for fluent responses, but for evidence-grounded reasoning, reproducibility, reliability, controllable autonomy, efficient resource usage and continuous measurable improvement.

PART 64 — KNOWLEDGE GRAPH AND SCIENTIFIC KNOWLEDGE REPRESENTATION ARCHITECTURE

64.1 PURPOSE

The GSIR knowledge graph shall provide a structured representation of scientific entities, concepts, relationships, claims, evidence, methods, experiments, datasets, publications and research findings.

The knowledge graph shall complement document retrieval and AI reasoning by representing relationships that are difficult to capture through ordinary text search.

The architecture shall support:

Entities

Relationships

Claims

Evidence

Methods

Experiments

Datasets

Publications

Researchers

Organizations

Concepts

Processes

Materials

Models

Measurements

END OF 64.1

64.2 KNOWLEDGE GRAPH ARCHITECTURE

The high-level architecture shall be:

Scientific Sources

↓

Document Processing

↓

Entity Extraction

↓

Relation Extraction

↓

Claim Extraction

↓

Evidence Linking

↓

Knowledge Validation

↓

Knowledge Graph

↓

Graph Retrieval

↓

AI Reasoning

The graph shall preserve links back to the original source material.

END OF 64.2

64.3 KNOWLEDGE OBJECTS

GSIR shall represent scientific information as structured knowledge objects.

A knowledge object may contain:

Object ID

Object Type

Canonical Name

Aliases

Properties

Relationships

Source References

Confidence

Validation Status

Created At

Updated At

Version

END OF 64.3

64.4 ENTITY TYPES

The knowledge graph shall support extensible entity types.

Core types may include:

Person

Organization

Publication

Dataset

Experiment

Method

Material

Chemical

Protein

Gene

Disease

Drug

Device

Technology

Algorithm

Model

Concept

Measurement

Variable

Process

Phenomenon

Location

The schema shall allow domain-specific entity types to be added without redesigning the complete graph.

END OF 64.4

64.5 ENTITY IDENTITY

Every important entity shall have a stable internal identifier.

The system shall distinguish:

Internal Entity ID

External Identifier

Canonical Name

Alias

Source-Specific Name

Multiple references to the same scientific entity shall be linkable to one canonical entity where confidence is sufficient.

END OF 64.5

64.6 ENTITY RESOLUTION

Entity resolution shall determine whether two references represent the same entity.

The process may consider:

Name

Aliases

Identifiers

Context

Metadata

Source

Domain

Relationships

Semantic Similarity

Uncertain matches shall remain unresolved rather than being merged incorrectly.

END OF 64.6

64.7 ENTITY ALIASES

Entities may contain multiple names.

Example:

Entity:

CRISPR-Cas9

Aliases:

CRISPR Cas9

Cas9

CRISPR/Cas9

Cas9 system

Aliases shall improve retrieval while preserving one canonical entity identity.

END OF 64.7

64.8 RELATIONSHIP MODEL

Relationships shall connect entities through typed edges.

Example:

Entity A

   │

   ├── causes ──→ Entity B

   ├── treats ──→ Entity C

   ├── uses ──→ Entity D

   ├── measures ──→ Entity E

   └── published_by ──→ Entity F

Relationships shall have explicit semantics rather than being represented only as generic links.

END OF 64.8

64.9 RELATIONSHIP TYPES

The graph shall support relationships such as:

causes

associated_with

inhibits

activates

treats

produces

measures

uses

depends_on

derived_from

tested_on

contains

part_of

developed_by

published_by

supports

contradicts

extends

reproduces

The relationship vocabulary shall remain extensible.

END OF 64.9

64.10 TYPED RELATIONSHIPS

Relationships shall carry type information.

Example:

Drug A

   └── treats ──→ Disease B

shall be distinct from:

Drug A

   └── studied_for ──→ Disease B

This distinction is essential for scientific reasoning.

END OF 64.10

64.11 RELATIONSHIP PROPERTIES

Edges may contain:

Relationship ID

Type

Source Entity

Target Entity

Confidence

Evidence

Temporal Information

Source

Validation Status

Version

This allows relationships to be evaluated independently.

END OF 64.11

64.12 CLAIM REPRESENTATION

Scientific claims shall be represented separately from ordinary entity relationships when necessary.

Claim

├── Statement

├── Subject

├── Predicate

├── Object

├── Evidence

├── Source

├── Confidence

└── Validation Status

This allows GSIR to distinguish a claim from an established graph fact.

END OF 64.12

64.13 CLAIM STATUS

Claims shall support states such as:

PROPOSED

EXTRACTED

SUPPORTED

PARTIALLY_SUPPORTED

CONTRADICTED

VERIFIED

REJECTED

UNKNOWN

The graph shall not treat every extracted statement as verified knowledge.

END OF 64.13

64.14 EVIDENCE LINKING

Every important scientific claim should link to evidence.

Claim

↓

Evidence

↓

Source Document

↓

Exact Location

Evidence may reference:

Page

Section

Paragraph

Table

Figure

Dataset Row

Code Location

Experiment Result

END OF 64.14

64.15 PROVENANCE

Knowledge graph objects shall preserve provenance.

The system shall be able to answer:

Where did this information come from?

When was it extracted?

Which processing version created it?

Which source supports it?

Was it independently verified?

END OF 64.15

64.16 SOURCE PROVENANCE

Source metadata may include:

Source ID

Document ID

Publisher

Author

Publication Date

URL

Version

Retrieval Time

Processing Version

64.17 KNOWLEDGE LINEAGE

Original Source

↓

Extracted Entity

↓

Extracted Relationship

↓

Claim

↓

Validated Knowledge

64.18 TEMPORAL KNOWLEDGE

Valid From

Updated At

↓

New Evidence

↓

↓

Validation

↓

Recency

Independent Confirmation

64.22 SCIENTIFIC METHOD REPRESENTATION

A method may contain:

Method ID

Name

Purpose

Inputs

Steps

Parameters

Outputs

Required Equipment

Applicable Domains

Sources

Validation

Hypothesis

↓

Method

↓

Inputs

↓

Conditions

↓

Measurements

↓

Results

↓

Interpretation

Dataset

├── Source

Topics

Methods

Experiments

Datasets

Claims

Identifiers

Research Areas

64.27 ORGANIZATION REPRESENTATION

University

Laboratory

Research Institute

64.28 CONCEPT HIERARCHIES

↓

Molecular Biology

↓

Genetics

↓

64.29 ONTOLOGY SUPPORT

Classes

Properties

Constraints

Hierarchy

Definitions

→ authored → Publication

Aliases

Properties

↓

A graph path shall not automatically be interpreted as causal evidence.

does not automatically establish:

64.85 KNOWLEDGE GRAPH COMPLETION CRITERIA

The knowledge graph architecture shall be considered complete when:

- Core scientific entities are represented.

- Stable entity identifiers exist.

- Entity resolution is supported.

- Aliases are supported.

- Typed relationships exist.

- Relationship properties are supported.

- Claims are represented separately where required.

- Evidence links are preserved.

- Provenance is preserved.

- Temporal knowledge is supported.

- Versioning exists.

- Contradictory evidence can coexist.

- Scientific methods are represented.

- Experiments are represented.

- Datasets are represented.

- Publications are represented.

- Researchers and organizations can be represented.

- Ontologies are supported.

- Graph constraints exist.

- Automatic extraction is supported.

- Extraction confidence is recorded.

- Human validation is supported.

- Duplicate detection exists.

- Graph traversal is supported.

- Multi-hop retrieval is supported.

- Graph and RAG integration exists.

- Graph and AI-agent integration exists.

- Knowledge writes are controlled.

- Knowledge deprecation exists.

- Retracted sources can trigger re-evaluation.

- Incremental updates are supported.

- Graph snapshots are supported.

- Graph storage is abstracted.

- Graph access is authorized.

- Graph operations are auditable.

- Knowledge quality metrics exist.

- Graph reasoning can be evaluated.

- Multimodal knowledge can be represented.

- Research gaps can be identified.

- Candidate hypotheses remain distinguishable from verified knowledge.

- Authoritative knowledge is protected by quality gates.

- AI context retains graph provenance.

64.86 FINAL KNOWLEDGE GRAPH PRINCIPLE

The GSIR knowledge graph shall function as a structured scientific knowledge layer connecting raw information, evidence, claims, entities, methods, experiments and validated relationships.

The complete flow shall be:

                       SCIENTIFIC SOURCES

                              │

                              ▼

                     DOCUMENT PROCESSING

                              │

                              ▼

                         VALIDATION

                              │

                              ▼

                              │

             ┌────────────────┼────────────────┐

             ▼                ▼                ▼

             │                │                │

             └────────────────┼────────────────┘

                              ▼

                    VERIFIED CONCLUSIONS

The knowledge graph shall not be treated as a static database of facts. It shall operate as a versioned, provenance-aware and evidence-linked scientific knowledge system that continuously connects new information with existing knowledge while preserving uncertainty, contradictions and historical lineage.

PART 65 — SCIENTIFIC DATA INGESTION, NORMALIZATION AND KNOWLEDGE ACQUISITION ARCHITECTURE

65.1 PURPOSE

The GSIR data ingestion architecture shall collect scientific information from heterogeneous sources and transform it into reliable, traceable and machine-readable representations for downstream retrieval, reasoning, knowledge graph construction and research workflows.

The ingestion system shall support:

Scientific Papers

Datasets

Web Sources

Structured Databases

Laboratory Data

Experimental Results

Code Repositories

Tables

Figures

Images

External APIs

User-Provided Files

The ingestion pipeline shall preserve provenance from the original source through every transformation.

END OF 65.1

The high-level flow shall be:

Source

↓

Source Registration

↓

Acquisition

↓

Integrity Verification

↓

Parsing

↓

Normalization

↓

Content Classification

↓

Metadata Extraction

↓

Content Segmentation

↓

Quality Validation

↓

Knowledge Extraction

↓

Indexing / Storage

The architecture shall support both batch and incremental ingestion.

END OF 65.2

Every external source shall be registered before being processed.

A source record shall contain:

Source ID

Source Type

Location

License

Status

Transformation

Transformation Version

Latency

Duplicate Extraction

Storage Overhead

↓

Batch Scheduler

↓

Parallel Workers

↓

Processing

↓

Validation

↓

Storage

END OF 65.58

Memory

Storage

New Experimental Result

Important Update

↓

Process

↓

Update Knowledge

Timestamp

ETag

Checksum

Content Hash

↓

↓

↓

↓

↓

Normalize

↓

Validate

↓

↓

65.98 INGESTION ARCHITECTURE COMPLETION CRITERIA

The ingestion architecture shall be considered complete when:

- Source registration exists.

- Multiple source types are supported.

- Source adapters isolate external formats.

- Stable source identifiers exist.

- Source versioning exists.

- Integrity validation exists.

- Duplicate detection exists.

- Acquisition modes are supported.

- Ingestion jobs are tracked.

- Ingestion states are defined.

- Documents are normalized.

- PDF and OCR processing are supported.

- HTML processing is supported.

- Structured datasets are supported.

- Tables are preserved.

- Figures and images are preserved.

- Multimodal documents are represented.

- Metadata extraction exists.

- Metadata validation exists.

- Language detection exists.

- Translation preserves the original.

- Semantic chunking exists.

- Source locations are preserved.

- Content quality is measured.

- Quarantine exists.

- Untrusted files are sandboxed.

- Resource limits are enforced.

- References are extracted.

- Citation linking exists.

- Dataset profiling exists.

- Units can be normalized.

- Experimental data can be ingested.

- Raw data can remain immutable.

- Derived data preserves lineage.

- Processing versions are recorded.

- Reprocessing is supported.

- Incremental processing is supported.

- Batch processing is supported.

- Parallel processing is controlled.

- Scheduled ingestion is supported.

- Change detection exists.

- Queue-based processing exists.

- Pipeline orchestration exists.

- Retry behavior is defined.

- Idempotent processing is supported.

- Errors are classified.

- Observability exists.

- Source reliability can be represented.

- Licensing and permissions are tracked.

- Security controls exist.

- Data classification exists.

- Content indexing exists.

- Hybrid indexing is supported.

- Knowledge graph integration exists.

- RAG integration exists.

- AI extraction is controlled.

- AI-generated information remains distinguishable from source data.

- Quality gates exist.

- Retractions can propagate through derived knowledge.

- Complete data lineage is maintained.

- Reproducible processing is supported.

- Administrative controls are audited.

- The architecture can scale independently across ingestion stages.

- Cost-efficient processing is supported.

66.99 EXPERIMENT ARCHITECTURE COMPLETION CRITERIA

The experiment architecture shall be considered complete when:

- Experiment definitions exist.

- Experiment versioning exists.

- Multiple experiment types are supported.

- Experimental design is structured.

- Variables are represented.

- Parameters are represented.

- Controls are represented.

- Samples can be tracked.

- Sample lineage is preserved.

- Protocols are versioned.

- Protocol validation exists.

- Execution instances are persistent.

- Execution states are defined.

- Computational experiments are supported.

- Simulations are supported.

- Parameter sweeps are supported.

- Optimization experiments are supported.

- Experiment scheduling exists.

- Resource allocation exists.

- Laboratory integration is supported.

- Instrument registry exists.

- Instrument capabilities are represented.

- Physical commands are controlled.

- Safety checks exist.

- Emergency stop is independent of AI.

- Calibration status is supported.

- Measurements are structured.

- Measurement uncertainty is supported.

- Raw measurements can remain immutable.

- Analysis pipelines are versioned.

- Statistical analysis is supported.

- Analysis plans can be locked.

- Replication is supported.

- Experiment comparison exists.

- Blinding is supported where required.

- Randomization is supported where required.

- Stopping rules are supported.

- Pause and resume are supported.

- Cancellation is supported.

- Failure classification exists.

- Recovery mechanisms exist.

- Checkpointing exists.

- Provenance is complete.

- Reproducibility integration exists.

- Scientific validation exists.

- Experiment results are versioned.

- Reports are generated.

- Visualizations preserve provenance.

- Export is controlled.

- Security controls exist.

- Computational sandboxing exists.

- AI-assisted experiment design is controlled.

- AI experiment execution is bounded.

- AI interpretation remains distinguishable from measurements.

- Validated experimental knowledge can feed the knowledge graph.

- Experiment observability exists.

- Experiment costs are measurable.

PART 67 — SCIENTIFIC WORKFLOW ORCHESTRATION AND EXECUTION ENGINE

67.1 PURPOSE

The GSIR Scientific Workflow Engine shall provide the core infrastructure for defining, compiling, scheduling, executing, monitoring, pausing, resuming, validating and reproducing complex scientific workflows.

A scientific workflow shall connect:

Research Objective

↓

Tasks

↓

Data

↓

Models

↓

Tools

↓

Experiments

↓

Validation

↓

Results

The workflow engine shall support both computational and non-computational research processes while preserving complete execution provenance.

END OF 67.1

67.2 CORE PRINCIPLE

A workflow shall be treated as a versioned executable scientific plan rather than a simple sequence of commands.

The workflow shall explicitly define:

Inputs

Tasks

Dependencies

Conditions

Parameters

Resources

Outputs

Validation

Failure Handling

Execution Policies

Scientific workflow systems benefit from automatic provenance because manual reconstruction of complex data transformations becomes difficult as workflows grow.

PART 68 — SCIENTIFIC KNOWLEDGE GRAPH AND RESEARCH KNOWLEDGE REPRESENTATION ARCHITECTURE

68.1 PURPOSE

The GSIR Scientific Knowledge Graph shall provide the structured knowledge layer connecting scientific entities, concepts, evidence, experiments, observations, models, datasets, publications, researchers, hypotheses and validated results.

The knowledge graph shall transform disconnected research information into an interconnected scientific representation.

Research

   │

   ├── Concepts

   ├── Hypotheses

   ├── Experiments

   ├── Observations

   ├── Datasets

   ├── Models

   ├── Publications

   ├── Methods

   ├── Evidence

   └── Results

A provenance-aware knowledge representation is important because scientific results must remain traceable to the processes and entities that produced them. 

END OF 68.1

Entities

Domain Context

The system shall distinguish between:

Observed Fact

68.98 FINAL SCIENTIFIC KNOWLEDGE ARCHITECTURE

The GSIR Scientific Knowledge Graph shall become the structured memory and evidence layer connecting all major scientific subsystems.

                         SCIENTIFIC WORLD

                                │

                                ▼

                     DOCUMENTS / EXPERIMENTS

                                │

                                ▼

                                │

                                │

                 ▼              ▼              ▼

              CLAIMS        RELATIONS       ENTITIES

                 │              │              │

                 └──────────────┼──────────────┘

                                ▼

                         KNOWLEDGE GRAPH

                                │

                ┌───────────────┼───────────────┐

                ▼               ▼               ▼

             SEARCH         REASONING        INFERENCE

                │               │               │

                └───────────────┼───────────────┘

                                ▼

                         SCIENTIFIC AGENTS

                                │

                                ▼

                          NEW HYPOTHESES

                                │

                                ▼

                            EXPERIMENTS

                                │

                                ▼

                          NEW EVIDENCE

                                │

                                ▼

                         KNOWLEDGE UPDATE

The knowledge graph shall therefore serve as the central structured scientific memory of GSIR.

It shall preserve not only what GSIR knows, but also where the knowledge came from, what evidence supports it, when it was valid, how confident the system is, which claims disagree, and which experiments or workflows generated the evidence.

This architecture provides the foundation for traceable scientific reasoning, evidence-grounded AI, hypothesis generation, research-memory formation and continuous discovery. Provenance-aware workflow systems are specifically intended to connect computational processes with their resulting scientific outputs and support reproducibility. 

END OF PART 68

PART 69 — SCIENTIFIC KNOWLEDGE GRAPH STORAGE, QUERY, AND PROVENANCE IMPLEMENTATION

69.1 PURPOSE

The GSIR knowledge graph storage layer shall provide persistent, versioned, provenance-aware storage for scientific entities, claims, relationships, evidence, sources, hypotheses, experiments and derived knowledge.

The implementation shall prioritize:

- Traceability

- Version control

- Evidence linkage

- Graph traversal

- Scientific queryability

- Efficient retrieval

- Reproducibility

- Controlled updates

Scientific knowledge graphs benefit from combining structured relationships with evidence and provenance, particularly for reproducibility and verification.

69.76 FINAL ARCHITECTURAL REQUIREMENT

The GSIR knowledge layer shall be designed around one fundamental rule:

Every important scientific statement must remain connected to its identity, evidence, source, provenance, version and validation state.

The knowledge graph is therefore not merely a database of scientific facts.

It is the persistent, traceable representation of:

WHAT GSIR KNOWS

+

WHY GSIR KNOWS IT

+

WHERE IT CAME FROM

+

WHEN IT WAS VALID

+

WHAT SUPPORTS IT

+

WHAT CONTRADICTS IT

+

HOW IT WAS DERIVED

+

WHICH VERSION PRODUCED IT

This architecture enables GSIR to maintain scientific knowledge as a continuously evolving but historically traceable research asset.

END OF PART 69.

PART 70 — SCIENTIFIC KNOWLEDGE GRAPH PROVENANCE, LINEAGE, AND REPRODUCIBILITY ENGINE

70.1 PURPOSE

The GSIR Provenance and Lineage Engine shall maintain the complete history of how scientific knowledge is created, transformed, validated, updated, and consumed.

Scientific knowledge graphs require explicit connections between assertions, evidence, sources, and provenance to support reproducibility and trustworthy knowledge discovery. 

The engine shall answer:

Where did this knowledge come from?

What data produced it?

Which process transformed it?

Which model generated it?

Which researcher or agent performed the operation?

Which software version was used?

Which evidence supports it?

Which version of the knowledge existed at that time?

Can the process be reproduced?

END OF 70.1

70.2 CORE PROVENANCE MODEL

SOURCE

   ↓

INPUT ARTIFACT

   ↓

PROCESS / ACTIVITY

   ↓

OUTPUT ARTIFACT

   ↓

ANALYSIS

   ↓

RESULT

   ↓

CLAIM

   ↓

KNOWLEDGE GRAPH

Every important transition shall be represented as provenance rather than being recorded only as an unstructured log.

70.89 FINAL ARCHITECTURAL REQUIREMENT

The GSIR Provenance and Lineage Engine shall ensure that scientific knowledge is never represented only as an isolated conclusion.

Every important conclusion shall remain connected to:

SOURCE

DATA

METHOD

PROCESS

MODEL

SOFTWARE

AGENT

EVIDENCE

RESULT

CLAIM

VERSION

TIME

VALIDATION

The system shall therefore make scientific knowledge traceable, reproducible, inspectable, versioned, and auditable.

END OF PART 70.

PART 71 — SCIENTIFIC WORKFLOW ORCHESTRATION AND EXECUTION ENGINE

71.1 PURPOSE

The GSIR Scientific Workflow Orchestration Engine shall coordinate complex research workflows involving data acquisition, document processing, scientific computation, AI reasoning, experiments, validation, knowledge updates, and reporting.

The workflow engine shall make research processes:

Deterministic where possible

Reproducible

Versioned

Observable

Recoverable

Auditable

Parallelizable

Scalable

Scientific workflow systems are valuable because they can automatically capture computational provenance, connect results to the processes that produced them, and support rerunning computational tasks. 

END OF 71.1

71.98 FINAL ARCHITECTURAL REQUIREMENT

The GSIR workflow engine shall transform complex research processes into explicit, executable, observable, recoverable, and reproducible computational workflows.

The fundamental rule shall be:

EVERY IMPORTANT RESEARCH PROCESS

        ↓

MUST HAVE

        ↓

DEFINED INPUTS

DEFINED TASKS

DEFINED DEPENDENCIES

DEFINED OUTPUTS

DEFINED VALIDATION

DEFINED PROVENANCE

DEFINED RECOVERY

DEFINED VERSION

The workflow engine shall therefore become the execution backbone connecting GSIR's research questions, agents, data, experiments, models, knowledge graph, validation systems, provenance layer, and final scientific outputs.

END OF PART 71.

PART 72 — SCIENTIFIC DATA INGESTION, NORMALIZATION, AND DATA QUALITY ENGINE

72.1 PURPOSE

The GSIR Scientific Data Ingestion and Quality Engine shall provide the controlled entry point for scientific data entering the system.

The engine shall transform heterogeneous external and internal data into validated, normalized, versioned, provenance-linked scientific artifacts suitable for downstream analysis, reasoning, experimentation, and knowledge construction.

Scientific workflows depend on reliable handling of data products through collection, transformation, and analysis, while provenance connects resulting products to the processes that produced them. 

END OF 72.1

72.98 FINAL ARCHITECTURAL REQUIREMENT

The GSIR Data Engine shall enforce the following fundamental rule:

RAW DATA MUST NEVER BE LOST.

EVERY TRANSFORMATION MUST BE TRACEABLE.

EVERY IMPORTANT DATASET MUST BE VERSIONED.

EVERY SCIENTIFIC VALUE MUST RETAIN ITS UNIT AND CONTEXT.

EVERY QUALITY DECISION MUST BE EXPLAINABLE.

EVERY CORRECTION MUST PRESERVE THE ORIGINAL.

EVERY DOWNSTREAM RESULT MUST BE TRACEABLE TO ITS INPUT DATA.

The resulting architecture shall provide GSIR with a reliable scientific data foundation connecting external sources, raw artifacts, validated datasets, AI/ML processing, scientific workflows, provenance, experiments, and the knowledge graph. This is essential because reproducible scientific workflows depend not only on execution logic but also on preserving the data products and provenance needed to understand and rerun the resulting analysis. 

END OF PART 72.

PART 73 — SCIENTIFIC METADATA, SEMANTIC INTEROPERABILITY, AND RESEARCH OBJECT CATALOG ENGINE

73.1 PURPOSE

The GSIR Metadata and Semantic Interoperability Engine shall provide the machine-readable descriptive layer connecting datasets, documents, experiments, models, workflows, software, evidence, claims, publications, agents, and knowledge.

The engine shall ensure that GSIR research objects are:

Findable

Accessible

Interoperable

Reusable

Machine-Readable

Semantically Connected

Versioned

Provenance-Aware

The FAIR principles explicitly emphasize persistent identifiers, rich metadata, interoperable vocabularies, qualified relationships, licensing, provenance, and domain standards.

73.96 FINAL ARCHITECTURAL REQUIREMENT

The GSIR Metadata and Semantic Interoperability Engine shall enforce:

EVERY RESEARCH OBJECT MUST HAVE AN IDENTITY.

EVERY IMPORTANT OBJECT MUST HAVE VERSIONED METADATA.

EVERY IMPORTANT RELATIONSHIP MUST BE EXPLICIT.

EVERY SEMANTIC MAPPING MUST HAVE A DEFINED CONFIDENCE.

EVERY EXTERNAL TERM MUST RETAIN ITS ORIGINAL FORM.

EVERY ONTOLOGY DEPENDENCY MUST BE VERSIONED.

EVERY IMPORTANT OBJECT MUST BE DISCOVERABLE BY MACHINES.

EVERY EXPORTED OBJECT MUST RETAIN ENOUGH METADATA FOR INTERPRETATION.

EVERY METADATA CHANGE MUST BE TRACEABLE.

EVERY SCIENTIFIC OBJECT MUST REMAIN LINKED TO ITS PROVENANCE.

The resulting architecture shall make GSIR's scientific data, software, workflows, experiments, models, evidence, claims, and knowledge machine-discoverable, semantically interoperable, version-aware, provenance-linked, and reusable across research environments. FAIR guidance applies these principles not only to datasets but also to workflows and other research objects, making metadata and interoperability foundational to the complete GSIR architecture. 

END OF PART 73.

PART 74 — SCIENTIFIC KNOWLEDGE GRAPH AND ONTOLOGY ENGINE

74.1 PURPOSE

The GSIR Scientific Knowledge Graph and Ontology Engine shall provide the semantic intelligence layer that connects scientific entities, concepts, observations, measurements, experiments, datasets, publications, models, workflows, evidence, and claims.

The engine shall convert validated information into a structured, queryable representation while preserving provenance, uncertainty, temporal context, source identity, and semantic relationships.

Semantic interoperability increasingly depends on explicit ontologies, vocabularies, identifiers, and machine-actionable metadata rather than simple exchange of files.

74.99 FINAL ARCHITECTURAL REQUIREMENT

The GSIR Knowledge Graph and Ontology Engine shall enforce:

EVERY IMPORTANT SCIENTIFIC ENTITY MUST HAVE A STABLE IDENTITY.

EVERY IMPORTANT RELATIONSHIP MUST HAVE A DEFINED SEMANTIC MEANING.

EVERY CLAIM MUST BE DISTINGUISHED FROM ITS EVIDENCE.

EVERY INFERENCE MUST BE DISTINGUISHED FROM AN OBSERVATION.

EVERY IMPORTANT ASSERTION MUST BE TRACEABLE TO ITS SOURCE.

EVERY ONTOLOGY DEPENDENCY MUST BE VERSIONED.

EVERY CONFLICTING CLAIM MUST REMAIN REPRESENTABLE.

EVERY KNOWLEDGE CHANGE MUST BE VERSIONED.

EVERY RETRACTION MUST PRESERVE HISTORICAL TRACEABILITY.

EVERY AI-GENERATED KNOWLEDGE CANDIDATE MUST REMAIN IDENTIFIABLE AS AI-GENERATED.

EVERY SCIENTIFIC ANSWER GENERATED FROM THE GRAPH MUST BE TRACEABLE TO SUPPORTING EVIDENCE.

END OF PART 74.

PART 75 — SCIENTIFIC KNOWLEDGE GRAPH AND EVIDENCE GRAPH ENGINE

75.1 PURPOSE

The GSIR Scientific Knowledge Graph Engine shall provide the structured knowledge layer connecting scientific entities, observations, measurements, experiments, datasets, publications, evidence, claims, models, workflows, researchers, and derived conclusions.

The engine shall transform validated information into an interconnected graph while preserving source context, uncertainty, provenance, temporal state, and evidence.

Modern scientific data interoperability increasingly relies on semantic representations, ontologies, qualified relationships, and provenance to make research objects interpretable and reusable across systems. 

END OF 75.1
